arxiv_record.abstract:
The deployment of large language models (LLMs) faces considerable challenges
concerning resource constraints and inference efficiency. Recent research has
increasingly focused on smaller, task-specific models enhanced by distilling
knowledge from LLMs. However, prior studies have often overlooked the diversity
and quality of knowledge, especially the untapped potential of negative
knowledge. Constructing effective negative knowledge remains severely
understudied. In this paper, we introduce a novel framework called
quality-guided contrastive rationale distillation aimed at enhancing reasoning
capabilities through contrastive knowledge learning. For positive knowledge, we
enrich its diversity through temperature sampling and employ self-consistency
for further denoising and refinement. For negative knowledge, we propose an
innovative self-adversarial approach that generates low-quality rationales by
sampling previous iterations of smaller language models, embracing the idea
that one can learn from one's own weaknesses. A contrastive loss is developed
to distill both positive and negative knowledge into smaller language models,
where an online-updating discriminator is integrated to assess qualities of
rationales and assign them appropriate weights, optimizing the training
process. Through extensive experiments across multiple reasoning tasks, we
demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing distillation
techniques, yielding higher-quality rationales.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: contrastive distillation of positive and negative rationales, quality-based weighting, and improved student performance and rationales. Greater emphasis on diversity and self-adversarial generation does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive limitations concerning training overhead and dependence on prompt/decoding choices, while distinguishing training cost from deployment storage. It newly explains why teacher-negative rationales may still benefit smaller students and interprets discriminator-score distributions. Section 4.2 also narrows the T5-base comparison from superiority on all datasets to most datasets.

D1.justification: V2 supplies important missing reproduction details: learning rate 1e-5, 10,000 training steps, measured runtimes, task prefixes, discriminator max pooling, masking augmentation, and 500 discriminator-pretraining steps. These are newly documented details, not necessarily newly implemented procedures. The abstract promises future code release but provides no released code.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate SVAMP arithmetic problems, CQA commonsense questions, and ANLI1/e-SNLI natural-language inference. The added analyses use existing datasets and task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 adds the mutual-information method MI (Chen et al., 2024b) to Tables 1–3. It also adds Single-Task to the T5-small comparison in Table 2, where v1 evaluated only Finetuning, DSS, and QCRD. The existing comparators remain.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the reported batch size from 32 to 8 and margin delta from 4 to 3. New diagnostic protocols compare checkpoint lags 3, 5, and 10, fixed and teacher-derived negative sources, and discriminator scores at different temperatures. These reported changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds direct examinations of discriminator behavior (Section 5.5), positive/negative annotation imbalance (Appendix A.1), negative-generator alternatives and checkpoint sensitivity (A.2), and computational cost (A.5). These substantially extend checks of central design choices. Existing ablations and case studies remain; the relocated temperature analysis omits the temperature-1 result.

E5.justification: Section 5.5 and Figure 6 introduce probability-density estimation of sampled rationale-quality scores, absent from v1. This characterizes score distributions rather than uncertainty in benchmark accuracy. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for benchmark results.

E6.justification: V2 adds comparator, annotation-distribution, discriminator-score, negative-generator, and timing results. MI exceeds QCRD on T5-base ANLI1, 54.20 versus 54.00. QCRD's e-SNLI result changes from 90.15 to 90.26 in Table 1 and the training-size plot; revised settings prevent treating this as a verified same-setting gain. The temperature-1 result of 67.5 is removed, and the erroneous best-k statement is corrected from 5 to 1.

M1.justification: Section 3.3.2 changes the specified negative-rationale margin loss from max(delta - CE, 0) to min(CE - delta, 0), reversing its contribution under Equation 3. This is a localized objective correction within the retained framework. Renaming self-play as self-adversarial does not establish another method change; implementation changes are not documented.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial portions of the introduction, related work, methodology, and discussion are rewritten. Section 3.2 is consolidated, terminology shifts toward self-adversarial generation, and discussion/appendix material is reorganized with a new Limitations section. The editorial changes extend well beyond inserting new results.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redrawn, v1's MinMax illustration is removed, and v2 adds the score-density figure and appendix diagnostic/cost tables. The temperature case study moves into the main text, while the judging prompt and temperature-results table move to the appendix. Benchmark tables gain comparator rows and highlighted winners.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to MAGDI, mutual-information CoT distillation, and SCOTT. Related work more specifically positions prior contrastive approaches as incorporating negative knowledge through model inputs. The overall research positioning and claimed novelty of contrastive rationale distillation remain.

T1.justification: The margin-loss definition in Section 3.3.2 changes mathematically: under Equation 3's negative coefficient, v2 produces a positive hinge penalty instead of v1's negative penalty. This changes optimization direction and is not equivalent notation. The remaining formal framework is retained, with no new theorem or proof.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the paper by correcting the loss sign to match intended negative-rationale repulsion, testing generator alternatives and discriminator behavior, and supplying essential reproduction settings. The added MI comparison exposes an exception to superiority, while measured training costs and explicit limitations make practical claims more assessable. These gains outweigh the removed illustration and temperature point, although benchmark uncertainty remains unreported and the broad abstract claim is still insufficiently qualified.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe QCRD, with the same authors, central framework, and benchmarks. All pages, equations, figures, tables, and appendices were readable and support comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains original benchmark experiments and adds comparator results, discriminator-score analysis, negative-generator comparisons, and measured training costs.

before.justification: V1 reports original T5-base and T5-small benchmark experiments, component ablations, sampling analyses, and rationale-quality evaluations.

arxiv_record.abstract: Decoder-only large language models typically rely solely on masked causal attention, which limits their expressiveness by restricting information flow to one direction. We propose Bitune, a method that enhances pretrained decoder-only LLMs by incorporating bidirectional attention into prompt processing. We evaluate Bitune in instruction-tuning and question-answering settings, showing significant improvements in performance on commonsense reasoning, arithmetic, and language understanding tasks. Furthermore, extensive ablation studies validate the role of each component of the method, and demonstrate that Bitune is compatible with various parameter-efficient finetuning techniques and full model finetuning.
arxiv_record.authors: Dawid J. Kopiczko, Tijmen Blankevoort, Yuki M. Asano
arxiv_record.title: Bitune: Leveraging Bidirectional Attention to Improve Decoder-Only LLMs

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list extend the compatibility claim from PEFT methods to full model finetuning. The conclusion removes v1's explicit claims to be the first such method and first instruction-tuning-specific adaptation. The central claim that bidirectional prompt processing improves decoder-only models remains intact.

C2.justification: Section 4 adds an explanation that retaining causal features helps adaptation relative to naive prefix-LM conversion, while leaving comparisons under training from scratch open. Section 3.3 newly argues that generated reasoning better represents usage and reduces contamination risk, without directly testing contamination. The original training-time and memory limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix A.9 adds the reasoning-data generation prompts, response tags, teacher identification, and example completions. Appendix A.6 supplies the cleaned Alpaca access link, and Table 9 explicitly lists the default mixing initialization. Most existing implementation details, hyperparameters, hardware information, and prompt templates are retained.

E1.justification: Appendix A.6 adds cleaned Alpaca as an instruction-training corpus. Section 3.3 adds GPT-4.1-generated reasoning data for four existing benchmarks, extending explicit generative reasoning evaluation beyond GSM8K to PIQA, ARC, and CSQA. This substantially broadens training coverage and task requirements; the proposed multi-turn setting is not evaluated.

E2.justification: v2 Table 2 adds parameter-matched LoRA16 comparisons for every model in downstream-task training; v1 used LoRA16 only in instruction-tuning comparisons. Table 7 adds a standard full-finetuning baseline. These are focused extensions to an otherwise retained comparator set.

E3.justification: New protocols include training on distilled reasoning traces and evaluating generated answers, full-weight optimization, and Codestral-22B evaluation. The timing experiment changes from 50:200 and 200:50 prompt-to-answer lengths on two models to separate prefilling and generation measurements at 2000:2000 tokens on Gemma-2B. Existing main experimental settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds a full-finetuning ablation testing whether gains extend beyond PEFT, attention-map case studies for two GSM8K questions in Appendix A.12, and revised inference-cost analysis. The original component, PEFT-method, attention-mask, and mixing-initialization analyses are retained; moving the initialization analysis to Appendix A.5 is not new evidence.

E5.justification: The original three-seed practice, seeds 42–44, and appendix standard deviations are unchanged. However, v1's explicit ten-run averaging for inference timing disappears with the replacement timing experiment. Several added accuracy comparisons also lack the detailed standard deviations supplied for the original experiments. Neither version establishes an increase in repetitions.

E6.justification: Matched original benchmark and ablation values, including appendix means and standard deviations, are unchanged. New results include chain-of-thought averages of 61.5 versus 59.1 for Gemma-2B and 81.2 versus 79.9 for Llama3-8B (Table 3), and Codestral GSM8K accuracy of 73.6 versus 69.3 (Table 17), comparing Bitune with LoRA. Full-finetuning, Alpaca, LoRA16, and timing results are also added; the old short-sequence timing entries are removed.

M1.justification: The core two-pass feature extraction, learned mixing, training algorithm, and causal decoding remain unchanged. Appendix A.8 adds two proposed multi-turn inference procedures: recomputing the entire history and alternating instruction prefilling with cached causal responses. These are limited procedural extensions without reported multi-turn experiments.

P1.justification: The title and abstract are rewritten, affiliations updated, and the discussion reorganized into a conclusion and separate limitations section. Mixing-initialization material moves to the appendix, alongside newly organized experimental sections. Most existing method and experimental prose is retained.

P2.justification: The main text switches from one to two columns, with extensively reformatted tables and pseudocode. Figures 2–3 and the initialization table move to the appendix; the main-text qualitative example disappears while remaining in the appendix. New experimental tables, data-generation displays, and attention heatmaps substantially change the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds focused positioning against prefix-LM conversion and citations for Alpaca, Codestral, and GPT-4.1. It removes the image/video-generation references used in v1's introduction. The broader related-work discussion remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The autoregressive factorization, attention masks, feature definitions, and convex mixing equations are mathematically unchanged. Equation splitting, notation compression, and correction of the answer-length notation do not introduce new mathematical reasoning. Neither version contains new theorems or proofs relative to the other.

improvement.justification: The multi-benchmark generative reasoning evaluation and parameter-matched downstream controls address important gaps in v1's evidence. Full-finetuning, Alpaca, and 22B-model results further strengthen the applicability argument while preserving the original detailed results. These gains outweigh limited reporting weaknesses: several new comparisons lack standard deviations, timing repetition information is lost, and the contamination argument remains untested.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Bitune, with matching core equations, algorithms, and original experiments despite the changed title and formatting. Their text, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds chain-of-thought experiments, full finetuning, Alpaca training, Codestral-22B evaluation, and attention visualizations.

before.justification: v1 reports original instruction-tuning and downstream-task experiments, component ablations, runtime measurements, and qualitative outputs, with detailed results in the appendix.

arxiv_record.abstract: Information retrieval models that aim to search for documents relevant to a query have shown multiple successes, which have been applied to diverse tasks. Yet, the query from the user is oftentimes short, which challenges the retrievers to correctly fetch relevant documents. To tackle this, previous studies have proposed expanding the query with a couple of additional (user-related) features related to it. However, they may be suboptimal to effectively augment the query, and there is plenty of other information available to augment it in a relational database. Motivated by this fact, we present a novel retrieval framework called Database-Augmented Query representation (DAQu), which augments the original query with various (query-related) metadata across multiple tables. In addition, as the number of features in the metadata can be very large and there is no order among them, we encode them with the graph-based set-encoding strategy, which considers hierarchies of features in the database without order. We validate our DAQu in diverse retrieval scenarios, demonstrating that it significantly enhances overall retrieval performance over relevant baselines.
arxiv_record.authors: Soyeong Jeong, Jinheon Baek, Sukmin Cho, Sung Ju Hwang, Jong C. Park
arxiv_record.title: Database-Augmented Query Representation for Information Retrieval

snapshot_arxiv_record.abstract: Information retrieval models that aim to search for documents relevant to a query have shown multiple successes, which have been applied to diverse tasks. Yet, the query from the user is oftentimes short, which challenges the retrievers to correctly fetch relevant documents. To tackle this, previous studies have proposed expanding the query with a couple of additional (user-related) features related to it. However, they may be suboptimal to effectively augment the query, and there is plenty of other information available to augment it in a relational database. Motivated by this fact, we present a novel retrieval framework called Database-Augmented Query representation (DAQu), which augments the original query with various (query-related) metadata across multiple tables. In addition, as the number of features in the metadata can be very large and there is no order among them, we encode them with the graph-based set-encoding strategy, which considers hierarchies of features in the database without order. We validate our DAQu in diverse retrieval scenarios, demonstrating that it significantly enhances overall retrieval performance over relevant baselines.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain multi-table database augmentation of query representations and order-invariant hierarchical encoding, with claimed retrieval benefits. The additional datasets and comparisons broaden supporting evidence. Removing the introduction's contribution bullets does not remove their substantive claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for weak LLM expansion results, interpretations of metadata-selection controls, and claims about robustness to noisy metadata and limited retrieval redundancy. Its limitations additionally discuss scarce public enterprise databases, subtle metadata bias, and the relevance-versus-exploration tradeoff. Earlier efficiency and privacy concerns remain.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a code-access URL, full database schema diagrams, H&M construction details, an explicit lambda-search range, and identification of DPR for the metadata-category ablation. It removes v1's batch-size-16 disclosure. The optimizer, learning rate, metadata-sampling counts, and A100 hardware information remain.

E1.justification: v2 adds future-purchase retrieval on H&M fashion data using article, customer, and transaction tables. The existing Stack Exchange answer-retrieval and Amazon book-purchase coverage remains, expanding evaluation from six scenarios across two databases to seven scenarios across three databases.

E2.justification: Tables 1 and 6 add LLM expansion, LameR, query-table expansion, user-table expansion, and evaluations with BGE-M3. Auxiliary comparisons add reranked controls, special-token expansion, BM25-based LameR, and Contriever-based metadata selection. Naïve Expansion and Expansion with BM25 are retained under the names Expansion with Full and Expansion with Retriever.

E3.justification: New protocols include H&M temporal splits with 24,479 training, 1,133 validation, and 1,124 test queries; H&M-specific retrieval cutoffs; BGE-M3 and reranking evaluations; and within-user retrieval-diversity measurement using overlap and Jaccard similarity. Existing Stack Exchange and Amazon splits are retained. The omitted batch-size statement does not establish a training-setting change.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained pooling, metadata-category, hyperparameter, and efficiency analyses, v2 adds reranking analysis, metadata word-length statistics, a special-token control, alternative retrieval components, within-user diversity analysis, and a noisy-metadata error case. These examine additional explanations, practical constraints, and robustness questions.

E5.justification: Both versions state that results average three runs and report ± values in the main and supplementary result tables. v2 extends this practice to additional results without introducing new seed information, uncertainty definitions, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures.

E6.justification: Matched DPR and Contriever results in the main and additional-metric tables are unchanged after baseline renaming. Extensive new entries cover H&M, BGE-M3, additional baselines, reranking, and supplementary analyses. The new results include exceptions to universal superiority: H&M Contriever Acc@50 is 15.40 for DAQu versus 15.66 for query-table expansion in Table 1.

M1.justification: The core DAQu encoder, hierarchical mean aggregation, query interpolation, training loss, and metadata sampling remain unchanged. Section 5 and Table 2 add an auxiliary DAQu-plus-reranker variant, extending the inference pipeline with post-retrieval reranking.

P1.justification: v2 substantially rewrites the introduction's examples and encoding explanation, streamlines the method prose, removes the contribution bullet list, consistently renames expansion baselines, and reorders the analyses. Appendix B is reorganized into a much more extensive subsection structure, alongside expanded limitations.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is revised, and v1's combined Figure 2 is split into v2 Figures 2 and 3 while retaining its analyses. The main and additional-results tables gain substantial row and column groups. New diagnostic tables, an error-case table, and three database-schema figures substantially expand the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references covering BGE-M3, RelBench, LameR, reranking, multi-field retrieval, product retrieval, and heterogeneous-data RAG. These update the surrounding literature and experimental context; the central positioning against textual query expansion and table retrieval remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The retrieval loss, query-interpolation formula, relational-link and attribute-set definitions, and hierarchical mean aggregation are retained. Equation renumbering and rewritten explanations introduce no substantive mathematical revision, theorem, or proof.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical justification beyond v1's narrow baseline set through direct comparisons with LLM and single-table expansion, another retrieval backbone, and an additional domain. New controls and diversity/noise analyses make the method's benefits and boundaries easier to assess. Some reporting weaknesses remain: batch size is omitted, new experimental configurations are incompletely specified, and universal-superiority wording overlooks exceptions in Table 1. These shortcomings temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial improvement in comparative evidence.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DAQu, Database-Augmented Query Representation for Information Retrieval. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, including v2's image-based database schemas, and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds H&M experiments, additional comparison methods and backbones, reranking results, and supplementary analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval experiments on Stack Exchange and Amazon, together with metadata ablations, sensitivity analyses, efficiency measurements, and qualitative cases.

arxiv_record.abstract: Vision-language-action models have gained significant attention for their ability to model multimodal sequences in embodied instruction following tasks. However, most existing models rely on causal attention, which we find suboptimal for processing sequences composed of interleaved segments from different modalities. In this paper, we introduce Astra, a novel Transformer architecture featuring trajectory attention and learnable action queries, designed to efficiently process segmented multimodal trajectories and predict actions for imitation learning. Furthermore, we propose a contrastive dynamics learning objective to enhance the model's understanding of environment dynamics and multimodal alignment, complementing the primary behavior cloning objective. Through extensive experiments on three large-scale robot manipulation benchmarks, Astra demonstrates substantial performance improvements over previous models.

C1.justification: A central contribution is redefined: v1 emphasizes explicit alignment of vision, language and action, while v2 claims that CDL learns environment dynamics and provides a lightweight alternative to generative dynamics learning. This claim appears throughout the abstract, introduction and conclusion. The trajectory-attention/action-query contribution remains.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations for negative-sample difficulty and CDL's reduced VIMA-Bench L4 performance, while dropping v1's explicit component-synergy interpretation. It replaces the earlier computational and multi-embodiment limitations with discussion of simulation-based evaluation and possible 3D inputs. Appendix A.4 newly explains that direct integration into autoregressive large VLAs requires substantial retraining.

D1.justification: V2 adds a repository link, benchmark-specific encoders, action representations, training budgets and hyperparameters, including the 38M configuration and five ManiSkill training epochs. Conversely, it omits v1's segment/timestep positional-embedding specification, frozen-T5 statement and explicit contrastive warmup schedule. These omissions do not establish corresponding implementation changes.

E1.justification: V2 adds VIMA-Bench, including multimodal instructions and novel meta-tasks, and CALVIN, including generalization to an unseen environment. ManiSkill remains, while Franka Kitchen and Push-T move to Appendix A.10. Thus coverage expands from three environments to five rather than replacing the two relocated benchmarks.

E2.justification: New reported comparisons include DT, Flamingo and object-token Gato on VIMA-Bench, and MCIL, OpenVLA, MDT, RoboFlamingo and GR-1 on CALVIN. Appendix A.9 also reports an unsuccessful π0 evaluation without numerical results. The existing ManiSkill and Franka Kitchen/Push-T comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: V2 introduces substantial new protocols: VIMA-Bench's four generalization levels and 10-epoch training, and CALVIN's ABC-to-D evaluation using the language-annotated 1% subset, five-task sequences and 20-epoch training. It adds a 38M configuration. ManiSkill's reported Gato and VIMA sizes change from 309M/695M to 198M/525M; this does not establish that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 extends component ablations to VIMA-Bench, adds training loss/accuracy curves and with/without-CDL execution examples, but removes the separate vision-, language- and action-negative ablations. The attention heatmaps are retained in Appendix A.3, and the regrasp example remains the same underlying case.

E5.justification: V2 newly specifies 100 evaluation trials per VIMA-Bench task. The existing 50-trial ManiSkill, 50-run Franka Kitchen and 30-trial Push-T counts remain. Neither version specifies independent training-seed replication, confidence intervals or significance tests; the added trial count does not establish increased replication of retained experiments.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive VIMA-Bench and CALVIN results, including Astra's 97.08% VIMA-Bench L1 success and 3.29 CALVIN average sequence length. Retained benchmark comparison scores largely match v1. However, ManiSkill's 'w/o Both' ablation changes from 83.3/79.4/68.0 to 72.33/76.00/67.00 for easy/medium/hard tasks. Separate negative-type results and several aggregate results are removed.

M1.justification: Trajectory attention and parallel action queries are retained. However, Section 3.3 substantially revises contrastive learning: positives gain image augmentation, the separate prompt/state/action negative families become mixed state/action negatives incorporating augmented samples, and trajectory encoding gains a linear layer after pooling. These are procedural changes beyond renaming the objective CDL.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, related work and contrastive-learning narrative, renames Actra to Astra, and changes the title and author list. It reorganizes the experimental sections and appendices, moves two benchmarks out of the main text, and adds a notation glossary and several explanatory subsections.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Architecture and contrastive-learning diagrams are redesigned; attention comparisons, training curves and execution panels are added. Attention heatmaps move to the appendix, the generalization bar chart disappears, and the combined Franka Kitchen/Push-T table becomes two appendix tables.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially repositioned around a distinction between large and generalized VLAs and between generative and contrastive dynamics learning. New discussions include OpenVLA, π0, GR-2 and world-model research such as Dreamer. This goes beyond the change from numbered to author-year citations.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 revises the formal construction of negative trajectories from three modality-specific families to mixed state/action negatives, changing the negative set used in the contrastive objective. The standard InfoNCE form, attention-mask mathematics, connection-count expression and diffusion-loss formulas remain. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: V1's generalization evidence chiefly concerns held-out object attributes in ManiSkill. V2 directly tests multimodal instructions, novel meta-tasks and transfer to an unseen CALVIN environment, with additional component ablations and stronger comparison sets. This substantially strengthens support for the architecture's applicability and exposes a CDL generalization limitation. Omitted implementation details and unexplained ManiSkill parameter-count revisions weaken reproducibility, but the expanded, targeted validation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, renamed from Actra to Astra. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revisions and relocation of material.

after.justification: V2 reports original VIMA-Bench and CALVIN evaluations and retains the ManiSkill, Franka Kitchen and Push-T results, alongside ablations and qualitative analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original robot-learning evaluations on ManiSkill, Franka Kitchen and Push-T, including quantitative comparisons, component ablations and qualitative execution examples.

arxiv_record.abstract: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) has emerged as a promising approach for detecting hallucinations and low-quality output of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, obtaining proper uncertainty scores is complicated by the conditional dependency between the generation steps of an autoregressive LLM because it is hard to model it explicitly. Here, we propose to learn this dependency from attention-based features. In particular, we train a regression model that leverages LLM attention maps, probabilities on the current generation step, and recurrently computed uncertainty scores from previously generated tokens. To incorporate the recurrent features, we also suggest a two-staged training procedure. Our experimental evaluation on ten datasets and three LLMs shows that the proposed method is highly effective for selective generation, achieving substantial improvements over rivaling unsupervised and supervised approaches.
arxiv_record.authors: Artem Vazhentsev, Ekaterina Fadeeva, Rui Xing, Gleb Kuzmin, Ivan Lazichny, Alexander Panchenko, Preslav Nakov, Timothy Baldwin, Maxim Panov, Artem Shelmanov
arxiv_record.journal-ref: Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
arxiv_record.title: Unconditional Truthfulness: Learning Unconditional Uncertainty of Large Language Models

C1.justification: v1 centers its contribution on learning a conditional confidence gap with an efficient regressor. v2 emphasizes attention and recurrent confidence features, and claims two-stage training is necessary to avoid overfitting. Its abstract and contribution statements extend claimed superiority to supervised competitors, while the conclusion explicitly claims cross-domain generalization.

C2.justification: v1 explains limited short-answer benefits and identifies the strict Markov assumption as a limitation. v2 develops attention-head and recurrent-training explanations, and distinguishes transfer within QA from poor transfer to different task types. Its limitations instead emphasize task-specific training data and distant-domain transfer. These materially revise the mechanism and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: v1 already contains substantial hyperparameter, dataset-size and compute documentation. v2 adds a repository link, explicit feature-padding and initialization instructions, Algorithm 1 and Captum/LIG implementation details. It newly specifies a 50% PRR rejection cutoff and updates configuration tables and hardware information. The retained LinReg/MLP search grids and reported GPU-hour totals remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Coverage changes from nine to eleven evaluated datasets: PubMedQA disappears, while WMT19 German-to-English translation, MMLU multiple-choice QA and GSM8k mathematical reasoning are added. Eight original datasets remain. v2 also introduces QA-to-summarization/translation transfer scenarios. Table 21 establishes eleven datasets despite inconsistent nine/ten-dataset descriptions elsewhere.

E2.justification: The benchmark comparisons add Factoscope, SAPLMA, MIND, Sheeps, LookBackLens and SATRMD as supervised comparators, alongside CCP, Simple Focus, EigenScore, LUQ and Semantic Density. NumSemSets, MC NSE, MC SE and SentenceSAR disappear from the corresponding comparisons. Transfer and runtime comparator sets also change substantially.

E3.justification: Gemma 7b, Llama-3 8b and StableLM-2 12b are replaced by Llama-3.1 8b, Gemma-2 9b and Qwen-2.5 7b. Sample sizes change, including CNN training examples decreasing from 2,000 to 500. Evaluation drops ROUGE-L outcomes and adds COMET and ROC-AUC with quality-label thresholds. Transfer training becomes QA-only; runtime evaluation changes from 900 instances on A100 to all test instances on H100.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of one-stage versus two-stage training, preceding-token count, token-level versus sequence-level training, LIG attribution features, attention-layer importance and attention patterns in correct versus incorrect answers. It substantially revises transfer experiments. Existing regressor, aggregation and feature ablations are revised; CatBoost and v1's G-versus-direct-confidence comparison are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates for benchmark quality and unexplained plus/minus summaries for runtime (v1 Table 6; v2 Table 4). Neither specifies seed counts, repeated-run estimation or significance testing. Changed runtime values and sample populations do not establish a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Benchmark, transfer and runtime results are extensively replaced under changed methods and settings. New ROC-AUC tables report mean scores of 0.814, 0.806 and 0.807 for Llama, Gemma and Qwen respectively. v2 Table 16 reports mean PRR of 0.238 versus 0.545 for one-stage versus two-stage training. Reported TAD runtime overhead changes from 0.10% for v1 LinReg to 5% in v2, under different hardware and evaluation populations.

M1.justification: v1 learns a conditional-on-error term G and reconstructs confidence using the immediately preceding token. v2 directly trains C on sequence-quality targets, incorporates multiple preceding tokens, and introduces probability-only training followed by training with predicted recurrent features. Direct confidence learning existed as a v1 ablation, but the multi-token, two-stage procedure is a substantive redesign.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, related work, method exposition, results discussion and limitations. It separates problem background from the method and moves dataset descriptions into Appendix D. The title and contribution bullets are also revised. The changes constitute substantial narrative restructuring beyond added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 redraws Figure 1, removes v1's attention-frequency plot, and adds attention-head case-study and layer-weight heatmaps. The win-rate matrix expands, benchmark tables replace paired metric columns with revised task columns, and several ablation displays move to the appendix. New ROC-AUC tables and an algorithm box further change the presentation substantially.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands coverage of density-based, retrieval-related and supervised UQ research, including CH-Wang et al., Su et al., Factoscope, LookBackLens and SATRMD. v2 more specifically positions TAD around recurrent confidence features and raw attention weights, including an explicit distinction from LookBackLens feature engineering. These exceed bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: Both retain the binary-token total-probability argument. v2 removes the explicit solved-G target and reconstruction derivation from v1 Equations 2–3, and revises the confidence and target definitions for direct recurrent prediction. This is a limited formal reformulation; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important weakness of v1 by evaluating its supervised method against six supervised competitors. Targeted training and feature ablations, together with cross-task failure tests, substantially strengthen evidence about the method's advantages and limits. Reporting inconsistencies remain: Section 5.2 says all supervised methods trail MSP on cross-task transfer, whereas Table 10 shows SATRMD ahead. These flaws qualify the claims but do not outweigh the stronger comparative validation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TAD for uncertainty quantification of LLM generations. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial methodological and experimental revisions.

after.justification: v2 reports original PRR and ROC-AUC benchmarks, training and feature ablations, transfer experiments, attention analyses and runtime measurements in Section 5 and Appendix A.

before.justification: v1 reports original selective-generation benchmarks across nine datasets and three LLMs, together with ablations, generalization experiments and runtime measurements in Section 4 and Appendix A.

arxiv_record.abstract: Recent advancements in large language model alignment leverage token-level supervisions to perform fine-grained preference optimization. However, existing token-level alignment methods either optimize on all available tokens, which can be noisy and inefficient, or perform selective training with complex and expensive key token selection strategies. In this work, we propose Selective Preference Optimization (SePO), a novel selective alignment strategy that centers on efficient key token selection. SePO proposes the first token selection method based on Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), which trains an oracle model to estimate a token-level reward function on the target data. This method applies to any existing alignment datasets with response-level annotations and enables cost-efficient token selection with small-scale oracle models and training data. The estimated reward function is then utilized to score all tokens within the target dataset, where only the key tokens are selected to supervise the target policy model with a reference model-free contrastive objective function. Extensive experiments on three public evaluation benchmarks show that SePO significantly outperforms competitive baseline methods by only optimizing 30% key tokens on the target dataset. SePO applications on weak-to-strong generalization show that weak oracle models effectively supervise strong policy models with up to 16.8x more parameters. SePO also effectively selects key tokens from out-of-distribution data to enhance strong policy models and alleviate the over-optimization problem.

metadata.abstract: Recent advancements in LLM alignment leverage token-level supervisions to perform fine-grained preference optimization. However, existing token-level alignment methods either optimize on all available tokens, which can be noisy and inefficient, or perform selective training with complex and expensive key token selection strategies. In this work, we propose Selective Preference Optimization (SePO), a novel selective alignment strategy that centers on efficient key token selection without requiring strong, fine-grained supervision signals. We theoretically prove the feasibility of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) as token-level reward function estimators, which applies to any existing alignment datasets and enables cost-efficient token selection with small-scale model sizes and training data. We then train an oracle model with DPO on the target data and utilize the estimated reward function to score all tokens within the target dataset, where only the key tokens are selected to supervise the target policy model with a contrastive objective function. Extensive experiments on three public evaluation benchmarks show that SePO significantly outperforms competitive baseline methods by only optimizing on 30% key tokens with up to 60% reduction in GPU training hours. We also explore SePO as a new paradigm for weak-to-strong generalization, showing that weak oracle models effectively supervise strong policy models with up to 16.8 more parameters. SePO also selects useful supervision signals from out-of-distribution data, alleviating the over-optimization problem.

arxiv_record.abstract: Backdoor attacks, in which a model behaves maliciously when given an attacker-specified trigger, pose a major security risk for practitioners who depend on publicly released language models. As a countermeasure, backdoor detection methods aim to detect whether a released model contains a backdoor. While existing backdoor detection methods have high accuracy in detecting backdoored models on standard benchmarks, it is unclear whether they can robustly identify backdoors in the wild. In this paper, we examine the robustness of backdoor detectors by manipulating different factors during backdoor planting. We find that the success of existing methods based on trigger inversion or meta classifiers highly depends on how intensely the model is trained on poisoned data. Specifically, backdoors planted with more aggressive or more conservative training are significantly more difficult to detect than the default ones. Our results highlight a lack of robustness of existing backdoor detectors and the limitations in current benchmark construction.
arxiv_record.authors: Jun Yan, Wenjie Jacky Mo, Xiang Ren, Robin Jia
arxiv_record.title: Rethinking Backdoor Detection Evaluation for Language Models

C1.justification: The abstract now explicitly limits its finding to methods based on trigger inversion or meta classifiers, where v1 referred generally to existing methods. The three stated contributions and central claim about weaknesses exposed by non-moderate training remain intact.

C2.justification: Appendix F adds explanations for exceptions involving conservative training and easily reversed word triggers. Appendix G expands v1's brief defense suggestion into search improvements, more generalizable features, and online monitoring. Revised limitations explain resource and detector-availability constraints while retaining the absence of a validated solution.

D1.justification: Appendix A.1 newly identifies the HuggingFace dataset entries and use of OpenBackdoor defaults. Section 5.1 corrects the conservative 5 × 10−6 parameter's label from poisoning rate to learning rate. Detector features and random-forest settings in Appendix B were already documented in v1 Section 5.2.

E1.justification: SST-2, HSOL, TrojAI, and the three trigger forms are retained. Appendix E adds clean-label poisoning of target-class samples on HSOL with sentence triggers, expanding the attack scenario. The Llama experiment still evaluates SST-2 classification.

E2.justification: PICCOLO, DBS, and Meta Classifier remain the evaluated detectors. V2 additionally supplies an unpoisoned RoBERTa-Base reference for the clean-accuracy comparison: 93% on SST-2 and 95% on HSOL in Table 1's caption, absent from the corresponding v1 Table 2.

E3.justification: Appendix D extends evaluation beyond RoBERTa-Base to Electra-Base, RoBERTa-Large, and Llama 3.2 1B. Appendix E introduces a clean-label protocol with 10% poisoning for every intensity. These are added experimental settings; the original metrics, TrojAI evaluation, and meta-training split are retained.

E4.justification: Appendices D–E substantially extend the controlled training-intensity robustness tests, examining whether detector weaknesses persist across model architectures and without label tampering. The original loss-landscape and T-SNE case study in Figure 3 is unchanged; the new defense suggestions are not experimentally tested.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or error bars for the experimental results. The retained standard deviation statistic is a model-weight feature, not an uncertainty estimate.

E6.justification: Figure 2 and the original three tables retain their results after renumbering. V2 adds Tables 4–7 and clean-model reference accuracies. For example, Llama Meta Classifier detection is 77%, 17%, and 7% under moderate, conservative, and aggressive training; clean-label DBS detection is 70%, 30%, and 0%. These are newly reported settings.

M1.justification: The proposed strategy of manipulating poisoning rate, learning rate, and training duration is unchanged. The Llama experiment reuses the weight-statistic Meta Classifier; no new detector component or optimization objective is specified.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized prose and author-affiliation edits, renames Section 5.4 from Analysis to Case Study, and adds acknowledgments. Detector details and standard-benchmark discussion move into Appendices B–C; most existing prose and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds four result tables covering additional architectures and clean-label attacks, substantially expanding the appendix displays. The TrojAI table moves from the main text to Appendix C, and the original attack tables receive reordered rows and revised captions. Figures 1–3 retain their graphics.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations for model merging, online defenses, obfuscated gradients, and additional models and implementation tools, while removing Touvron et al.'s Llama reference. The core positioning against more elaborate evasive attacks remains unchanged. The Li survey's bibliographic update represents the same work.

T1.justification: The trigger-inversion objective in Equation 1 and the mathematical problem formulation are unchanged. No theorem, proof, or substantive formal derivation is added.

improvement.justification: V1 explicitly acknowledged relying on one victim model. V2 addresses that important limitation with additional model families and sizes, and tests clean-label poisoning, substantially strengthening support for the central robustness finding. Implementation disclosures and explanations of exceptions also improve the paper. These gains outweigh the minor inconsistency in Table 5's clean-reference caption.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equation, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: V2 retains those experiments and adds results for additional model architectures and clean-label attacks in Tables 4–7.

before.justification: V1 reports original detector evaluations under different training intensities on SST-2 and HSOL, plus attack success and clean accuracy measurements in Appendix A.

arxiv_record.abstract: Information retrieval (IR) is the task of finding relevant documents in response to a user query. Although Spanish is the second most spoken native language, there are few Spanish IR datasets, which limits the development of information access tools for Spanish speakers. We introduce MessIRve, a large-scale Spanish IR dataset with almost 700,000 queries from Google's autocomplete API and relevant documents sourced from Wikipedia. MessIRve's queries reflect diverse Spanish-speaking regions, unlike other datasets that are translated from English or do not consider dialectal variations. The large size of the dataset allows it to cover a wide variety of topics, unlike smaller datasets. We provide a comprehensive description of the dataset, comparisons with existing datasets, and baseline evaluations of prominent IR models. Our contributions aim to advance Spanish IR research and improve information access for Spanish speakers.
arxiv_record.authors: Francisco Valentini, Viviana Cotik, Dami\'an Furman, Ivan Bercovich, Edgar Altszyler, Juan Manuel P\'erez
arxiv_record.title: MessIRve: A Large-Scale Spanish Information Retrieval Dataset

C1.justification: The central contribution remains a large, naturally sourced Spanish retrieval dataset covering country variation. The introduction extends the stated contributions to cross-dataset evaluation and release of a fine-tuned baseline model. The abstract revises dataset size from around 730,000 to almost 700,000 queries.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of weak cross-dataset transfer, dataset-dependent lexical retrieval performance, and annotation problems behind retrieval failures. Appendix B qualifies raw agreement through class imbalance and low kappa. Expanded limitations discuss underrepresented communities, Wikipedia and Google biases, incomplete offensive-content screening, and missing statistical uncertainty estimates.

D1.justification: New Appendix A documents software versions, two 24GB A30 GPUs, training hyperparameters, token limits, frozen position embeddings and approximately 15 hours of training. Appendix C explains the existing autocomplete expansion procedure more precisely. v2 also supplies code and fine-tuned-model links and updates the dataset access location.

E1.justification: Retrieval evaluation expands from MessIRve alone to include MIRACL, mMARCO, SQAC, Multi-EuP and PRES (v2 Figure 4), adding parliamentary and health retrieval domains. These datasets were previously reviewed, and some underwent topic analysis, but v1 did not report retrieval evaluations on them.

E2.justification: The MessIRve comparison retains BM25, MIRACL-mdpr-es, E5-large and OpenAI-large, adding E5-large-ft-messirve as a fifth baseline. OpenAI-large is excluded from the newly introduced cross-dataset experiment for cost reasons, rather than removed from an existing comparison.

E3.justification: Tables 1–2 revise the reported full training/test counts from 571,120/160,099 to 537,730/156,528, with changes across country splits. v2 adds two-epoch fine-tuning, cross-dataset testing using MIRACL's development set and other datasets' test sets, and a three-rater assessment of 100 pairs plus LLM assessments of 650 pairs. The original author audit remains; the cause of the split revisions is unexplained.

E4.justification: v2 adds query-length and prefix-diversity analyses, a manual investigation of 30 retrieval failures, and examples diagnosing ambiguous queries and incorrect relevance judgments (Section 4.1, Section 5, Appendix B). It also examines Wikipedia editor representation. The earlier topic and country-vocabulary analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix B adds rating distributions and chance-adjusted Fleiss' kappa alongside percentage agreement, reporting 0.186, 0.146 and 0.089 for correctness, non-ambiguity and relevance. v2 explicitly acknowledges the absence of confidence intervals and significance testing. No repeated-run or seed reporting is introduced.

E6.justification: Full-set nDCG@10/Recall@100 change from 0.433/0.899 to 0.476/0.916 for OpenAI-large and from 0.430/0.847 to 0.463/0.865 for E5-large. Revised splits prevent interpreting these as gains under identical conditions. v2 adds fine-tuned E5 results of 0.491/0.887, cross-dataset rankings, and new quality and error-analysis findings; the original author-audit results remain unchanged.

M1.justification: v2 introduces E5-large-ft-messirve, adapting the existing E5 model through fine-tuning with BM25-mined hard negatives (Section 5, Appendix A). v1 explicitly deferred fine-tuning to future work. This is a limited model adaptation; the core Google/Wikipedia collection approach and retrieval architecture are retained.

P1.justification: Substantial portions of related work, dataset comparison and topic discussion are rewritten and condensed. v2 introduces a query-format subsection, consolidates the former experimental setup/results subsections, and reorganizes the single supporting appendix into Appendices A–C, including relocation of the original author audit.

P2.justification: v2 adds query-length boxplots, cross-dataset performance plots, prefix-entropy/count panels and a query-document example table. The MessIRve performance plot gains a fifth series and revised legend and captions. The original topic heatmap and Tables 3–5 are retained with renumbering or relocation.

R1.justification: v2 adds references concerning RAG, annotation sparsity, AnCora, E5 training and implementation libraries, and replaces the BM25 reference to Robertson et al. (2009) with Robertson et al. (1994). The central positioning against the same five Spanish retrieval datasets remains.

T1.justification: Neither version presents formal theoretical contributions, proofs or substantive mathematical derivations. The added entropy and agreement statistics are empirical analysis tools, without new mathematical definitions or formal properties.

improvement.justification: v1 relied on author-only quality assessment and left training utility and cross-dataset evaluation largely untested. v2 adds independent validation, demonstrates fine-tuning utility and transfer limitations, diagnoses annotation failures, and substantially improves reproducibility information. These strengthen the dataset's credibility and usefulness. The small independent audit, weak chance-adjusted agreement, absent confidence intervals and unexplained split/score revisions remain limitations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MessIRve Spanish information-retrieval dataset. Their readable text, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained material across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical analyses and adds fine-tuning, cross-dataset retrieval evaluation, independent human and LLM assessments, and error analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval experiments, a human quality assessment of 650 query-document pairs, and analyses of topics and country-specific vocabulary.

arxiv_record.abstract: Tree search methods have demonstrated impressive performance in code generation. Previous methods combine tree search with reflection that summarizes past mistakes to achieve iterative improvement. However, these methods face significant challenges. First, they search directly within the code language space, neglecting the underlying reasoning process critical for effective code generation. Second, reflection-based approaches merely accumulate historical errors in memory without providing correct reasoning pathways, making it difficult for subsequent search iterations to identify optimal solutions, resulting in decreased search quality. In this work, we propose RethinkMCTS, a framework that systematically explores and refines the reasoning process for code generation. Specifically, we employ MCTS to search for thoughts before code generation and integrate MCTS with a refinement mechanism called rethink, which incorporates fine-grained code execution feedback to refine erroneous thoughts during the search. It ensures the search path aligns with better reasoning, improving overall search quality. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that RethinkMCTS outperforms previous search-based and feedback-enhanced code generation baselines.
arxiv_record.authors: Qingyao Li, Wei Xia, Kounianhua Du, Xinyi Dai, Ruiming Tang, Yasheng Wang, Yong Yu, Weinan Zhang
arxiv_record.title: RethinkMCTS: Refining Erroneous Thoughts in Monte Carlo Tree Search for Code Generation

First, they search directly within the code language space, neglecting the underlying reasoning process critical for effective code generation. Second, reflection-based approaches merely accumulate historical errors in memory without providing correct reasoning pathways, making it difficult for subsequent search iterations to identify optimal solutions, resulting in decreased search quality. In this work, we propose RethinkMCTS, a framework that systematically explores and refines the reasoning process for code generation. Specifically, we employ MCTS to search for thoughts before code generation and integrate MCTS with a refinement mechanism called rethink, which incorporates fine-grained code execution feedback to refine erroneous thoughts during the search. It ensures the search path aligns with better reasoning, improving overall search quality. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that RethinkMCTS outperforms previous search-based and feedback-enhanced code generation baselines. 2025.emnlp-main.410 2025.emnlp-main.410.checklist.pdf li-etal-2025-rethinkmcts 10.18653/v1/2025.emnlp-main.410

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning feedback-dependent generalization, selection of the thought to refine, and unexplored fine-tuning. It discusses token overhead and new experimental mechanisms. However, the reward-weight discussion claims poorer performance on both datasets despite Table 3 showing improvements on introductory and interview APPS problems.

D1.justification: Appendices A, C, and D add baseline implementation descriptions, explicit prompts, example traces and feedback, and pseudocode. Appendix B newly discloses temperature zero. Conversely, v1's explicit instruction to split APPS test cases evenly into public and private sets is omitted. The resource link remains unchanged.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate HumanEval and the same three APPS difficulty levels. The added experiments reuse this coverage; mathematical reasoning and tool use are discussed only as potential applications.

E2.justification: The six named external baselines remain. v2 adds Base(16) alongside Base(1), introduces a controlled variant replacing rethink with reflection, and adds ToT and PG-TD to the rollout comparison in Figure 5.

E3.justification: The main backbone models, 16-rollout budget, branching limit, and default reward weights remain. New experiments introduce controlled reflection substitution, alternative reward weights (1.0, 0.2) and (1.0, 1.0), and per-question token and monetary-cost measurements. These extend the evaluation design without establishing changes to the original data split.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled rethink-versus-reflection analysis, reward-weight sensitivity, token-cost analysis, and GPT-4o-mini component and search-granularity studies. The rollout comparison gains additional comparators. The self-evaluation versus generated-tests study is retained from v1 Table 2 as v2 Table 6.

E5.justification: v1 supplies point estimates without run-count or uncertainty reporting. v2 Appendix B and Table 7 report means and standard deviations across three runs with different seeds for RethinkMCTS, ToT, LATS, and PG-TD, while identifying the main results as single-run results.

E6.justification: RethinkMCTS's Table 1 scores remain unchanged, but ToT scores for both backbones and GPT-4o-mini PG-TD scores are revised. For example, ToT's GPT-3.5-turbo HumanEval entry changes from 84.15 to 76.22; the reason is not fully specified. Substantial new results cover Base(16), reflection, reward weights, costs, additional ablations, and repeated runs.

M1.justification: Thought-level MCTS, block-level verbal feedback, leaf-thought refinement, and dual evaluation remain unchanged. The additional prompts and Algorithm 1 document the existing procedure without establishing a new method component.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and method exposition are extensively rewritten. The narrative emphasizes rethink versus reflection, removes the standalone MCTS primer, relocates the generated-tests analysis, and introduces structured appendices, limitations, and ethics sections.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column report to a two-column layout. v2 adds a reflection-comparison diagram, redraws the framework illustration, revises chart arrangements and rollout displays, expands Table 1 with averages and additional rows, and introduces numerous experimental tables and prompt panels.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands the cited background on code agents, semantic reasoning, and tree search. It adds explicit grounding in natural-language planning for code generation through Wang et al. (2024b), semantic reasoning through Tang et al. (2023), and newer refinement work. improvement.justification: The controlled reflection comparison, cost accounting, repeated-run uncertainty estimates, and explicit prompts substantially strengthen the evidence and reproducibility of the unchanged method. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RethinkMCTS. All 11 pages of v1 and 19 pages of v2, including v2's appendices, are readable and support comparison of text, equations, tables, and figures.

after.justification: v2 retains original benchmark results and adds controlled comparisons, reward-weight experiments, token-cost measurements, and repeated-run results.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large Language Models' (LLM) reasoning can be improved using test-time aggregation strategies, i.e., generating multiple samples and voting among generated samples. While these improve performance, they often reach a saturation point. Refinement offers an alternative by using LLM-generated feedback to improve solution quality. However, refinement introduces 3 key challenges: (1) Excessive refinement: Uniformly refining all instances can over-correct and reduce the overall performance. (2) Inability to localize and address errors: LLMs have a limited ability to self-correct and struggle to identify and correct their own mistakes. (3) Insufficient refinement: Deciding how many iterations of refinement are needed is non-trivial, and stopping too soon could leave errors unaddressed. To tackle these issues, we propose MAgICoRe, which avoids excessive refinement by categorizing problem difficulty as easy or hard, solving easy problems with coarse-grained aggregation and hard ones with fine-grained and iterative multi-agent refinement. To improve error localization, we incorporate external step-wise reward model (RM) scores. Moreover, to ensure effective refinement, we employ a multi-agent loop with three agents: Solver, Reviewer (which generates targeted feedback based on step-wise RM scores), and the Refiner (which incorporates feedback). To ensure sufficient refinement, we re-evaluate updated solutions, iteratively initiating further rounds of refinement. We evaluate MAgICoRe on Llama-3-8B and GPT-3.5 and show its effectiveness across 5 math datasets. Even one iteration of MAgICoRe beats Self-Consistency by 3.4%, Best-of-k by 3.2%, and Self-Refine by 4.0% while using less than half the samples. Unlike iterative refinement with baselines, MAgICoRe continues to improve with more iterations. Finally, our ablations highlight the importance of MAgICoRe's RMs and multi-agent communication.
arxiv_record.authors: Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Archiki Prasad, Swarnadeep Saha, Elias Stengel-Eskin, Mohit Bansal
arxiv_record.title: MAgICoRe: Multi-Agent, Iterative, Coarse-to-Fine Refinement for Reasoning

metadata.abstract: Large language model (LLM) reasoning can be improved by scaling test-time compute with aggregation, i.e., generating multiple samples and aggregating over them. While improving performance, this strategy often reaches a saturation point beyond which additional compute provides no return. Refinement offers an alternative by using model-generated feedback to improve answer quality. However, refinement faces three key challenges: (1) Excessive refinement: Uniformly refining all instances can cause over-correction and reduce overall performance. (2) Inability to localize and address errors: LLMs struggle to identify and correct their own mistakes. (3) Insufficient refinement: Stopping refinement too soon could leave errors unaddressed. To tackle these issues, we propose MAgICoRe, a framework for Multi-Agent Iteration for Coarse-to-fine Refinement. MAgICoRe mitigates excessive refinement by categorizing problems as easy or hard, solving easy problems with coarse-grained aggregation, and solving the hard ones with fine-grained multi-agent refinement. To better localize errors, we incorporate external step-wise reward model scores, and to ensure sufficient refinement, we iteratively refine the solutions using a multi-agent setup. We evaluate MAgICoRe on Llama-3-8B and GPT- 3.5 and show its effectiveness across seven reasoning datasets. One iteration of MAgICoRe beats Self-Consistency by 3.4%, Best-of-k by 3.2%, and Self-Refine by 4.0% even when these baselines use k = 120, and MAgICoRe uses less than 50% of the compute.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction broaden the claimed effectiveness from five math datasets to seven reasoning datasets, including commonsense and logical reasoning. The introduction also adds explicit claims of scaling to stronger base models and reward models and emphasizes jointly addressing all three refinement issues.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning component interaction, reward-model modularity, reliable feedback, and smaller gains with stronger models. Its new Limitations section explicitly discusses inference overhead, the initial sampling requirement, and domain-specific reward-model availability; Appendix D discusses using strong LLMs when trained reward models are unavailable.

D1.justification: v2 supplies the GPT4o-mini scoring prompt, additional-baseline implementation recipes, token-accounting details, and dataset licenses and language information. The code link and original reviewer/refiner templates remain; v1's explicit one-shot descriptions disappear without establishing that the prompting procedure changed.

E1.justification: v2 extends the retained five math benchmarks to ARC-Challenge commonsense reasoning and Date Understanding logical reasoning (Table 7). Appendix D also evaluates step-annotated Math-Shepherd instances for the oracle-feedback analysis. This substantially broadens the evaluated data and reasoning requirements.

E2.justification: v2 Table 9 adds evaluated comparisons with 120-way SC + PRM, Self-correct + 120-way SC, Least-to-Most + 120-way SC, and Multi-Agent Debate + SC. These substantially expand comparator coverage beyond v1's principal prompting, aggregation, and Self-Refine baselines.

E3.justification: Original math splits and default settings remain. New protocols evaluate Qwen2.5-Math-7B and GPT4o-mini, alternative ORM/PRM configurations, 200 instances per non-math task, and 500 Math-Shepherd instances. Appendix D also introduces generation-matched debate settings and token-cost evaluation counting agent and reward-model inputs.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests addressing each refinement issue separately (Table 3), reward-model substitutions (Table 4), oracle versus predicted step scores (Table 12), and token-efficiency analysis (Figure 5). Earlier difficulty-classification, agent-role, aggregation, and qualitative analyses remain, sometimes relocated.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, across-run uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The repeated debates in v2 are part of the baseline's generation procedure, not statistical uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Substantial new results include Qwen-based MAGICORE averaging 93.3 versus 91.8 for 120-way SC (Table 2), and third-iteration accuracies of 88.5 on ARC and 80.5 on Date Understanding (Table 7). Original Table 1 accuracies and extended iteration results are retained; the Llama SAT improvement annotation changes from +6.8% to +5.8%.

M1.justification: The difficulty-routing rules, Solver–Reviewer–Refiner loop, and answer selection remain unchanged. v2 adds a limited scoring adaptation: prompting GPT4o-mini to output stepwise scores in place of a trained PRM for non-math tasks, documented in Section 4.2 and Appendix F.

P1.justification: v2 substantially condenses and rewrites the abstract, introduction, and method exposition. It removes the introductory contribution bullets, moves related work and several analyses into the appendices, consolidates appendix analyses, and adds dedicated limitations and documentation sections.

P2.justification: The paper changes from predominantly single-column to two-column presentation, extensively resizing and relocating displays. v2 adds eight numbered tables and the five-panel token-cost Figure 5. Existing figures, tables, prompts, and qualitative examples are retained with revised placement, formatting, or captions.

R1.justification: The existing aggregation, refinement, and multi-agent positioning is retained. v2 adds discussion of reward-guided MCTS and reasons for excluding it from comparisons, plus references supporting new models, datasets, and baselines. The Christiano et al. reference is removed; moving related work to Appendix A is structural.

T1.justification: The weighted-voting, majority-quality, and entropy-based confidence definitions remain unchanged across the renumbered appendices. v2 Appendix D adds an explicit normalized-cost definition, 0.25 times input tokens plus output tokens, with its input/output cost-ratio assumption. No theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's math-focused, two-model evaluation. Additional baselines, non-math tasks, stronger-model tests, and reward-quality analyses address important gaps in comparative and generalization evidence. Token accounting includes agent and reward-model overhead omitted by sample-count comparisons, while explicit limitations improve transparency. The cost conclusions remain conditional on the stated token-weighting assumption, but the overall evidential gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MAGICORE with the same authors and core framework. Text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support matching retained, relocated, and added material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds experiments on other reasoning domains, stronger models, alternative reward models, additional baselines, and refinement variants.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on five mathematical-reasoning datasets, with two base models, ablations, iteration analyses, and qualitative examples.

arxiv_record.abstract: Auto-evaluation is crucial for assessing response quality and offering feedback for model development. Recent studies have explored training large language models (LLMs) as generative judges to evaluate and critique other models' outputs. In this work, we investigate the idea of learning from both positive and negative data with preference optimization to enhance the evaluation capabilities of LLM judges across an array of different use cases. We achieve this by employing three approaches to collect the preference pairs for different use cases, each aimed at improving our generative judge from a different perspective. Our comprehensive study over a wide range of benchmarks demonstrates the effectiveness of our method. In particular, our generative judge achieves the best performance on 10 out of 13 benchmarks, outperforming strong baselines like GPT-4o and specialized judge models. Further analysis show that our judge model robustly counters inherent biases such as position and length bias, flexibly adapts to any evaluation protocol specified by practitioners, and provides helpful language feedback for improving downstream generator models.
arxiv_record.authors: Peifeng Wang, Austin Xu, Yilun Zhou, Caiming Xiong, Shafiq Joty
arxiv_record.title: Direct Judgement Preference Optimization

metadata.abstract: To meet the increasing need for timely and accurate evaluation of large language model (LLM) responses, training LLM-as-judges to evaluate and critique other model responses has emerged as a popular paradigm. However, existing judge models are largely trained with supervised finetuning (SFT) on small data scales to perform limited types of evaluation tasks, fundamentally limiting generalization.To meet the need for strong, generalized judge models, we explore training foundational judge models at large data scales (680K) with direct preference optimization (DPO). Using four training tasks, we form three types of DPO preference pairs targeting different aspects of evaluation: Generating meaningful critiques, making accurate judgements, and understanding what comprises good and bad responses. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we train judge models of three sizes: 8B parameters, 12B, and 70B, and evaluate on a comprehensive suite of 13 benchmarks (7 pairwise, 4 single rating, and 2 classification). Our models achieve the best aggregate performance, with even our 8B model outperforming GPT-4o in pairwise benchmarks. Further analysis shows that our judge models produce factual and actionable critiques and serve as strong foundational judges for continued finetuning.

      <abstract>To meet the increasing need for timely and accurate evaluation of large language model (LLM) responses, training LLM-as-judges to evaluate and critique other model responses has emerged as a popular paradigm. However, existing judge models are largely trained with supervised finetuning (SFT) on small data scales to perform limited types of evaluation tasks, fundamentally limiting generalization.To meet the need for strong, generalized judge models, we explore training foundational judge models at large data scales (680K) with direct preference optimization (DPO). Using four training tasks, we form three types of DPO preference pairs targeting different aspects of evaluation: Generating meaningful critiques, making accurate judgements, and understanding what comprises good and bad responses. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we train judge models of three sizes: 8B parameters, 12B, and 70B, and evaluate on a comprehensive suite of 13 benchmarks (7 pairwise, 4 single rating, and 2 classification). Our models achieve the best aggregate performance, with even our 8B model outperforming GPT-4o in pairwise benchmarks. Further analysis shows that our judge models produce factual and actionable critiques and serve as strong foundational judges for continued finetuning.</abstract>
