C1.justification: v3 replaces the headline claim of best performance on 10 of 13 benchmarks with best aggregate performance. It also adds central claims that the judges produce factual critiques and provide strong starting points for domain-specific continual finetuning, substantially expanding the foundational-judge contribution.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive limitations concerning annotation freshness, English-only evaluation, complete versus partial responses, and inference cost. It also interprets harder negatives as mitigating positional bias, discusses specialization/generalization tradeoffs, and explains possible GPT-4-reference effects on MetaCritique recall.

D1.justification: v3 adds the training-source inventory in Table 5, teacher sampling settings, an EvalBiasBench prompt, and continual-finetuning construction and training details. A repository URL replaces v1's future-release promise. These substantially improve documentation, although v1's explicit 1024-token output limit is no longer specified.

E1.justification: The original 13-benchmark suite remains, while v3 adds MetaCritique evaluation of critique factuality and completeness and ContextualJudgeBench evaluation of contextual pairwise judgements. The newly listed sources for the original training mixture are additional disclosure, not evidence that its coverage changed.

E2.justification: Tables 1–3 add Con-J-7B, Skywork-Critic-70B, Self-taught-evaluator-70B, and Themis-8B in relevant tasks. Prometheus-2-BGB and some FLAMe variants disappear from these comparisons, and Skywork-8B is removed from classification. Appendix E.9 additionally compares against DeepSeek-GRM and its inference-time scaling variants.

E3.justification: The existing benchmark metrics and response-order swapping procedure remain. New protocols include GPT-4-based MetaCritique scoring and contextual adaptation using 12,500 training samples, 2,000 test samples, an 80:20 CoT/standard-judgement mixture, three training epochs, and a five-value DPO beta sweep (Section 5.5; Appendix B.1).

E4.justification: v3 adds a strong-versus-weak negative-sample teacher ablation (Appendix E.8, Table 11) and a specialization/generalization sensitivity study through continual-finetuning beta values (Figure 6). Existing task ablations, prompting tests, bias analyses, and qualitative examples are retained, often in relocated sections.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent-seed variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The two response-order evaluations are retained. Newly disclosed sampling of 20 teacher responses concerns training-data generation, not statistical uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: The SFR scores in Tables 1–3 and the original ablation and downstream-refinement results remain unchanged. Substantial new results include MetaCritique F1 of 77.60 for SFR-Judge-70B, contextual accuracy of 55.6% versus 45.2% when finetuning from Llama-3.1-8B, and hard/easy-negative comparisons. These are additional experiments, not improvements to the retained benchmark scores.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same CoT critique, standard judgement, and response deduction constructions, combined DPO+SFT objective, and underlying 8B/12B/70B models. The added studies investigate the existing recipe and its adaptation settings without introducing a new judge algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Dataset descriptions and several main-text analyses move into reorganized appendices, while new analyses and limitations reshape the narrative. Model names are also shortened consistently.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column layout, relocates and resizes existing displays, and adds training-source, critique-quality, teacher-ablation, and inference-scaling tables plus a continual-finetuning figure. Main-table highlighting changes from best overall/non-proprietary to best/second-best.

R1.justification: v1 positions DPO as a departure from predecessors described as SFT-trained. v3 explicitly discusses DPO-based Themis, Self-taught Evaluator, and Con-J, distinguishing its multitask preference construction from their approaches. It also adds positioning relative to multitask learning and inference-time scaling.

T1.justification: The preference constructions and DPO+SFT mathematical objective are unchanged. Expanded notation and explanations of borrowed evaluation metrics introduce no new theorem, proof, derivation, or substantive formal assumption.

improvement.justification: Direct critique-quality evaluation addresses an important gap between correct judgements and trustworthy explanations, while controlled contextual finetuning strengthens evidence for transfer. More competitive baselines, revised novelty positioning, explicit training-source documentation, and substantive limitations substantially improve credibility and transparency. The original results remain stable, though statistical uncertainty is still unreported.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Direct Judgement Preference Optimization work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial rewriting and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds critique-quality evaluation, contextual continual-finetuning experiments, and a teacher-quality ablation.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations across 13 benchmarks, training ablations, bias and prompting analyses, and downstream model-training experiments.

arxiv_record.abstract: Traditional robot simulators focus on physical process modeling and realistic rendering, often suffering from high computational costs, inefficiencies, and limited adaptability. To handle this issue, we concentrate on behavior simulation in robotics to analyze and validate the logic behind robot behaviors, aiming to achieve preliminary evaluation before deploying resource-intensive simulators and thus enhance simulation efficiency. In this paper, we propose BeSimulator, a modular and novel LLM-powered framework, as an attempt towards behavior simulation in the context of text-based environments. By constructing text-based virtual environments and performing semantic-level simulation, BeSimulator can generalize across scenarios and achieve long-horizon complex simulation. Inspired by human cognition paradigm, it employs a ``consider-decide-capture-transfer'' four-phase simulation process, termed Chain of Behavior Simulation (CBS), which excels at analyzing action feasibility and state transition. Additionally, BeSimulator incorporates code-driven reasoning to enable arithmetic operations and enhance reliability, and reflective feedback to refine simulation. Based on our manually constructed behavior-tree-based simulation benchmark, BTSIMBENCH, our experiments show a significant performance improvement in behavior simulation compared to baselines, ranging from 13.60% to 24.80%. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Dawn888888/BeSimulator.

C1.justification: The central BeSimulator, CBS and BTSIMBENCH contributions remain. However, v2's abstract and introduction explicitly frame the system as preliminary logic validation before conventional simulation, and the separate contribution claiming to introduce behavior simulation is dropped. This refines the intended role without replacing the main contribution.

C2.justification: New Section 7 explicitly acknowledges that FSMs and HTNs were not evaluated and that conventional simulators remain essential for physical fidelity and visual information. Appendices C–D add substantive explanations involving missing, redundant or incorrect preconditions and faulty state transitions. These considerably qualify the earlier reliability and generalization discussion.

D1.justification: v2 adds CBS prompt templates, JSON fields and Python-output conventions in Appendix A, detailed task/node descriptions and XML behavior trees in Appendix B, and a code/data repository pointer in the abstract. These substantially expand reproducibility information beyond v1's procedural descriptions and py_trees link.

E1.justification: Both evaluate BTSIMBENCH with 75 behavior trees derived from 25 BEHAVIOR-1K tasks, covering good, logically defective and unreachable solutions. The renamed Counterfactuals category matches Bad Logic. Appendix B documents existing tasks, and the new diagnostic analyses remain within the retained benchmark.

E2.justification: v1 compares against few-shot CoT prompting. v2 retains that comparator and adds Best of N with LLM Judge for each backbone in Table 3, selecting among three CoT-generated answers. This is a limited extension of the comparison methods.

E3.justification: DeepSeek-V2-Chat is replaced by DeepSeek-V3 in the main experiments and ablations. Added evaluations introduce three-candidate selection for BoN and separate accuracy metrics for precondition extraction and world-state updating. The benchmark size, main delivery/accuracy metrics and five-feedback limit remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The three existing mechanism ablations remain, while Appendix C adds quantitative analysis separating precondition extraction from state updating. Appendix D adds a traced GetDrink failure in which an incorrect state transition causes rejection of a Good tree. These additions substantially expand the analysis of where simulation fails.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without repeated-run counts or uncertainty. v2 Table 3 explicitly reports five repeated experiments and per-category means with standard deviations. This introduces substantial uncertainty reporting, although it does not establish an increase from a known earlier run count.

E6.justification: The main and ablation results are revised, and BoN and component-accuracy results are added. For example, Claude-based BeSimulator averages are 93.3% in v1 Table I and 92.80% in v2 Table 3. v2's five-run summaries and replacement DeepSeek-V3 experiments should not be interpreted as same-setting performance changes. Table 5 newly shows higher state-update than precondition-extraction accuracy across all four models.

M1.justification: Both retain case generation, the world states manager, four-phase CBS, numerical code execution, reflective feedback and BPS evaluation. Action and condition nodes retain their four-phase and two-phase procedures. Renaming Bad Logic to Counterfactuals and supplying more explicit descriptions and prompts do not establish a changed simulation algorithm.

P1.justification: Existing introduction, method and experimental paragraphs are extensively rewritten, contributions and baseline descriptions are reorganized, and Bad Logic becomes Counterfactuals. Dedicated limitations and ethics sections and organized appendices expand the document structure. The changes extend well beyond copyediting or inserting new results.

P2.justification: v2 adds a workflow figure, substantially redraws the architecture diagram, reorganizes the main comparison table by backbone, and adds explanatory, diagnostic and appendix tables plus a failure-tree figure. Earlier benchmark illustrations are retained as Figures 3–4. Typography and page layout also change substantially.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion or citations for Reflect, Matsuo et al.'s world-model review, DKPrompt and BEHAVIOR Robot Suite, and replaces the DeepSeek-V2 reference with DeepSeek-V3. Some background references, including GPT-4 and Claude-3, are removed. The three related-work themes remain, with clearer positioning alongside conventional simulators.

T1.justification: Section III in v1 and Section 3 in v2 retain the same planning quintuple, state-transition formulation and goal condition in Equation 1. No new theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation appears in the later appendices.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves transparency and assessment of reliability: Table 3 adds repeated-run uncertainty and another comparator, Appendices A–B disclose implementation and benchmark details, and Appendices C–D diagnose failures. Section 7 also makes applicability limits explicit. These address important reporting and reproducibility gaps in v1. Evaluation remains confined to behavior trees, and efficiency claims still lack direct timing evidence, but the overall quality gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BeSimulator and the same core BTSIMBENCH evaluation. Their text, equations, tables and figures are readable and support comparison. v1 ends with references and has no appendices; v2 includes readable Appendices A–D.

after.justification: v2 reports original comparative experiments and ablations in Tables 3–4, component accuracy results in Appendix C, and a failure case in Appendix D.

before.justification: v1 reports original BTSIMBENCH experiments across four LLMs in Table I and component ablations in Table II.

arxiv_record.abstract:
Forecasting weather and climate events is crucial for making appropriate
measures to mitigate environmental hazards and minimize losses. However,
existing environmental forecasting research focuses narrowly on predicting
numerical meteorological variables (e.g., temperature), neglecting the
translation of these variables into actionable textual narratives of events and
their consequences. To bridge this gap, we proposed Weather and Climate Event
Forecasting (WCEF), a new task that leverages numerical meteorological raster
data and textual event data to predict weather and climate events. This task is
challenging to accomplish due to difficulties in aligning multimodal data and
the lack of supervised datasets. To address these challenges, we present
CLLMate, the first multimodal dataset for WCEF, using 26,156 environmental news
articles aligned with ERA5 reanalysis data. We systematically benchmark 23
existing MLLMs on CLLMate, including closed-source, open-source, and our
fine-tuned models. Our experiments reveal the advantages and limitations of
existing MLLMs and the value of CLLMate for the training and benchmarking of
the WCEF task.

      <abstract>Forecasting weather and climate events is crucial for making appropriate measures to mitigate environmental hazards and minimize losses. However, existing environmental forecasting research focuses narrowly on predicting numerical meteorological variables (e.g., temperature), neglecting the translation of these variables into actionable textual narratives of events and their consequences. To bridge this gap, we proposed Weather and Climate Event Forecasting (WCEF), a new task that leverages numerical meteorological raster data and textual event data to predict weather and climate events. This task is challenging to accomplish due to difficulties in aligning multimodal data and the lack of supervised datasets. To address these challenges, we present CLLMate, the first multimodal dataset for WCEF, using 26,156 environmental news articles aligned with ERA5 reanalysis data. We systematically benchmark 32 existing models on CLLMate, including closed-source, open-source, and our fine-tuned models. Our experiments reveal the advantages and limitations of existing MLLMs and the value of CLLMate for the training and benchmarking of the WCEF task. The dataset is available at <url>https://github.com/hobolee/CLLMate</url>.</abstract>

C1.justification: CLLMate changes from a proposed forecasting model claimed to outperform baselines into a dataset and benchmark exposing existing MLLMs' capabilities and limitations. The abstract, contributions, and conclusion drop the original model-superiority and WCRP deployment contributions. The WCEF task proposal remains, but the central contribution and claimed outcome are substantially redefined.

C2.justification: v1 attributes success primarily to knowledge-graph learning and raster-text alignment. v2 instead discusses class imbalance, geographic reporting bias, difficulties predicting consequences, model-dependent modality redundancy, and limits of scaling. Knowledge-graph incorporation becomes future work. Appendix A.4 also distinguishes potential generative applications from the multiple-choice evaluation actually conducted.

D1.justification: Appendices A–C add the dataset schema, annotation and adjudication procedures, detailed forecasting prompts, ERA5 access/license information, and a planned CC BY 4.0 release after review. Fine-tuning documentation specifies frozen components, DeepSpeed ZeRO-3, learning rate 2e-5, batch size 16, eight A800 GPUs, and training times. v1 largely referred readers to recommended training hyperparameters; public dataset availability is still only promised in v2.

E1.justification: The ERA5 and Wisers sources remain, but coverage expands from China to 1,049 regions distributed globally. Evaluation changes from generating daily event lists for China to selecting hierarchical categories for individual regional meteorological phenomena and consequences. These are substantive changes in geographic coverage and task requirements.

E2.justification: v1 quantitatively compares CLLMate with top-1 similarity and LLaVA-based tuning, with additional MLLMs appearing in qualitative cases. v2 removes top-1 similarity and evaluates random/majority guessing alongside 23 model variants. Table 2 includes newly evaluated comparators such as Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Janus-Pro, Cambrian, and Qwen2.5-VL, plus expanded LLaVA comparisons.

E3.justification: The chronological test allocation changes from approximately 13% to 10%. Text-generation metrics are replaced by classification accuracy at two hierarchical levels. v2 introduces standardized answer codes, randomized option ordering, and structured zero-shot reasoning prompts. Its one-epoch LLaVA fine-tuning experiments replace v1's knowledge pretraining followed by three multimodal tuning epochs.

E4.justification: v1's knowledge-graph, context, and raster ablations are replaced by image, statistics, and zero-shot reasoning ablations on Gemini-2.0-flash and LLaVA-1.6-mistral-7B. Appendix D adds model-scale and architectural comparisons. The original China-wide examples are replaced by detailed Guangzhou heat and California wildfire cases with expert-marked model errors.

E5.justification: Appendix B.2 newly reports three annotators, pairwise agreement of 81.83%, and Fleiss's kappa of 0.63, adding statistical assessment of annotation reliability. v1 has no corresponding analysis. Neither version reports repeated model runs, seed variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests for forecasting performance.

E6.justification: The original generation results, including CLLMate's BERTScore of 73.56 versus top-1 similarity's 71.37, are removed. v2 reports new classification results, including 45.93% primary-phenomena accuracy for fine-tuned LLaVA-1.5-7B and 16.25% subordinate-consequence accuracy for Qwen2.5-VL-72B, alongside new ablation and case outcomes. These replace results under different tasks and settings; they do not establish same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: v1 proposes a Llama3-8B model with knowledge-graph pretraining, trainable raster encoding/projection, and LoRA tuning. v2 removes that model and graph-training stage, benchmarking existing MLLMs and fine-tuning LLaVA with frozen vision encoders/adapters instead. Dataset construction also changes from Llama3-70B extraction and geopy filtering to GPT-4o-mini extraction, expert validation, regional alignment, and hierarchical categorization.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contributions, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around a benchmark contribution. Related work moves before problem formulation, the original methodology narrative becomes dataset construction and benchmarking, and supporting material is reorganized into structured Appendices A–D. These are substantial narrative and organizational changes beyond added experiments.

P2.justification: The framework diagram is revised and resized; the original graph/instruction illustrations and case displays are replaced. v2 adds geographic and temporal distributions, category charts, a taxonomy diagram, a dataset-comparison table, and substantially redesigned performance tables. Appendix scale plots redisplay Table 2 results, while prompts and cases receive new boxed layouts. The document template also changes throughout.

R1.justification: v2 replaces the extensive instruction-tuning dataset discussion with substantive positioning against meteorological and event datasets. Section 2.3 and Table 1 compare CLLMate with SEVIR, Mesogeos, Digital Typhoon, NeuralNERE, ClimateIQA, and WeatherQA, emphasizing verified event records and downstream impacts. Model and annotation references also change substantially.

T1.justification: The raster/event definitions and core forecasting Equations 1–2 remain substantively unchanged. v2 removes the knowledge-graph definition and supporting mathematical specifications of the former model, including embedding, training-loss, and nearest-neighbor prediction formulas. Neither version develops theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves the benchmark's empirical foundation: systematic expert validation and agreement reporting address v1's undocumented label-validation process, while explicit prompts, data schemas, and training settings improve reproducibility. Broader comparisons support more qualified conclusions about model limitations. These gains outweigh the narrower multiple-choice evaluation. A material caveat remains: Section 5.4 selects a majority baseline whose primary category differs from Figure 6's largest training category, weakening that comparison. The improvement concerns benchmark credibility and auditability, not demonstrated gains in open-ended forecasting.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the CLLMate/WCEF research project using ERA5 meteorology and news-derived events. Although v2 substantially reframes the work, the main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original model benchmarking in Table 2, ablations in Table 3, expert annotation agreement in Appendix B.2, and case studies in Appendix D.

before.justification: v1 reports original forecasting experiments and component ablations in Tables 1–2, plus qualitative model comparisons in Figures 5–6.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) exhibit remarkable multi-tasking ability by learning mixed instruction datasets. However, novel tasks would be encountered sequentially in dynamic world, which urges for equipping LMMs with multimodal continual instruction learning (MCIT) ability especially for diverse and challenging generative tasks. Existing MCIT methods do not fully exploit the unique attribute of LMMs and often gain performance at the expense of efficiency. In this paper, we propose a novel prompt learning framework for MCIT to effectively alleviate forgetting of previous knowledge while managing computational complexity with natural image-text supervision. Concretely, we learn prompts for each task and exploit efficient prompt fusion for knowledge transfer and prompt selection for complexity management with dual-modality guidance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves substantial +14.26% performance gain on MCIT benchmarks with remarkable $\times$ 1.42 inference speed free from growing computation. Code is available at https://github.com/AuroraZengfh/ModalPrompt.
arxiv_record.authors: Fanhu Zeng, Fei Zhu, Haiyang Guo, Xu-Yao Zhang, Cheng-Lin Liu
arxiv_record.title: ModalPrompt: Towards Efficient Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning with Dual-Modality Guided Prompt

C1.justification: The abstract and contributions replace the headline +20% improvement with +14.26%, reflecting the Avg comparison against CODA-Prompt. The central contribution of multimodally guided prompt fusion and selection, and the claimed 1.42-fold inference speed, remain.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly acknowledges limited forward transfer to unseen tasks. Appendix C adds explanations for retaining CLIP/L and interprets Qwen-VL results as architectural generalizability. The explanation of interference when selecting two versus one or three prompt sets disappears with that analysis.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future code release; v2 states that code is available and supplies a ModalPrompt URL. Appendices B–D add instruction templates, baseline configurations such as MoELoRA's eight experts and rank 16, a LLaVA repository reference, and the GPU's 48 GB capacity. These substantially expand documented reproducibility information.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same eight CoIN datasets covering question answering, classification, and grounding. The new encoder experiment uses a subset of these datasets, while Qwen-VL introduces a different model configuration without extending data or task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds L2P, Dualprompt, and CODA-Prompt to the main comparison, and LWF, EWC, and Model Tailor in Appendix C. CODA-Prompt also enters the stagewise, efficiency, and prompt-count comparisons. v1's appendix comparator named CoIN corresponds to the retained MoELoRA baseline.

E3.justification: v2 adds Qwen-VL evaluation, six-dataset encoder comparisons using CLIP/L with BPE and CLIP/G for both modalities, and prompt/expert-count sweeps across methods. The original CoIN task order and metric formulas remain: Last and Avg rename ContinualT and CAA.

E4.justification: v2 adds encoder sensitivity testing and extends prompt-count analysis to MoELoRA and CODA-Prompt. Existing component ablations gain longitudinal metrics. Conversely, v1's study of selecting one, two, or three prompt sets disappears. The similarity maps, selection maps, and qualitative examples are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests. Averaging accuracy across tasks does not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive baseline, encoder, and Qwen-VL results while retaining ModalPrompt's main final-task scores. Existing values also change: multi-task ScienceQA rises from 46.22 to 81.43, and appendix final VQAv2/OCRVQA entries change from 65.02/57.59 to 66.90/59.68, matching the main table. The control-score revisions lack an explanation of changed settings.

M1.justification: The frozen backbone, learned projection, and top-k prompt fusion/selection are retained. The stated prototype loss changes from duplicated text-similarity terms in v1 Eq. 12 to image-plus-text similarity in v2 Eq. 6. This is a limited objective correction; whether the implementation changed is not established.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, method, and results undergo extensive rewriting. The method is reorganized into guidance features, training-time fusion, and inference-time selection. Metric definitions move to Appendix A, appendices are reorganized by function, and limitations, ethical impact, and acknowledgments sections are added.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, replaces the introductory radar chart with a conceptual diagram, and redraws the method figure. It merges and relabels the heatmaps, restructures benchmark and ablation tables, and adds notation, instruction, comparison, and trajectory tables plus a Qwen-VL radar chart.

R1.justification: Related work shifts from a broad continual-learning taxonomy toward continual instruction tuning and multimodal adaptation. It adds substantial literature, including MaPLe, M2PT, conditional LoRA, and HIDE-LLaVA, while removing several generic replay references. Appendix C additionally positions the method against Model Tailor and regularization approaches.

T1.justification: The visual projection's dimensional mapping is corrected from text-to-vision dimensions in v1 Eq. 4 to vision-to-text dimensions in v2 Eq. 1, alongside the prototype-loss correction. These are local mathematical corrections. The explicit O(T)/O(k) notation restates the existing complexity argument, and renamed evaluation metrics retain their formulas.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important validation gap: v1's prompt-based method was compared primarily with Finetune and MoELoRA. Relevant prompt baselines, broader controls, encoder/backbone checks, and expanded technical disclosure substantially strengthen empirical support and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the removed selection-count analysis and remaining reporting problems, including Finetune B8 being 31.16 in Table 4 versus approximately 35.61 calculated from Table 10.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ModalPrompt research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, allowing reliable matching across substantial rewriting and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds baseline comparisons, encoder studies, and Qwen-VL results in Section 4 and Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original CoIN benchmark results, component ablations, efficiency measurements, and detailed continual-learning trajectories in Section 4 and Appendix A.

arxiv_record.abstract: This paper compares the effectiveness of traditional machine learning methods, encoder-based models, and large language models (LLMs) on the task of detecting depression and anxiety. Five Russian-language datasets were considered, each differing in format and in the method used to define the target pathology class. We tested AutoML models based on linguistic features, several variations of encoder-based Transformers such as BERT, and state-of-the-art LLMs as pathology classification models. The results demonstrated that LLMs outperform traditional methods, particularly on noisy and small datasets where training examples vary significantly in text length and genre. However, psycholinguistic features and encoder-based models can achieve performance comparable to language models when trained on texts from individuals with clinically confirmed depression, highlighting their potential effectiveness in targeted clinical applications.

arxiv_record.title: Exploring Large Language Models for Detecting Mental Disorders

      <abstract>This paper compares the effectiveness of traditional machine learning methods, encoder-based models, and large language models (LLMs) on the task of detecting depression and anxiety. Five Russian-language datasets were considered, each differing in format and in the method used to define the target pathology class. We tested AutoML models based on linguistic features, several variations of encoder-based Transformers such as BERT, and state-of-the-art LLMs as pathology classification models. The results demonstrated that LLMs outperform traditional methods, particularly on noisy and small datasets where training examples vary significantly in text length and genre. However, psycholinguistic features and encoder-based models can achieve performance comparable to language models when trained on texts from individuals with clinically confirmed depression, highlighting their potential effectiveness in targeted clinical applications.</abstract>

It also adds interpretations of influential words and BDI-subgroup differences.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a code-repository link, additional prompt templates, information about AutoML-selected Random Forest ensembles, and hardware and compute disclosures totaling 533 GPU hours in Table 9. E1.justification: The five Russian datasets, diagnostic tasks, pooled datasets, and transfer scenario remain unchanged. v3 extends evaluation coverage to clinical correctness of generated explanations on correctly classified depressed DE cases, a limited additional evaluation task using existing data.

E2.justification: Matching the full benchmark tables confirms the same AutoML approaches, four encoder models, and seven LLMs in corresponding evaluations. Changes in the best-model summary rows reflect revised rankings; the clinically informed prompt adapts an existing model.

E3.justification: v3 introduces averaging over alternative system prompts for zero-shot and five-shot evaluations, replacing the previously documented single-template evaluation. It also adds a two-psychologist, five-point explanation-rating protocol restricted to correctly detected depressed cases and BDI-score subgroup evaluations. The original 80/20 stratified split and fine-tuning hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained pooling and transfer analyses, v3 adds prompt-sensitivity evaluation, clinician-rated explanation error analysis, and a clinically informed prompt comparison. Appendix E adds Captum word ablations for label and explanation generation, while Appendix F examines performance within BDI-score subgroups.

E5.justification: Prompted LLM results change from appendix point estimates and zero-variance summary entries to means and standard deviations across prompt variants. Appendix D additionally reports Fleiss' kappa of 0.39 for psychologist agreement. The existing six-seed AutoML procedure is unchanged; the new prompt variation is not an increase in random-seed runs.

E6.justification: Many prompted results are replaced under the averaging protocol: DSM five-shot Vikhr 7B IT 0.4 macro-F1 changes from 66.06 to 63.69 ± 1.18 in Table 2. Appendix LLM precision/recall entries are also corrected. New results include explanation ratings of 2.84/5 and 2.47/5 for ordinary and clinically informed prompting, respectively, plus feature-ablation and subgroup findings.

M1.justification: Appendix D introduces a clinically informed five-shot variant that includes psychologist-selected depression markers alongside demonstration labels. The underlying classifiers, model architectures, LoRA procedure, and original explanation-generating prompts are retained.

P1.justification: v3 changes the title and author information, streamlines related-work passages, and clarifies dataset and methodological prose. The existing narrative and section sequence largely remain, with Section 5.4 and Appendices D–G added for the new material.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens reliability by correcting swapped precision/recall reporting and evaluating sensitivity to prompt wording. A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Russian-language mental-disorder detection study despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original classification experiments and adds psychologist evaluations, clinically informed prompting, feature ablations, and questionnaire-score subgroup analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification experiments on five datasets, pooled-dataset evaluations, and transfer from clinically diagnosed essays to social-media data.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large Language Models(LLMs) excel in general tasks but struggle in specialized domains like healthcare due to limited domain-specific knowledge.Supervised Fine-Tuning(SFT) data construction for domain adaptation often relies on heuristic methods, such as GPT-4 annotation or manual data selection, with a data-centric focus on presumed diverse, high-quality datasets. However, these methods overlook the model's inherent knowledge distribution, introducing noise, redundancy, and irrelevant data, leading to a mismatch between the selected data and the model's learning task, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address this, we propose a two-stage model-centric data selection framework, Decomposed Difficulty Data Selection (3DS), which aligns data with the model's knowledge distribution for optimized adaptation. In Stage1, we apply Prompt-Driven Data Selection via Explicit Alignment, where the the model filters irrelevant or redundant data based on its internal knowledge. In Stage2, we perform Decomposed Difficulty Data Selection, where data selection is guided by our defined difficulty decomposition, using three metrics: Instruction Understanding, Response Confidence, and Response Correctness. Additionally, an attention-based importance weighting mechanism captures token importance for more accurate difficulty calibration. This two-stage approach ensures the selected data is not only aligned with the model's knowledge and preferences but also appropriately challenging for the model to learn, leading to more effective and targeted domain adaptation. In the case study of the medical domain, our extensive experiments on real-world healthcare datasets demonstrate the superiority of 3DS over exisiting methods in accuracy by over 5.29%. Our dataset and code has been open-sourced at https://github.com/PuppyKnightUniversity/3DS.

metadata.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in general language tasks, motivating their adaptation to specialized domains such as healthcare. Effective domain adaptation typically involves supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on carefully selected instruction-tuning data. Current data selection methods adopt a data-centric approach, relying on external annotations and heuristics to identify externally defined high-quality or challenging data. Our exploratory experiments highlight this approach fails to improve the model’s domain performance, due to misalignment between selected data and the model’s knowledge distribution. To tackle this, we propose Decomposed Difficulty-based Data Selection (3DS), a two-stage model-centric data selection framework that aligns data selection with the model’s distribution. 3DS employs Prompt-Driven Data Selection to filter out noise based on the model’s knowledge via explicit alignment in Stage#1, then adopts Decomposed Difficulty-based Data Selection to guide selection via three novel data difficulty metrics, including Instruction Understanding, Response Confidence, and Response Correctness in Stage#2, enhanced by an attention-based importance weighting mechanism for accurate calibration.Extensive experiments in the healthcare domain show 3DS outperforms existing methods by up to 2.97% accuracy, with additional validation in law and general domains, confirming its generalization ability. Our dataset and code are open-sourced at https://github.com/PuppyKnightUniversity/3DS.

C1.justification: The central 3DS contribution remains, but v2 broadens its claimed demonstrated applicability from Chinese medicine to English law and general-domain tasks. The abstract's superiority claim changes from 'over 5.29%' to 'up to 2.97%' under a revised comparison set. v1's claim of successful real-world medical deployment is omitted.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of stage-ablation effects, coarse verbal difficulty scores and complementary difficulty signals. It removes v1's domain-shift and reduced-overconfidence interpretation. New substantive limitations address selection occurring only before training, potentially valuable discarded samples, bias amplification through self-assessment, and population-specific limitations of Chinese medical data.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents LoRA rank, sequence cutoff, scheduler, warmup, precision, hardware, software versions, embedding extraction and the 280-example threshold-validation set. Appendices substantially expand baseline instructions, prompts and dataset provenance and maintenance information. The anonymous release pointer is replaced by stated public code and dataset access information; external availability was not checked.

E1.justification: v2 retains the Chinese medical training collection and CMB-Exam, MMCU-Medical and CMB-Clin evaluations, while adding English legal reasoning on CaseHOLD and general-domain evaluation across MMLU's 57 subjects. This substantially expands domain, language and task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds Alpagasus and DEITA to the medical benchmark and pairwise comparisons. Its pilot study compares DeepSeek-R1 scoring with target-model scoring, and Appendix G.2 adds evaluated medical-model comparators Meditron-7B, HuatuoGPT-II-7B and HuatuoGPT-II-34B. The original main comparison methods remain represented.

E3.justification: v2 removes Baichuan2-7B and adds Qwen2.5-7B and LLaMA3-8B configurations. New protocols include external-versus-self-scoring controls, stage and budget experiments, and CaseHOLD evaluation using 5K selected training samples and 1K test samples. Pairwise judging is reported as GPT-4o instead of GPT-4, without establishing that retained comparisons were rerun. The original basic medical fine-tuning budget and hyperparameters are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds stage-removal and stage-collapse ablations, difficulty-metric correlation and overlap analyses, 3K–7K budget sensitivity, and K-Center versus full-pool evaluation. Existing component ablations and two threshold curves are retained or relocated. v1's 500-sample domain-shift analysis, max-attention comparison, only-D1 variant and Baichuan2-7B analyses are removed.

E5.justification: Unlike v1, v2 explicitly reports that most main experiments use one run, supplies three-run random-selection variability in Appendix E, and reports three-seed means and standard deviations for CaseHOLD. This adds limited uncertainty reporting; it does not establish repeated-run validation of the main 3DS results.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive pilot, backbone, baseline, ablation and cross-domain result entries, including CaseHOLD accuracy of 76.13% and MMLU accuracy of 65.08%. Matched mean-attention results are retained: Baichuan2-13B's CMB-Exam/MMCU scores remain 47.37/51.08, and Qwen1.5-7B's remain 61.96/66.09. Baichuan2-7B results and several variant and domain-shift findings disappear.

M1.justification: The target-model quality filtering, three perplexity-based difficulty measures, attention weighting, intermediate difficulty selection and K-Center sampling remain intact. v2 selects the already-existing mean-attention variant as its principal configuration. Added K-Center pseudocode and embedding details explain the existing procedure rather than introduce a new component.

P1.justification: The introduction and motivation are extensively rewritten around a hypothesis, research questions and pilot findings. Related Work moves from Section 2 to Section 6, threshold analysis becomes Section 4.4, and algorithm and dataset material move into expanded appendices. The dataset description becomes a structured datasheet, alongside title, terminology and author-information edits.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, redraws Figure 1, restructures the main result tables with different backbone columns and averages, and separates ablations into dedicated tables. Dataset statistics and expanded pairwise plots move to appendices. New analytical tables, dataset examples and Algorithm 2 are added, while v1's domain-shift figure is removed.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands literature coverage to V-usable information, active learning, human problem-solving and confidence, additional medical models and datasets, cross-domain benchmarks, and fairness and safety. Section 6 explicitly distinguishes LLM data selection from active learning while retaining the central model-centric positioning. Earlier citations including D-CPT Law and Gemini Goes to Med School are omitted.

T1.justification: The difficulty definitions and attention-weighted calculations retain their mathematical substance. v2's explicit fixed-budget optimization objective, K-Center pseudocode and standard evaluation formulas elaborate the existing task and procedures. No substantive new theoretical assumptions, results or proofs are introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation of previously unisolated design choices through stage/collapse and K-Center ablations, and addresses v1's medical-only validation with CaseHOLD and MMLU experiments. Expanded implementation and dataset documentation materially improves reproducibility. These gains outweigh the removal of some earlier analyses, although most main experiments are single-run and reporting errors remain, including Table 15's Baichuan2-13B comparison against removal of Stage 2, whose win/tie/loss percentages total 110%.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same 3DS framework, with matching medical datasets, method components and retained results. All 17 pages of v1 and 23 pages of v2, including their equations, figures, tables and appendices, support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original pilot experiments, medical evaluations and ablations, plus CaseHOLD and MMLU experiments in Section 5.

before.justification: v1 reports original medical fine-tuning results, component ablations, GPT-4 comparisons, threshold experiments and a domain-shift analysis.

arxiv_record.abstract: NLP benchmarks rely on standardized datasets for training and evaluating models and are crucial for advancing the field. Traditionally, expert annotations ensure high-quality labels; however, the cost of expert annotation does not scale well with the growing demand for larger datasets required by modern models. While crowd-sourcing provides a more scalable solution, it often comes at the expense of annotation precision and consistency. Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to enhance the annotation process, particularly for detecting label errors in existing datasets. In this work, we consider the recent approach of LLM-as-a-judge, leveraging an ensemble of LLMs to flag potentially mislabeled examples. We conduct a case study on four factual consistency datasets from the TRUE benchmark, spanning diverse NLP tasks, and on SummEval, which uses Likert-scale ratings of summary quality across multiple dimensions. We empirically analyze the labeling quality of existing datasets and compare expert, crowd-sourced, and LLM-based annotations in terms of the agreement, label quality, and efficiency, demonstrating the strengths and limitations of each annotation method. Our findings reveal a substantial number of label errors, which, when corrected, induce a significant upward shift in reported model performance. This suggests that many of the LLMs' so-called mistakes are due to label errors rather than genuine model failures. Additionally, we discuss the implications of mislabeled data and propose methods to mitigate them in training to improve performance.
arxiv_record.authors: Omer Nahum, Nitay Calderon, Orgad Keller, Idan Szpektor, Roi Reichart
arxiv_record.title: Are LLMs Better than Reported? Detecting Label Errors and Mitigating Their Effect on Model Performance

C1.justification: The central claims remain: confident ensemble disagreements identify label errors, LLM annotations compare favorably with human annotations, and correcting labels affects training and evaluation performance. The headline improvements of up to 4% and 15% are retained. SummEval supplies additional support without materially changing these claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning crowd-worker qualifications, contamination, prompting, aggregation, and task coverage. It explicitly frames SummEval as a simulated crowd-label setting, discusses legitimate annotation variation, and adds interpretations of individual-model calibration and fine-tuned models’ learned label bias.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies the GPT-4 snapshot and documents SummEval model versions, JSON outputs, and probability extraction. Conversely, v1’s Table 7 containing full dataset sizes is removed. Existing binary prompts, annotation instructions, hardware, and fine-tuning hyperparameters remain available.

E1.justification: The four TRUE datasets are retained, and SummEval adds CNN/DailyMail summaries evaluated for coherence, relevance, consistency, and fluency. Its ordinal ratings substantially extend coverage beyond the earlier binary factual-consistency setting.

E2.justification: The added SummEval agreement comparison individually evaluates GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Flash as annotator groups (Table 5), extending the model comparisons beyond those in the corresponding TRUE analysis. The existing TRUE comparator sets, nine-model performance comparison, and training controls remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The new SummEval protocol uses median-aggregated crowd and expert ratings, relative distance to expert labels, Pearson correlation, and ordinal Krippendorff’s alpha. Appendix E also introduces model-specific confidence bins. These are substantial additions to evaluation design; the existing TRUE sampling and fine-tuning settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds separate confidence/error-detection analyses for four LLMs (Appendix E, Figure 13) and examines fine-tuned models’ class predictions on corrected versus unchanged examples (Appendix F.2). It also extends confidence and ensemble-size analyses to SummEval. Earlier filtering/flipping and validation-set ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report five fine-tuning seeds, 95% bootstrap confidence intervals using 100 resamples, and Clopper–Pearson intervals with finite-population correction. Additional plots extend the existing reporting practices without establishing a changed uncertainty procedure or increased run count.

E6.justification: v2 adds SummEval results, including expert–LLM correlation of 0.57 versus expert–crowd correlation of 0.04 (Figure 7), agreement statistics (Table 5), and confidence/ensemble curves. Model-specific findings and class-prediction frequencies are also new. Corresponding TRUE Tables 2–4 and training-result plots retain their earlier values.

M1.justification: v2 adapts the ensemble procedure to five-level ordinal predictions, requiring a rating difference greater than one before confidence-based flagging (Section 3; Appendix A.2). The underlying probability averaging and binary filtering/flipping procedures remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The narrative is extensively reorganized: related work moves forward and incorporates annotation background, the method receives a separate rewritten section, and detailed dataset descriptions and annotation comparisons move to appendices. v2 also adds an appendix contents list and a dedicated limitations section.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figures 2, 3, and 7 combine TRUE and SummEval panels; Figure 13 and Table 5 add new displays. Existing displays are relocated or relabeled, and the earlier dataset-size Table 7 is removed.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against annotation-error detection research, distinguishing its zero-shot confident-disagreement approach from trained detectors. It adds works including Klie, Weber-Genzel, Yang, and Bavaresco. The earlier dedicated factual-consistency survey and references such as QAFactEval and WeCheck are removed.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 introduces a precise ordinal-disagreement definition requiring a score gap greater than one, extending the earlier binary disagreement relation. This is a limited mathematical-definition addition; no theorems, proofs, or substantive derivations are introduced.

improvement.justification: SummEval substantially strengthens validation beyond v1’s binary setting by evaluating ordinal, multidimensional annotations against independently supplied expert ratings. The new model-specific and label-bias analyses improve support for the ensemble rationale and interpretation of fine-tuned-model behavior. Explicit qualifications also sharpen the crowdsourcing conclusions. SummEval remains a simulated crowd-label setting, and some dataset-size documentation is lost, but the gains in validation and interpretation are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, references, appendices, tables, and rendered figures support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds LLM annotations and analyses of SummEval, alongside new model-specific analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original annotation comparisons, label-error analyses, ensemble experiments, and fine-tuning results on four TRUE datasets.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large language models have many beneficial applications, but can they also be used to attack content-filtering algorithms in social media platforms? We investigate the challenge of generating adversarial examples to test the robustness of text classification algorithms detecting low-credibility content, including propaganda, false claims, rumours and hyperpartisan news. We focus on simulation of content moderation by setting realistic limits on the number of queries an attacker is allowed to attempt. Within our solution (TREPAT), initial rephrasings are generated by large language models with prompts inspired by meaning-preserving NLP tasks, such as text simplification and style transfer. Subsequently, these modifications are decomposed into small changes, applied through beam search procedure, until the victim classifier changes its decision. We perform (1) quantitative evaluation using various prompts, models and query limits, (2) targeted manual assessment of the generated text and (3) qualitative linguistic analysis. The results confirm the superiority of our approach in the constrained scenario, especially in case of long input text (news articles), where exhaustive search is not feasible.
arxiv_record.authors: Piotr Przyby{\l}a, Euan McGill, Horacio Saggion
arxiv_record.title: Attacking Misinformation Detection Using Adversarial Examples Generated by Language Models

C1.justification: The central claim that LLM-based rephrasing enables effective attacks under restricted queries is retained. v2 adds human assessment and linguistic analysis to its stated contributions, asserts human-supported meaning-preservation advantages, and explicitly claims first use of edit-operation decomposition and state-of-the-art BODEGA results in its Conclusions.

C2.justification: v2 replaces the text-length explanation of prompt success with an interpretation based on changing the source register. It develops the tradeoff between aggressive direct rephrasing and conservative edits, discusses repetition and naturalness failures, and newly qualifies deployment realism through the requirement for continuous victim scores. Human evidence replaces v1's explicitly untested expectation about meaning preservation.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a repository link and states that code and annotation results are shared. Appendix C provides annotation instructions, while method footnotes explain the development observations behind the existing 60-character threshold and beam size of five. These are additional disclosures rather than changes to those parameters.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same four English BODEGA tasks: propaganda recognition, fact-checking, rumour detection and hyperpartisan news classification. The new human assessment and budget experiments use this retained coverage. Additional citations identifying source corpora do not establish new datasets.

E2.justification: v2 adds TREPAT-simple as a comparator in the main attack evaluation and query-budget experiment. BERT-ATTACK, F-BERT-ATTACK and BeamAttack remain. FAST-BERT-ATTACK in v1 and F-BERT-ATTACK in v2 describe the same random-word-priority modification.

E3.justification: v2 changes the selected HN prompt from FORMAL to INFORMAL, adds query limits of 10, 100 and 250 around the retained 50-query default, and introduces a 350-case human evaluation. That evaluation samples successful attack pairs, randomizes method presentation and assesses meaning preservation and naturalness.

E4.justification: v2 adds an ablation testing direct rephrasing against decomposition and beam search, query-budget sensitivity analysis, and linguistic case studies of repetition, grammatical problems and meaning changes. Table 2 additionally examines semantic similarity across prompts. The original model and prompt comparisons are retained.

E5.justification: v2 introduces annotation-reliability reporting: two linguists, 25% overlapping assignments, and agreement of 75% for meaning preservation and 63% for naturalness among cases where both made explicit preferences. Neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests for the automatic results.

E6.justification: Development and final-evaluation values change extensively. Under the retained reported BERT/FC configuration, TREPAT's BODEGA score changes from 0.2744 in v1 Table 4 to 0.3348 in v2 Table 3. HN results use a changed prompt. New results cover TREPAT-simple, query budgets and human preferences. The revised 15-of-16 winning count includes both TREPAT variants and ties; v1's 9-of-16 count concerns the original method.

M1.justification: The original splitting, rephrasing, edit decomposition, filtering and beam-search procedure is retained as TREPAT-full. v2 adds TREPAT-simple, which uses generated rephrasings directly without decomposition or beam search. This introduces a procedural variant without redesigning the original method.

P1.justification: v2 recasts the introduction around an explicit contribution list, reorders experiments and baselines, expands the method walkthrough, and reorganizes Results into automatic, manual and linguistic subsections. The closing Discussion becomes Conclusions, Ethical impact and Limitations, and the appendix structure expands substantially.

P2.justification: v2 adds an architecture diagram, query-budget plot, annotation-guideline figure and human-evaluation table. The prompt table gains a semantic-score section, and attack tables gain TREPAT-simple rows. BiLSTM and GEMMA tables move to Appendix D, while the BERT table remains in the main text.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of RAFT and adversarial prompting, plus citations supporting human evaluation, dataset provenance and moderation ethics; the earlier spam-filter reference is removed. Its main research positioning remains similar, with an additional explicit decomposition-novelty claim. The BODEGA preprint-to-journal citation update represents the same work.

T1.justification: The mathematical descriptions of edit decomposition, beam-search scoring and the BODEGA metric remain unchanged. Neither version develops formal theorems or proofs. New examples and parameter rationales provide explanation rather than new mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly lacked human validation of meaning preservation, a central requirement for valid adversarial examples. v2 substantially addresses that gap through a blinded 350-case assessment, annotation guidelines and agreement reporting. The ablation and budget sweep also clarify component tradeoffs and applicability. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses, including unexplained numerical revisions and prose/table inconsistencies: Section 5.1 says TREPAT-simple wins BERT/RD, whereas Table 3 favors TREPAT-full. The improvement rests on stronger validation and clearer boundaries, rather than the larger winning count.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TREPAT for adversarial attacks on misinformation detection. Their complete text, tables, figures and appendices support comparison, including matching results relocated to v2 Appendix D.

after.justification: v2 reports original automatic attack experiments, query-budget comparisons, human evaluations and qualitative analysis of generated adversarial examples.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments comparing language models, prompts and attack methods across four misinformation tasks and four victim architectures.

arxiv_record.abstract: SAEs have recently been employed as a promising unsupervised approach for understanding the representations of layers of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, with the growth in model size and complexity, training SAEs is computationally intensive, as typically one SAE is trained for each model layer. To address such limitation, we propose \textit{Group-SAE}, a novel strategy to train SAEs. Our method considers the similarity of the residual stream representations between contiguous layers to group similar layers and train a single SAE per group. To balance the trade-off between efficiency and performance, we further introduce \textit{AMAD} (Average Maximum Angular Distance), an empirical metric that guides the selection of an optimal number of groups based on representational similarity across layers. Experiments on models from the Pythia family show that our approach significantly accelerates training with minimal impact on reconstruction quality and comparable downstream task performance and interpretability over baseline SAEs trained layer by layer. This method provides an efficient and scalable strategy for training SAEs in modern LLMs.
arxiv_record.authors: Davide Ghilardi, Federico Belotti, Marco Molinari, Tao Ma, Matteo Palmonari
arxiv_record.title: Group-SAE: Efficient Training of Sparse Autoencoders for Large Language Models via Layer Groups

Experiments on models from the Pythia family show that our approach significantly accelerates training with minimal impact on reconstruction quality and comparable downstream task performance and interpretability over baseline SAEs trained layer by layer. This method provides an efficient and scalable strategy for training SAEs in modern LLMs.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes up to 6x training speedup, preserved causal-task performance, and human interpretability. v2 adds AMAD selection as a central contribution and claims roughly 50% computational savings, an efficiency-quality tradeoff, and superiority over compute-matched smaller SAEs. The contribution changes from demonstrating grouped training on one model to selecting groups and substantiating efficiency across three model sizes.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the AMAD turning point and layer-localized features with neighboring-layer support as explanations for effective grouping. Its limitations emphasize fixed TopK/expansion settings, Pythia/Pile-specific generalization, and restricted interpretability assessment. This replaces v1's emphasis on unresolved group-count selection, single-model scaling, and possible polysemantic interference when many layers share an SAE.

D1.justification: v2 replaces the release-upon-acceptance promise with a reported code/SAE release and access link. Appendices A–B disclose random layer sampling, detailed auxiliary-loss settings, normalization, software libraries, eight AMD MI250X GPUs, and an approximately 24-hour longest run. These substantially expand reproducibility information, although the inconsistent FVU formulas leave some implementation ambiguity.

E1.justification: The Pile remains the underlying corpus, but v1's Indirect Object Identification, Greater Than, and Subject-Verb Agreement evaluations disappear, including their appendix results. v2 retains Pile-based reconstruction and next-token evaluation, substantially narrowing coverage of distinct causal tasks. The additional Pythia sizes are model configurations, rather than new datasets.

E2.justification: Alongside individual per-layer SAEs, v2 evaluates two new efficiency comparators: Group SAEs with evenly spaced groups and smaller SAEs trained on every layer. Table 1 compares these at reportedly matched computational cost; v1 contains neither comparison.

E3.justification: v2 adds Pythia-410M and Pythia-1B configurations and broader group-count sweeps. Expansion increases from 8 to 16, angular-distance sampling from 5M to 10M tokens, and normalization, batch sizes, and optimizer settings change. Evaluation shifts to FVU and relative cross-entropy increase; Gemini detection/fuzzing on 64 features per SAE replaces human scoring of 96 sampled features. Appendix E also reverses MMCS matching from group-to-baseline to baseline-to-group.

E4.justification: v2 adds AMAD/compute versus quality analyses, expands MMCS comparisons to baseline layers against different groups, and introduces feature-activation distributions across layers in Appendix F. v1's feature-ablation tests of sufficiency and necessity, Attribution Patching/Integrated Gradients analyses, and detailed per-layer reconstruction/sparsity plots are removed. The supplementary analyses therefore change substantially.

E5.justification: v1 reports averages without uncertainty estimates. v2 Section 4.1 specifies layer-weighted means and standard deviations, and Figure 2 identifies shading as one standard deviation. This adds descriptive variability reporting, without establishing repeated training runs, seed variation, or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: The earlier causal-task and human scores are replaced by extensive new results under changed training and evaluation settings. v2 Table 2 reports 42.5%, 53.3%, and 53.7% computational savings. Table 1 reports Pythia-160M cross-entropy increases of 6.01% for AMAD grouping, 7.37% for smaller SAEs, and 5.40% for evenly spaced grouping, documenting an exception to AMAD superiority. These are new comparisons, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: Complete-linkage clustering using angular distance is retained, but v2 introduces AMAD-based selection of the smallest group count below a 0.2 distance threshold. Training also changes from v1's JumpReLU and squared-error-plus-L1 objective to TopK activation with FVU reconstruction and an auxiliary dead-latent loss (v2 Section 4.1 and Appendix B). These change the procedure beyond its Group-SAE renaming.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, background, and experimental narrative around Group-SAE and three research questions. Separate reconstruction, downstream-task, and human-evaluation sections become a consolidated experimental section. The appendices are reorganized into training, grouping, automated interpretation, feature similarity, and feature distribution, with retained material matched across these moves.

P2.justification: The single-column ICLR presentation becomes a two-column main text, and the method illustration is redrawn. Average bars and causal-task curves are replaced by AMAD/compute tradeoff plots with uncertainty shading, new comparison and cost tables, and automated-interpretability plots. Appendices add feature-distribution heatmaps and redesigned similarity plots; these are substantial display changes.

R1.justification: The new Shared SAEs subsection discusses Yun et al., Lawson et al., and Lindsey et al.'s crosscoders, explicitly positioning Group-SAE against earlier multilayer representation methods through its efficiency-performance tradeoff. v2 also adds mechanistic-interpretability challenges and automated-interpretation literature, while removing much of v1's causal-task evaluation positioning. This is a substantive revision beyond bibliographic updates.

T1.justification: v2 adds AMAD's mathematical definition and threshold-selection rule, plus elementary FLOP accounting that includes activation caching. v1's indirect-effect and approximation formulations are removed. These change the formal definitions and derivations without introducing theoretical guarantees. v2 also leaves an inconsistency between the squared-error FVU definition in Equation 6 and the unsquared Frobenius-norm ratio in Equation 9.

improvement.justification: v1 explicitly lacked a group-count selection rule and evaluated efficiency without compute-matched alternatives. v2 supplies an operational AMAD rule, caching-inclusive cost accounting, and reported matched-cost comparisons across three Pythia sizes, substantially strengthening the central efficiency argument. Expanded implementation details and release information also improve reproducibility. Removing causal-task tests and human judgments weakens direct interpretability validation, and the FVU formula inconsistency limits clarity. Nevertheless, the gains in method selection and controlled efficiency evidence constitute a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same layer-grouped SAE research. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and figures, tables, equations, and renamed or relocated material support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 reports original experiments on three Pythia sizes, including reconstruction, next-token prediction, automated interpretability, computational comparisons, and feature analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original Pythia-160M experiments covering reconstruction, feature similarity, three causal downstream tasks, and human interpretability.

arxiv_record.abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) offers a promising approach to aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences. Typically, a reward model is trained or supplied to act as a proxy for humans in evaluating generated responses during the reinforcement training phase. However, current reward models operate as sequence-to-one models, allocating a single, sparse, and delayed reward to an entire output sequence. This approach may overlook the significant contributions of individual tokens toward the desired outcome. To this end, we propose a more fine-grained, token-level guidance approach for RL training. Specifically, we introduce RED, a novel reward redistribition method that evaluates and assigns specific credit to each token using an off-the-shelf reward model. Utilizing these fine-grained rewards enhances the model's understanding of language nuances, leading to more precise performance improvements. Notably, our method does not require modifying the reward model or introducing additional training steps, thereby incurring minimal computational costs. Experimental results across diverse datasets and tasks demonstrate the superiority of our approach.
arxiv_record.authors: Jiahui Li, Lin Li, Tai-wei Chang, Kun Kuang, Long Chen, Jun Zhou, Cheng Yang
arxiv_record.title: RED: Unleashing Token-Level Rewards from Holistic Feedback via Reward Redistribution

C1.justification: Both versions claim that token-level credit from an existing reward model improves RLHF with little overhead, requires no additional fine-grained human labeling or reward-model retraining, and preserves the optimal policy. RED's name and stronger emphasis on computational simplicity reframe claims already present in v1.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for ABC's weaknesses, RLOO's behavior, and reward–cost conflicts. It newly acknowledges missing token-reward ground truth and difficulty rewarding reasoning steps in coding/math, while removing the no-human-evaluation limitation after adding human studies. The stability discussion also shifts from reduced fluctuations to acknowledging greater variability.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds implementation pseudocode, model-specific parameter tables, explicit KL coefficients, RLOO sample counts, mixture weights, and human-questionnaire templates. Dataset construction and training instructions are revised. Hardware/timing information and GPT-4 prompts remain, while the explicit cost-model training loss is replaced by a reference to prior work.

E1.justification: Both versions use Nectar, TL;DR, SafeRLHF, and Alpaca for the same question-answering, summarization, and helpfulness/harmlessness tasks. New model configurations, human assessments, and reward-perturbation controls retain this dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds attention-based credits (ABC) and RLOO comparisons, including PPO-ABC and RLOO-ABC on Nectar and TL;DR. LLaMA3 comparisons also gain DPO and, on SafeRLHF, Lagrangian variants. The earlier uniform terminal-reward Simple baseline disappears. These substantially expand and revise the evaluated comparator sets.

E3.justification: Appendix B changes Nectar reward-model training from 5,000 to 102,366 examples and broadens preference-pair construction. TL;DR SFT/RL counts change from 14,900/14,900 to 116,722/92,846, with revised learning rates, lengths, and other hyperparameters. Qwen2.5 configurations replace GPT-J evaluations, and human-evaluation and coherence/diversity protocols are added. These are reported setting changes, without establishing which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds reward-mixture ablations, return-preserving reward-noise tests, a dynamic-initialization control, human assessment of token-credit quality, coherence/diversity analyses, and reward–KL relationships. Its initialization control redistributes the prompt offset and is distinct from v1's removed uniform terminal-reward baseline. Case studies are also expanded and revised.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly reports three random seeds and train/test error bars in Section 4.6 and Figure 4. v2 removes that disclosure, labels learning-curve bands as standard deviations, and adds ablation error bars without specifying their repeated-run basis. This changes uncertainty reporting but does not establish an increase in runs.

E6.justification: Many reported scores are replaced: for example, LLaMA Nectar PPO-R3HF's reward score/win rate of 3.9008/92.72% becomes PPO-RED's 3.475/97.83% in Table 1. Changed training settings prevent interpreting these as same-setting performance changes. v2 also adds ABC, RLOO, Qwen2.5, human-evaluation, and ablation results, while removing GPT-J results.

M1.justification: The core temporal-difference redistribution remains unchanged. v2 adds a convex combination of redistributed token rewards and the original terminal reward, controlled by beta_c in Equation 7. This changes the training reward in configurations using beta_c below one, while retaining the existing reward model and central algorithm.

P1.justification: The paper is retitled and renamed, with extensive rewriting of the abstract, method explanation, experimental narrative, related work, and limitations. DPO/concurrent-work discussions and stability/showcase material move into the appendices, while the main text gains a dedicated ablation section and reorganized explanatory subheadings.

P2.justification: The main text switches to two columns, Figure 1 is redrawn, and new reward-computation, ablation, and pseudocode figures appear. SafeRLHF results move from a plot to expanded tables; learning curves become a multi-panel reward/KL analysis. Results tables are consolidated and expanded with model groupings, human assessments, and additional showcases.

R1.justification: Section 5 and Appendix A.2 substantially expand positioning around fine-grained rewards and RL alternatives. Chan et al.'s ABC becomes the closest comparator, alongside new discussion and citations covering KTO, SimPO, ORPO, REINFORCE variants, and GRPO/DeepSeek. Earlier Xia and Zhong comparisons are retained and relocated.

T1.justification: v2 adds a potential-based-shaping proof involving value-function shifts and unchanged advantages, explicit stochastic-approximation assumptions in Appendix A.2, and derivations for the mixed reward's return. The earlier DPO analysis is largely retained and relocated; the new proof and formal conditions constitute substantive theoretical additions.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's explicit lack of human evaluation through Appendix C.2/C.5 and Table 13, and adds the closely related ABC comparator plus controlled reward-noise and initialization tests. These substantially strengthen assessment of the central credit-assignment and alignment claims. Removal of seed-count reporting and inconsistent win/tie/loss totals in some new tables temper confidence in individual comparisons, but the added direct validation provides a substantial overall benefit.

A1.justification: Both PDFs contain readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices for the same reward-redistribution research, renamed from R3HF to RED. Corresponding methods and experiments can be matched despite substantial revision.

after.justification: Sections 4 and Appendix C report original training results, ablations, human evaluations, reward-quality assessments, and generated examples.

before.justification: Sections 4 and Appendix C report original model-training experiments, reward scores, GPT-4 evaluations, learning curves, and generated examples.

arxiv_record.abstract: Systems that answer questions by reviewing the scientific literature are becoming increasingly feasible. To draw reliable conclusions, these systems should take into account the quality of available evidence from different studies, placing more weight on studies that use a valid methodology. We present a benchmark for measuring the methodological strength of biomedical papers, drawing on the risk-of-bias framework used for systematic reviews. Derived from over 500 biomedical studies, the three benchmark tasks encompass expert reviewers' judgments of studies' research methodologies, including the assessments of risk of bias within these studies. The benchmark contains a human-validated annotation pipeline for fine-grained alignment of reviewers' judgments with research paper sentences. Our analyses show that large language models' reasoning and retrieval capabilities impact their effectiveness with risk-of-bias assessment. The dataset is available at https://github.com/RoBBR-Benchmark/RoBBR.

arxiv_record.title: Measuring Risk of Bias in Biomedical Reports: The RoBBR Benchmark

      <abstract>Systems that answer questions by reviewing the scientific literature are becoming increasingly feasible. To draw reliable conclusions, these systems should take into account the quality of available evidence from different studies, placing more weight on studies that use a valid methodology. We present a benchmark for measuring the methodological strength of biomedical papers, drawing on the risk-of-bias framework used for systematic reviews. Derived from over 500 biomedical studies, the three benchmark tasks encompass expert reviewers’ judgments of studies’ research methodologies, including the assessments of risk of bias within these studies. The benchmark contains a human-validated annotation pipeline for fine-grained alignment of reviewers’ judgments with research paper sentences. Our analyses show that large language models’ reasoning and retrieval capabilities impact their effectiveness with risk-of-bias assessment. The dataset is available at <url>https://github.com/RoBBR-Benchmark/RoBBR</url>.</abstract>
