C1.justification: V1 presents four tasks simulating the review process and emphasizes models falling short of expert performance. V2 centers one risk-labeling task and claims novelty specifically for its two diagnostic subtasks. Its abstract, introduction, and conclusion emphasize evidence that retrieval and reasoning capabilities affect risk assessment, substantially redefining the contribution.

C2.justification: V2 develops interpretations about retrieval bottlenecks, global context, and traditional models' generalization limits, while qualifying some reasoning and baseline comparisons as inconclusive. It adds licensing, English-language coverage, and over-reliance limitations. V1's explicit caveats about expert-label errors, reviewer disagreement, and exclusion of observational studies are removed.

D1.justification: V2 adds model snapshots, generation settings, annotation costs, annotator-training details, retrieval-intervention prompts, and LoRA training details including hardware, rank, batch size, optimizer, and schedule. These materially expand reproducibility information. Conversely, v1's explicit collection date and review-level split-construction description are omitted; the principal repository and licensing disclosures remain.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates four tasks using Cochrane-derived data. V2 removes study inclusion/exclusion and adds a non-Cochrane main-task test set containing 2,489 judgments from 496 reviews. It explicitly includes RoB2 assessments, including deviation bias and the 'some concern' label, substantially changing represented sources and assessment coverage.

E2.justification: V2 removes Claude3-Opus and Gemini-1.5-Pro from the retained task comparisons. It adds Llama-3.1-70B, untuned and fine-tuned Llama-3-8B, OpenAI-v3 and GritLM retrieval baselines, and logistic regression, SVM, and RobotReviewer comparisons. Sonnet-3.5 also joins the retrieval comparison, where v1 did not report it.

E3.justification: V2 replaces v1's capped evaluation subsets with revised task sets, including a reported 465-example SJS evaluation versus 310 previously. It changes overall reporting from pooled 'Full' scores to averages across bias categories, drops retrieval@3 and main-task accuracy/weighted accuracy, and adds task-specific fine-tuning and a restricted binary-label RobotReviewer protocol. Appendix Table 14 inconsistently retains older SJS sample counts.

E4.justification: V2 adds cross-task association analysis (Figure 4), controlled retrieval/reasoning combinations (Table 6), non-Cochrane evidence highlighting (Table 7), local-versus-global context analysis (Appendix F), and a detailed reasoning-error case study (Appendix G). These substantially extend v1's descriptive task comparisons and brief illustrative example.

E5.justification: Both versions already report bootstrapped standard errors and annotation-agreement hypothesis tests. V2 additionally reports explicitly labeled 95% confidence intervals in Tables 6–8. Its appendix benchmark tables retain per-category standard errors but omit uncertainty for aggregate scores that v1 supplied. Neither version establishes an increase in repeated runs.

E6.justification: The benchmark result tables are substantially replaced, with screening results removed and numerous new model and analysis results added. For example, v2 Table 3 reports Llama-3-8B retrieval scores of 22.7% before fine-tuning and 40.8% afterward; Table 6 reports 31.5% versus 46.1% for GPT-4o reasoning using Sonnet-retrieved versus ground-truth sentences. Changed datasets and aggregation prevent interpreting headline v1-to-v2 differences as same-setting performance changes.

M1.justification: V2 adds retrieval-conditioned inference variants: risk classification from retrieved sentences and classification from the full paper with highlighted evidence (Sections 6.3–6.4). These are limited procedural extensions; the central GPT-4 annotation and distractor-generation procedures retain their existing prompts and sliding-window approach. Omission of v1's separate negation-filter prompt does not establish whether that underlying filtering step changed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background, related work, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related work moves before benchmark development, the four-task narrative becomes a main-task/two-subtask hierarchy, and existing task explanations and illustrations move into reorganized appendices. Terminology is standardized around SSR and SJS.

P2.justification: V2 changes the document to two columns, redraws the reviewer-process illustration, adds an annotation-pipeline diagram and analytical plots, and substantially restructures result and dataset tables. Existing task illustrations move to the appendix, while the screening illustration is removed. Many prompt images are retained unchanged despite relocation and renumbering.

R1.justification: V2 replaces much of the broad screening, retrieval, and summarization survey with focused risk-labeling and support-sentence discussions. It adds work including Dias et al.'s RoBIn and contextual embedding research, and explicitly distinguishes its subtasks and annotation pipeline from prior label prediction, quotation extraction, and embedding methods.

T1.justification: V2's coverage definition and Equation 1 make the existing aspect-matching guidance and Bias Recall@Optimal metric explicit, renaming the latter Aspect Recall Ratio@Optimal. They do not establish a substantively different mathematical construction. Neither version provides theoretical guarantees or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the benchmark's diagnostic purpose. Broader data sources and baseline families address v1's narrow empirical evaluation, while retrieval interventions and error analyses provide direct evidence connecting the subtasks to risk assessment. Added implementation details improve reproducibility. Benefits outweigh remaining weaknesses, including inconsistent SJS sample counts, removed label-quality caveats, and the limited practical interpretation of gold-label-guided highlighting.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the RoBBR benchmark. Their main text, tables, figures, references, and appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial revisions to coverage and evaluation.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark evaluations, fine-tuning results, annotation comparisons, retrieval interventions, and error analyses in the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original model evaluations on four benchmark tasks and a human-versus-GPT annotation agreement study, with additional results and standard errors in Appendix E.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs), particularly smaller variants, still struggle with complex reasoning tasks. While inference-time prompting can guide reasoning, existing methods often rely on sequential queries. Ensemble approaches offer a promising path to performance gains, especially given recent batch inference speed-ups. This work introduces DIPPER, a novel, training-free framework that transforms a single LLM into an effective inference-time ensemble. By feeding the model an optimized and diverse set of prompts in parallel, DIPPER elicits varied reasoning paths, leading to performance gains. We empirically demonstrate significant improvements on reasoning benchmarks, such as MATH, where a DIPPER ensemble of three Qwen2-MATH-1.5B instances (via parallel prompting of a single model) outperforms a larger 7B model.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claim of training-free, prompt-diverse ensembles built from one base LLM, including three Qwen2-MATH-1.5B instances outperforming a 7B model. The new contribution bullets organize existing claims; additional experiments mainly extend their support.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands the fidelity-diversity interpretation, explaining why excessive fidelity weighting can hurt and why candidate-pool diversity matters. It adds an easier-task explanation for limited GSM8K gains, discusses applicability beyond reasoning, and explicitly acknowledges the homogeneous-model limitation. The earlier explanation of LLMA's reasoning-based advantage is removed.

D1.justification: v2 Appendix A newly identifies all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and specifies temperature 0.7, top-p 0.8, repetition penalty 1.05, and a 512-token generation limit. It also identifies the Best-of-N reward model. These disclosures do not establish changed settings for retained experiments. The detailed LLMA prompt template is removed.

E1.justification: MATH, GSM8K, and MMLU-STEM are retained. v2 Appendix C.3 adds BIG-Bench synonyms, word unscrambling, and word sorting, extending evaluation beyond the original mathematical and STEM reasoning coverage.

E2.justification: The main Self-ensemble, Random+, and Top-n comparator set is retained after renaming. The separate MV-versus-LLMA comparison in v1 Table 1 disappears. v2 Figure 8 instead compares FASV with Self-ensemble under Best-of-N; it does not display the other variants discussed in the accompanying text.

E3.justification: v2 adds LLaMA3.2-3B, Qwen3-0.6B/1.7B, and Llama3.1-8B configurations, Best-of-N evaluation with Qwen2.5-Math-RM-72B, and instruction induction from five input-output demonstrations. It also introduces a candidate-pool control using k-means with k=4. The original benchmark splits and 4/8/5-shot settings remain.

E4.justification: v2 adds clustered-versus-full candidate-pool analysis, GSM8K diversity sensitivity and scatter analyses, and a paraphrased-versus-diverse prompt case study. It removes the MV/LLMA override-ratio and unique-answer diagnostics. Self-reflection evidence is narrowed from an ensemble-size sweep to a single n=5 comparison.

E5.justification: The retained self-reflection result loses its displayed spread: v1 Figure 4 includes a shaded band, whereas v2 Section 5.5 reports only the n=5 accuracies. Neither version defines that band or specifies repeated-run counts or seeds. Other error-bar and shaded-spread displays remain.

E6.justification: v2 adds LLaMA, Qwen3, and BIG-Bench results and removes v1's MV/LLMA table. Retained curves also change: GSM8K Random+ at n=3 moves from approximately 84.10 to 83.73 (v1 Figure 7; v2 Figure 12), and MMLU-STEM scores are revised. The MATH correlation plot changes substantially, with its peak moving from about 0.41 to 0.82 (Figure 6 in both versions).

M1.justification: The prompt generator, fidelity-adjusted semantic-volume selection, and majority voting remain. The optional aggregation procedure changes from an LLM synthesizing constituent responses to Best-of-N selection using an external reward model. The rewritten selection objective is algebraically equivalent to v1's objective.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, contribution bullets are introduced, and problem formulation becomes a separate section. Prompt-generator material moves from the appendix into the main method description, while the experimental narrative and appendices are reorganized. Author order and affiliations also change.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from single-column to two-column layout, with substantially rearranged and resized figures. The algorithm and prompt-accuracy distribution move into the main text. New model, diversity-analysis, and BIG-Bench displays are added; the LLMA comparison table and self-reflection plot are removed.

R1.justification: v2 adds a dedicated prompt-optimization discussion distinguishing single-prompt search from ensemble composition, citing works including Zhou, Lin, Yang, and Hu. It also newly connects prompt selection to data-selection research and the diversity objective to determinantal point processes, substantially broadening v1's mainly ensemble-focused positioning.

T1.justification: v2 Equation 7 and Appendix B add an explicit derivation decomposing fidelity-adjusted semantic volume into log-determinant diversity plus alpha times total prompt fidelity. This derivation is absent from v1, although the underlying objective and existing submodularity-based argument are retained.

improvement.justification: v1's empirical support relies principally on one specialized constituent model. v2 substantially strengthens generality through additional model families and non-reasoning tasks, adds controlled analysis of candidate diversity, and improves reproducibility through encoder and decoding details. The explicit objective derivation also aids understanding. Lost LLMA diagnostics and reduced self-reflection reporting are drawbacks, and Table 5 contains exceptions to the claimed consistent superiority, but the broader and more examinable evidence provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DIPPER and provide readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices. The framework and retained experiments can be matched despite extensive restructuring.

after.justification: v2 Section 5 and Appendix C report original experiments, including retained reasoning benchmarks and additional model, BIG-Bench, and prompt-diversity evaluations.

before.justification: v1 Section 4 and the appendices report original experiments on MATH, GSM8K, and MMLU-STEM, including prompt diversity, aggregation, and self-reflection results.

arxiv_record.abstract: Despite significant advancements in Text-to-Audio (TTA) generation models achieving high-fidelity audio with fine-grained context understanding, they struggle to model the relations between audio events described in the input text. However, previous TTA methods have not systematically explored audio event relation modeling, nor have they proposed frameworks to enhance this capability. In this work, we systematically study audio event relation modeling in TTA generation models. We first establish a benchmark for this task by: 1. proposing a comprehensive relation corpus covering all potential relations in real-world scenarios; 2. introducing a new audio event corpus encompassing commonly heard audios; and 3. proposing new evaluation metrics to assess audio event relation modeling from various perspectives. Furthermore, we propose a finetuning framework to enhance existing TTA models ability to model audio events relation. Code is available at: https://github.com/yuhanghe01/RiTTA

C1.justification: The benchmark and relation-aware evaluation contributions remain. However, the abstract, contribution list, and conclusion replace ordinary finetuning as the principal intervention with gated prompt tuning, claiming improved relation modeling with approximately five million additional parameters. This substantially changes the paper's methodological contribution.

C2.justification: v4 introduces a domain-gap explanation for prompt-only adaptation failing, interprets the new agentic and component comparisons, and explicitly identifies the closed event/relation vocabulary as an applicability limitation. It removes v1's bag-of-words and unary-pretraining rationale and its explanation linking degraded Not performance to silent training targets. Earlier relation-difficulty interpretations are retained in Appendix F.

D1.justification: v4 supplies a substantially more concrete adaptation recipe: random 1024-dimensional prompts, specified trainable backbone components, Adam learning rate 3e-5, batch size 16, SNR gamma 5, 40 epochs, and four A100 GPUs. v1's Tango training description primarily names Adam and refers to the Tango 2 strategy. The PANNS recipe, original inference settings, and code link remain; TangoFlux inference settings are still absent from Table I.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same constructed benchmark covering four relation categories, 11 sub-relations, and 25 audio event classes, with seed audio from Freesound and VCTK. The PANNS training and testing coverage is also retained. New model and agentic comparisons use this existing coverage; open-ended generation is only proposed as future work.

E2.justification: v4 Table 4 retains the original seven model configurations and adds TangoFlux plus GPT-4 agentic decomposition-and-merging comparators using Tango, Tango 2, and TangoFlux. Table 5 additionally compares gated prompting against ordinary finetuning on both Tango and TangoFlux, substantially expanding the evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: Equation 2 changes the reported relation-scoring aggregation from a product to a maximum. New TangoFlux experiments introduce frozen-backbone, single-prompt-type, and ungated controls. Existing dataset splits and original baseline inference settings are retained; the PDFs do not establish whether the scoring correction changed the implementation or caused retained results to be rerun.

E4.justification: v4 Section 6.4 and Table 6 add four targeted ablations testing backbone adaptation, relation prompts, event prompts, and gating. v1 contains no corresponding component study. Earlier qualitative examples and relation-specific radar analyses remain, including material moved to the appendix.

E5.justification: The seed information in Appendix Table I is unchanged. Neither version reports repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests for the compared results. The detector confidence thresholds are retained evaluation settings, not new uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: The original benchmark values and Tango finetuning row are retained, while v4 adds TangoFlux, agentic, gated-prompt, and ablation results. Within v4 Table 5, gated prompting versus finetuning yields mAMSR values of 59.13 versus 48.67 for Tango and 127.98 versus 83.44 for TangoFlux, in the reported scaled units. Gains are not uniform: TangoFlux's gated variant scores lower on Count and Spatial Distance.

M1.justification: v1 Section 4 proposes finetuning Tango's diffusion model while fixing the other components. v4 Section 5 introduces relation and event prompts, text-conditioned cross-attention, sparse entmax gating, and auxiliary classification losses. These prompts are jointly trained with Tango's UNet or TangoFlux's Transformer blocks, constituting a substantive new method.

P1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, related work, method, and experimental narrative are substantially revised. Data creation becomes a separate main section, while evaluation details, detailed benchmark findings, and the original extended conclusion move into appendices. A new short conclusion and explicit limitations section further reorganize the narrative.

P2.justification: The document changes from a predominantly single-column to a two-column layout, with extensive resizing and relocation of displays. Figure 5 replaces the finetuning pipeline with the gated-prompt architecture; comparison tables gain new groupings and an ablation table is added. Earlier benchmark tables and radar plots remain, several relocated to the appendix.

R1.justification: v4 replaces the general audio-generation overview with positioning in NLP, visual, and acoustic prompt tuning, citing works such as Lester, Jia, Sohn, Liang, and Oiso. It adds TangoFlux and sparse-gating references while removing WavJourney and several references supporting v1's bag-of-words rationale. These changes substantially reposition the proposed intervention relative to prior research.

T1.justification: Equation 2 replaces the product of binary relation indicators with their maximum, aligning the mathematical expression with the retained statement that a satisfying subset is sufficient. This is a substantive but localized correction to the metric definition. The remaining scoring equations are retained, and no theoretical proofs are added.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens evidence for the proposed intervention beyond v1's Tango finetuning demonstration: it compares adaptation on two backbones, evaluates agentic alternatives, and tests component necessity through four ablations. Concrete training settings and the Equation 2 correction also improve assessability. Benefits are tempered by nonuniform subgroup gains, removal of the relevant WavJourney discussion, and retained erroneous below-1% statements in Appendix Table IV, but the central methodological claims now have substantially stronger experimental support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RiTTA and provide readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices. Retained material can be matched across the substantial revision and relocation of content.

after.justification: v4 retains original experimental results and adds TangoFlux benchmarking, GPT-4 agentic comparisons, gated prompt tuning experiments, and component ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original TTA benchmarking, Tango finetuning results, and PANNS detector experiments, including the appendix comparison of detector mAP before and after finetuning.

arxiv_record.abstract: As a crucial step to enhance LLMs alignment with human intentions, Instruction Fine-Tuning (IFT) has a high demand on dataset quality. However, existing IFT datasets often contain knowledge that is inconsistent with LLMs' internal knowledge learned from the pre-training phase, which can greatly affect the efficacy of IFT. To address this issue, we introduce NILE (iNternal consIstency aLignmEnt) framework, aimed at optimizing IFT datasets to unlock LLMs' capability further. NILE operates by eliciting target pre-trained LLM's internal knowledge corresponding to instruction data. The internal knowledge is leveraged to revise the answer in IFT datasets. Additionally, we propose a novel Internal Consistency Filtering (ICF) method to filter training samples, ensuring its high consistency with LLM's internal knowledge. Our experiments demonstrate that NILE-aligned IFT datasets sharply boost LLM performance across multiple LLM ability evaluation datasets, achieving up to 66.6% gain on Arena-Hard and 68.5% on Alpaca-Eval V2. Further analysis confirms that each component of the NILE}framework contributes to these substantial performance improvements, and provides compelling evidence that dataset consistency with pre-trained internal knowledge is pivotal for maximizing LLM potential.

metadata.abstract: Recent advances show that the world knowledge in the Instruction Fine-Tuning (IFT) dataset, which is incompatible with LLMs’ internal knowledge, can greatly hurt the IFT performance. However, the effective integration and balancing of the internal knowledge of LLMs, acquired during pre-training, with existing IFT datasets remains a largely underexplored area of research. To address this gap, this work introduces NILE, a novel framework to optimize the effectiveness of IFT by adjusting IFT datasets through carefully aligning the world and internal knowledge. NILE employs a three-stage pipeline to effectively quantify and adjust consistency with the internal knowledge of target LLMs. Our analysis provides compelling evidence that balancing such consistency with pre-trained internal knowledge is pivotal for unleashing LLM potential, and confirms that NILE can systematically contribute to these substantial performance improvements. Experimental results demonstrate that NILE-aligned IFT datasets sharply boost LLM performance across multiple LLM ability evaluation datasets, achieving up to 66.6% gain on Arena-Hard and 68.5% on Alpaca-Eval V2.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning external-knowledge use and computational practicality, explains threshold selection through manual screening, and discusses fixed-size answer reversion in Limitations. D1.justification: v2 supplies an access link for NILE-revised datasets, IKE runtime and token usage, and KSR token/cost measurements. It also discloses screening 100 samples per dataset for threshold selection and using Alpaca-style system prompts during evaluation. These supplement already detailed implementation information without establishing changes to existing experiments.

E1.justification: v2 retains Alpaca/OpenOrca training and the four original evaluation benchmarks, while adding SQuADv2 passage-based reading comprehension and MMLU multitask knowledge assessment in Appendices A.2–A.3. These extend evaluation to substantive additional task requirements.

E2.justification: Vanilla and SR remain the comparators in corresponding experiments, and the existing retriever and knowledge-source comparisons are retained. Additional evaluations reuse existing methods; SQuADv2 compares NILE with Vanilla. Newly cited methods are not evaluated as additional baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds Llama-3.2-3B and Qwen2.5-7B/14B configurations, substantially extending the evaluated model families and sizes. New protocols include SQuADv2 validation with EM/F1, MMLU accuracy using default harness settings, and a fifth-percentile ICF condition. Previously stated training and evaluation settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 7 extends the existing threshold sensitivity study with a MEDIUM condition for both training datasets. E5.justification: Both versions disclose vLLM seed 42 and chi-squared p-values below 0.01 for the existing 10,000-instruction similarity analysis. v2 adds no repeated-run counts, benchmark confidence intervals, or new uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: Table 4 and matched preexisting ablation results are unchanged. v2 adds results for three model configurations, MMLU, SQuADv2, the intermediate threshold, and resource usage. For example, the newly evaluated Qwen2.5-14B Alpaca configuration reports LCWR 28.55 for NILE versus 15.37 for Vanilla; these are additional results, not revisions of v1 scores.

arxiv_record.abstract: With the continuous advancement in the performance of large language models (LLMs), their demand for computational resources and memory has significantly increased, which poses major challenges for efficient inference on consumer-grade devices and legacy servers. These devices typically feature relatively weaker GPUs and stronger CPUs. Although techniques such as parameter offloading and partial offloading can alleviate GPU memory pressure to some extent, their effectiveness is limited due to communication latency and suboptimal hardware resource utilization. To address this issue, we propose Dovetail, a lossless inference acceleration method that leverages the complementary characteristics of heterogeneous devices and the advantages of speculative decoding. Dovetail deploys a draft model on the GPU to perform preliminary predictions, while a target model running on the CPU validates these outputs. By reducing the granularity of data transfer, Dovetail significantly minimizes communication overhead. To further improve efficiency, we optimize the draft model specifically for heterogeneous hardware environments by reducing the number of draft tokens to lower parallel verification latency, increasing model depth to enhance predictive capabilities, and introducing a Dynamic Gating Fusion (DGF) mechanism to improve the integration of feature and embedding information. We conduct comprehensive evaluations of Dovetail across various consumer-grade GPUs, covering multiple tasks and mainstream models. Experimental results on 13B models demonstrate that Dovetail achieves inference speedups ranging from 1.79x to 10.1x across different devices, while maintaining consistency and stability in the distribution of generated texts.
arxiv_record.authors: Libo Zhang, Zhaoning Zhang, Baizhou Xu, Rui Li, Zhiliang Tian, Songzhu Mei, Dongsheng Li

      <author id="libo-zhang" orcid="0009-0007-2093-0597" openreview="~Libo_Zhang6"><first>Libo</first><last>Zhang</last></author>
      <author id="zhaoning-zhang" orcid="0009-0009-9320-2798" openreview="~Zhaoning_Zhang1"><first>Zhaoning</first><last>Zhang</last><affiliation>National University of Defense Technology</affiliation></author>

      <author id="dongsheng-li" orcid="0000-0001-9743-2034" openreview="~Dongsheng_Li3"><first>Dongsheng</first><last>Li</last><affiliation>National University of Defense Technology</affiliation></author>
      <pages>17382-17395</pages>
      <abstract>With the continuous advancement in the performance of large language models (LLMs), their demand for computational resources and memory has significantly increased, which poses major challenges for efficient inference on consumer-grade devices and legacy servers. These devices typically feature relatively weaker GPUs and stronger CPUs. Although techniques such as parameter offloading and partial offloading can alleviate GPU memory pressure to some extent, their effectiveness is limited due to communication latency and suboptimal hardware resource utilization. To address this issue, we propose Dovetail—a lossless inference acceleration method that leverages the complementary characteristics of heterogeneous devices and the advantages of speculative decoding. Dovetail deploys a draft model on the GPU to perform preliminary predictions, while a target model running on the CPU validates these outputs. By reducing the granularity of data transfer, Dovetail significantly minimizes communication overhead. To further improve efficiency, we optimize the draft model specifically for heterogeneous hardware environments by reducing the number of draft tokens to lower parallel verification latency, increasing model depth to enhance predictive capabilities, and introducing a Dynamic Gating Fusion (DGF) mechanism to improve the integration of feature and embedding information. We conduct comprehensive evaluations of Dovetail across various consumer-grade GPUs, covering multiple tasks and mainstream models. Experimental results on 13B models demonstrate that Dovetail achieves inference speedups ranging from 1.79× to 10.1× across different devices, while maintaining consistency and stability in the distribution of generated texts.</abstract>

C1.justification: The heterogeneous-decoding and draft-model contributions remain the same. The abstract shifts its quantitative emphasis from 7B throughput under 3–7GB VRAM to 13B speedups of approximately 1.79–10.1x across devices, and the introduction adds the 10.14x result to its contribution statement.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly distinguishes accelerating a quantized target from preserving its pre-quantization accuracy. Appendix C.2 attributes the laptop's slowdown with an extra draft block to the int8-target/fp16-draft timing relationship and suggests quantizing the draft. The earlier long-prefill limitation and hardware-imbalance qualification are retained.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands configuration documentation through exact CPU/GPU layer allocations, laptop hardware and PyTorch dynamic-quantization details, and SpecExec draft-model and candidate-count settings. Training hardware and duration are revised from four GPUs and approximately 4–5 days to eight GPUs and approximately one day. The code link is retained, although v1's explicit 128GB server-RAM specification is omitted.

E1.justification: ShareGPT training and the MT-bench, HumanEval, GSM8K, and Alpaca evaluation tasks are retained. v2 additionally tests a constrained personal-computer deployment with an i5-9300H and 4GB GTX 1050 Mobile, extending the two Xeon-server scenarios evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: The principal comparators remain EAGLE-2, TinyLlama, ShearedLlama, SpecExec, CPU-only inference, and offloading. v2 Table 4 adds reported Offload comparisons on HumanEval, where v1 Table II had blank entries. Table 5 also introduces a GPTQ-4bit Offload comparator for the laptop experiment.

E3.justification: The reported training configuration changes from four A800 GPUs and 50 epochs to eight A800 GPUs and 24 epochs; the PDFs do not establish whether retained experiments were rerun. Evaluation adds LLaMA2-Chat 13B and Vicuna 13B, plus laptop settings using an int8 target, tree depth 4, and seven candidates, compared with depth 7 and 16 candidates on servers.

E4.justification: The original candidate-count sensitivity analysis and 7B ablations are retained. v2 adds hardware and stage-timing measurements, Vicuna 13B DGF/depth ablations on RTX 2080 and GTX 1050, and a SpecExec comparison using 16 versus 128 candidates (Tables 1 and 7–10). These examine deployment bottlenecks and the justification for comparator settings.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The additional averages and timing measurements in v2 retain point-estimate reporting.

E6.justification: The shared 7B benchmark and ablation values are retained, while substantial new result blocks appear. Examples include Vicuna 13B's 2.65x mean speedup at temperature 0 in Table 3, LLaMA2-Chat 13B HumanEval speedups of 10.14x for Dovetail versus 7.10x for SpecExec in Table 4, and quantized Vicuna 13B laptop throughput of 3.36 tokens/second in Table 5. These concern newly reported configurations.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure retains GPU drafting, CPU verification, probability-based draft-tree construction, Dynamic Gated Fusion, and multiple Transformer blocks. The additional model, precision, and hardware configurations do not introduce a new algorithmic component.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial portions of the introduction, methods, experiments, and related work are rewritten or condensed. The effectiveness analysis moves into Appendix B, the naming illustration moves into Appendix A, and limitations receive a separate section. Author and affiliation information also changes.

P2.justification: v2 changes the document template and table styling, expands the opening speedup chart to three deployment configurations, and adds hardware, timing, laptop, and supplementary-analysis tables. Architecture diagrams are restyled, the sensitivity plot gains separate axes, and v1's generic speculative-decoding illustration is removed. Other illustrations are relocated.

R1.justification: The research positioning remains largely stable. Citations are added for works including EAGLE, TinyLlama, KIVI, and lossless compression, while LLM.int8, SpinQuant, and Blockwise Parallel Decoding are removed. Changes to MagicDec and Judge Decoding references concern the same works' publication metadata.

T1.justification: v1 Equations 1–5 are retained as v2 Appendix B Equations 2–6, and v1 Equation 6 becomes v2 Equation 1. The latency model, overlap assumptions, and hardware-effectiveness inequality remain substantively unchanged; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1's broad consumer-device claims were evaluated with one 7B target on Xeon servers. v2 substantially strengthens their empirical basis through 13B targets and an actual constrained laptop, including evidence that additional draft depth can hurt performance. Added SpecExec controls and deployment details improve interpretability and reproducibility. The unexplained training-budget revision alongside unchanged 7B results remains a reporting weakness, but the expanded validation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Dovetail, and their text, figures, tables, and equations support reliable comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 includes Appendices A–C. Relocated material, including the hardware-effectiveness analysis, can be matched across versions.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds results for 13B models, laptop deployment, timing measurements, and supplementary ablations in Appendix C.

before.justification: v1 reports original inference-speed, acceptance-length, memory-use, and ablation results for Dovetail, including Tables I–III.

arxiv_record.abstract: Avoiding the propagation of undue (binary) gender inferences and default masculine language remains a key challenge towards inclusive multilingual technologies, particularly when translating into languages with extensive gendered morphology. Gender-neutral translation (GNT) represents a linguistic strategy towards fairer communication across languages. However, research on GNT is limited to a few resources and language pairs. To address this gap, we introduce mGeNTE, an expert-curated resource, and use it to conduct the first systematic multilingual evaluation of inclusive translation with state-of-the-art instruction-following language models (LMs). Experiments on en-es/de/it/el reveal that while models can recognize when neutrality is appropriate, they cannot consistently produce neutral translations, limiting their usability. To probe this behavior, we enrich our evaluation with interpretability analyses that identify task-relevant features and offer initial insights into the internal dynamics of LM-based GNT.

C1.justification: v1 principally contributes a multilingual resource for neutral translation, language modeling and rewriting. v3 additionally claims the first systematic multilingual evaluation of open LMs for GNT and establishes a recognition–generation gap, model/context effects and interpretability findings. These substantially broaden the abstract, introduction and conclusion beyond the resource contribution.

C2.justification: v3 interprets the recognition–generation gap through different contextual reliance and suggests possible lexical overfitting in source classification. It adds substantive limitations concerning prompt/model generalization, sentence-level context, proprietary evaluation and coarse attribution. v1's limitations mainly state that model experiments remain forthcoming.

D1.justification: v3 adds checkpoint identifiers, inference libraries, temperature and precision settings, decoding constraints, hardware/runtime estimates, annotation and attribution procedures, and code/artifact access information (Appendix B). v1 mainly documents corpus construction and translator guidelines. Its explicit CC BY 4.0 license statement is omitted in v3, without establishing a license change.

E1.justification: v3 adds English–Greek to the retained English–Italian/Spanish/German coverage, expanding the corpus from 4,500 to 6,000 triplets and introducing a lower-resource target with a distinct script. It also conducts model evaluations of source categorization and gendered/neutral translation. The Europarl domain and Set-G/Set-N distinction are retained.

E2.justification: v1 has no evaluated model comparisons. v3 compares Llama 3.1 8B, Llama 3.3 70B, Qwen2.5 72B, Gemma 2 9B and Phi-4 14B, with five additional models evaluated during screening (Appendix B.3). It also compares Qwen2.5 72B and GPT-4o as evaluators against human annotations (Table 5).

E3.justification: v3 introduces four prompt configurations, four-shot demonstrations excluded from evaluation, preliminary zero-/two-/four-shot comparisons, and explicit output-format controls. Evaluation adds source-label accuracy, xCOMET, GNT judgments, label–translation coherence and human validation of the judge (Section 4; Appendix B). These constitute a new evaluation design beyond v1's corpus analyses.

E4.justification: v3 adds ablations of system instructions and neutralization guidelines, shot-count and extraction-error analyses, and tests of label–translation coherence. Section 6 and Appendix C further analyze which context components contribute to classification versus translation using AttnLRP. These investigate model behavior absent from v1.

E5.justification: v3 newly reports mean ± standard deviation across prompt configurations (Table 6) and displays performance variability with error bars (Figure 3). This is limited descriptive variability reporting; neither version supplies a repeated-seed or significance-testing protocol.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive model and attribution results without corresponding v1 model scores. For example, Qwen2.5 72B with G+S achieves Set-N GNT accuracy of 0.75 for German and 0.46 for Italian (Figure 13). Existing identical-neutralization rates also change from 10.2% to 11% for Spanish and from 9% to 9.3% for German (Section 3.3).

M1.justification: v1 describes corpus construction without a model inference pipeline. v3 adds structured generation of a source-category label followed by its translation, using conversational demonstrations and constrained decoding, plus an adapted multilingual LLM judge (Section 4, Figure 2, Appendix B). These introduce substantive processing procedures while largely retaining the corpus-curation approach.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion are extensively rewritten around recognizing versus producing neutrality. Separate language-background and related-work discussions are consolidated into Background, while corpus explanations are condensed and details moved to Appendix A. The title, terminology and contribution narrative also change substantially.

P2.justification: v1 Figures 1–3 are expanded, redrawn or merged into appendix Figures 8 and 20; corpus statistics and examples are reorganized across main-text and appendix tables. v3 also adds study and prompt diagrams, performance plots, ablation heatmaps and attribution visualizations, substantially changing the visual presentation.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning around multilingual benchmarking, open-model evaluation and interpretability. Background/Table 1 compare resource coverage and evaluation support, including FairTranslate; the text contrasts its evaluation with earlier single-language studies. Section 6 adds a substantial attribution/interpretability lineage, including AttnLRP, beyond v1's inclusive-language and resource overview.

T1.justification: Appendix B.5 newly defines span-level attribution scores and derives the summed-logit gradient and absolute embedding–gradient dot product (Equations 1–3), followed by normalization. v1 has no corresponding mathematical development. This is a limited methodological formalization rather than a new theorem or theoretical guarantee.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the benchmark's demonstrated utility, completing the model evaluation explicitly deferred in v1. Multilingual comparisons, human validation of the evaluator, prompt analyses and attribution experiments establish a consequential recognition–generation gap and clarify conditions affecting GNT. Detailed implementation reporting further supports reuse. Proprietary judging and coarse attribution restricted to one model limit reproducibility and generalization, but these limitations are acknowledged and do not outweigh the substantial empirical gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same mGeNTE resource and corpus-construction pipeline. Text, tables, figures and v3 Appendices A–C support reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and a changed title. v1 contains no appendix.

after.justification: v3 reports original translation and source-label evaluations, evaluator validation against human annotations, prompt and shot analyses, and context-attribution experiments, alongside corpus analyses (Sections 3–6; Appendices B–C).

before.justification: v1 reports original corpus statistics, word-frequency analyses, annotator agreement and measurements of variation among translators' neutralizations (Section 3). These qualify as empirical data analyses even though model evaluation is explicitly deferred.

arxiv_record.abstract: Guesstimation -- the task of making approximate quantitative estimates about objects or events -- is a common real-world skill, yet remains underexplored in large language model (LLM) research. We introduce three guesstimation datasets: MARBLES, FUTURE, and ELECPRED, spanning physical estimation (e.g., how many marbles fit in a cup) to abstract predictions (e.g., the 2024 U.S. presidential election). Inspired by the social science concept of Wisdom of Crowds (WOC)- where the median of multiple estimates improves accuracy-we propose WOC decoding for LLMs. We replicate WOC effects in human participants and find that LLMs exhibit similar benefits: median aggregation across sampled responses consistently improves accuracy over greedy decoding, self-consistency decoding, and mean decoding. This suggests that LLMs encode a world model that supports approximate reasoning. Our results position guesstimation as a useful probe of LLM world knowledge and highlight WOC decoding as a strategy for enhancing LLM guesstimation performance on real-world tasks.
arxiv_record.authors: Yun-Shiuan Chuang, Sameer Narendran, Nikunj Harlalka, Alexander Cheung, Sizhe Gao, Siddharth Suresh, Junjie Hu, Timothy T. Rogers
arxiv_record.title: Probing LLM World Models: Enhancing Guesstimation with Wisdom of Crowds Decoding

Inspired by the social science concept of Wisdom of Crowds (WOC)- where the median of multiple estimates improves accuracy-we propose WOC decoding for LLMs. We replicate WOC effects in human participants and find that LLMs exhibit similar benefits: median aggregation across sampled responses consistently improves accuracy over greedy decoding, self-consistency decoding, and mean decoding. This suggests that LLMs encode a world model that supports approximate reasoning. Our results position guesstimation as a useful probe of LLM world knowledge and highlight WOC decoding as a strategy for enhancing LLM guesstimation performance on real-world tasks.

C1.justification: v3 expands the central contribution from physical, verbal/multimodal guesstimation to concrete and abstract forecasting. It adds claims of superiority over mean decoding and greater sampling efficiency. The original claims about visual information improving human/VLM performance disappear, while the broader world-model-probing thesis remains.

C2.justification: v3 replaces much of the embodied-experience rationale with a 'crowd within' account of internal probabilistic variability. It adds interpretations concerning outliers, distributional robustness, and Democratic prediction bias, alongside substantive limitations about cultural generalization, unresolved mechanisms, and temporal contamination. The German experiment explicitly qualifies WOC's applicability.

D1.justification: The original MARBLES questions, answers, and prompt template are retained and relocated. v3 additionally documents forecasting ground truths and sources, election-history prompts, model cutoff dates, a separate numeric-extraction model, up to three parsing retries, manual extraction verification, and a two-A100 compute setup (Appendices F–K). These substantially expand reproducibility information.

E1.justification: v3 retains the 15 MARBLES questions but removes the multimodal human/VLM condition. It adds FUTURE's 15 quantitative forecasting questions, ELECPRED's 51 U.S. state/DC election predictions, and predictions for Germany's 16 federal states. These substantially change domain and input-condition coverage.

E2.justification: v1 compares WOC with mode-based self-consistency and greedy decoding. v3 retains these comparators and adds arithmetic-mean decoding in Tables 1–3, providing an additional direct comparison between median and mean aggregation.

E3.justification: The new forecasting experiments introduce historical numerical context, election-history prompts, and model-cutoff eligibility controls, including excluding Mixtral-8x22B from FUTURE. FUTURE also adds an instruction to guess when information is insufficient. The evaluated model roster drops Vicuna and LLaVA configurations. Both versions already plot sampling through 30 responses.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained sample-size analysis, v3 adds outlier and missing-majority case studies, election-map error analysis, correlations between response-distribution properties and WOC gains, and a German-election generalization test (Appendices B–E and J). The earlier visual-input comparison is removed.

E5.justification: v1 reports standard errors, including errors based on 30 resamplings. v3 adds paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across models for all three principal datasets (Appendix D), explicitly describes bootstrapping in Tables 2–3, and reports 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for Germany in Table 11. This adds formal inference without establishing increased independent run counts.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial forecasting and German-election results and removes multimodal and Vicuna entries. Existing MARBLES entries also change: Mistral-7B self-consistency error rises from 157.94 to 1154.61 while WOC remains 26.60; the reason for recomputation is unspecified. New results include inconsistent WOC superiority in Germany and cases favoring mean decoding, such as FUTURE's Mistral row.

M1.justification: WOC remains median aggregation of chain-of-thought responses sampled at temperature 1. The MARBLES prompting and two-step extraction template are retained from v1 Table 3 in v3 Table 8. Newly disclosed extractor and retry details do not establish a replacement of the underlying method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, results narrative, related work, and conclusion are substantially rewritten around text-only forecasting and the revised conceptual framing. Human procedures move to Appendix I, supporting material is reorganized into Appendices A–K, and dedicated limitations and ethics sections are added.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column layout and separates the earlier combined schematic/results figure into a revised schematic and a three-dataset plot. It adds election maps and multiple result/data/prompt tables, restructures Table 1 with a mean column, and reformats and relocates retained appendix tables.

R1.justification: v1 emphasizes VLM spatial reasoning, citing work such as SpatialVLM and SpatialRGPT. v3 replaces that positioning with expanded discussion of median robustness, the 'crowd within,' and prompting/self-consistency research, adding works by Vul and Pashler, Hora, Davis-Stober, Kojima, Nguyen, and Byerly. It also explicitly claims the first application of WOC decoding to LLM reasoning.

T1.justification: The median-based formulation and normalized absolute-error equation are retained. Neither version develops formal theorems or proofs. v3's distributional investigation is empirical, while its discussion of internal world models supplies conceptual interpretation rather than new mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v1's broad claims relied on one physical task family without a mean baseline or explicit generalization limits. v3 supplies a more demanding comparative evaluation, forecasting tests, formal statistical analysis, and an informative German-election failure case with substantive limitations. These substantially strengthen assessment of the proposal. Removing multimodal evidence narrows coverage, and claims of consistent superiority remain overstated—for example, FUTURE's Mistral mean error is 0.58 versus WOC's 0.61 in Table 2—but these shortcomings do not outweigh the improved evaluation and qualification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WOC guesstimation research and retain the MARBLES benchmark. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial changes in scope.

after.justification: v3 retains human and LLM MARBLES results and reports additional forecasting experiments, statistical analyses, and German-election results in Tables 2, 3, and 11.

before.justification: v1 reports original human and LLM/VLM guesstimation experiments, including decoding comparisons and verbal versus multimodal results in Table 1 and Figure 1.

arxiv_record.abstract: Sequence labeling remains a significant challenge in low-resource, domain-specific scenarios, particularly for character-dense languages like Chinese. Existing methods primarily focus on enhancing model comprehension and improving data diversity to boost performance. However, these approaches still struggle with inadequate model applicability and semantic distribution biases in domain-specific contexts. To overcome these limitations, we propose a novel framework that combines an LLM-based knowledge enhancement workflow with a span-based Knowledge Fusion for Rich and Efficient Extraction (KnowFREE) model. Our workflow employs explanation prompts to generate precise contextual interpretations of target entities, effectively mitigating semantic biases and enriching the model's contextual understanding. The KnowFREE model further integrates extension label features, enabling efficient nested entity extraction without relying on external knowledge during inference. Experiments on multiple Chinese domain-specific sequence labeling datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, effectively addressing the challenges posed by low-resource settings.
arxiv_record.authors: Peichao Lai, Jiaxin Gan, Feiyang Ye, Yilei Wang and Bin Cui
arxiv_record.title: Improving Low-Resource Sequence Labeling with Knowledge Fusion and Contextual Label Explanations

C1.justification: v3 broadens the empirical applicability claim beyond Chinese: the introduction explicitly includes English, and the abstract and conclusion remove the Chinese-only qualification. The central contributions—extension-label fusion, contextual explanation synthesis and inference without external features—remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v3 adds explanations of synthetic-data LoRA failures through spurious co-occurrence and non-target overprediction, discusses full-data applicability and attention-head computational tradeoffs, and emphasizes benefits from larger augmentation LLMs. Its dedicated Limitations section largely restates v1’s existing warning that synthetic-data noise can outweigh benefits as data increases.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-access link and substantially expands implementation documentation in Appendix H: separate learning rates of 2e-5 and 1e-3, dataset-specific weight decay and beta settings, Transformers implementation, and two NVIDIA A6000 GPUs. Existing encoder dimensions, clustering thresholds and attention defaults are relocated rather than newly introduced.

E1.justification: The eight Chinese datasets are retained. v3 adds English NER on CoNLL’03 and MIT-Movie, Japanese NER on Stockmark-NER, and Korean NER on Naver Changwon NER. These evaluations substantially broaden represented languages and domains.

E2.justification: v3 adds MELM and brings CNN Nested NER and DiFiNet into the few-shot comparison alongside LLM-DA and ProgGen. Appendix A adds Llama3-8B to zero-shot and LoRA comparisons, and Llama3.1-70B and DeepSeek-V3 to zero-shot comparisons. The conventional comparator set in Table 1 remains unchanged.

E3.justification: v3 adds full-dataset training, synthetic-data LoRA experiments, and Llama3.1-70B, GPT-4o and DeepSeek-V3 augmentation configurations. It reports beta=0.4 for several retained NER datasets versus v1’s uniform 1.0. The attention-head study changes its stated augmentation model from GLM3-6B to GLM4-9B-Chat and extends the tested configurations. These reported changes do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 Table 3 adds removal of both local attention and label extension, plus replacement of local attention with masked CNNs. Appendix D extends head-count sensitivity testing through 14 heads. Appendix A adds source-only versus synthetic-augmented LoRA comparisons and discusses overprediction errors. The earlier t-SNE and label-logit analyses are retained.

E5.justification: v3 Table 2 adds standard deviations alongside few-shot scores; v1 reports point estimates only. This is a limited uncertainty-reporting addition: neither version specifies repeated-run counts or seeds, and v3 does not establish an increase in repetitions.

E6.justification: v3 adds substantial few-shot, multilingual, full-data and LLM results. Eleven retained Table 1 entries also change; for example, GLM4 fusion-only Weibo at 1000 samples changes from 72.01 to 72.59. Conventional-baseline scores remain unchanged. Because loss settings are also revised, these numerical revisions do not establish controlled same-setting gains.

M1.justification: v1 specifies a fixed extension-label loss weight, alpha=0.13. v3 Appendix H introduces label-frequency-dependent weights, alpha_i=0.5*Cbar/C_i, changing the training-loss procedure. The two enhancement pipelines, biaffine/local-attention architecture and inference masking remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 extensively rewrites the introduction around model-centric and data-centric approaches, condenses the method exposition, and reorganizes results into many-shot and few-shot subsections. It moves the t-SNE analysis into the main text and training details into Appendix H, standardizes variant names, and adds Limitations and Ethics sections.

P2.justification: v3 adds a conceptual comparison as Figure 1, incorporates the earlier illustrative example into a substantially expanded Figure 2, and redraws Figure 3 to clarify inference masking. Table 1 changes from two dataset panels to one wide table, several result tables are added, and the retained t-SNE visualization moves into the main text.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion adds InstructUIE, UniversalNER and GoLLIE, while synonymous-label handling is connected to surface-form competition. Additional references support MELM, newer LLMs, datasets and implementation software. The central positioning relative to span-based labeling and LLM augmentation remains intact.

T1.justification: Appendix H introduces Equation 15, formally defining frequency-dependent extension-label weights absent from v1. The existing clustering, attention and loss mathematics otherwise remain equivalent or are condensed into prose. Neither version contains theorem or proof developments.

improvement.justification: The new attention-removal and CNN-replacement ablations directly test a contribution whose benefit v1 inferred mainly from comparisons between different models. Multilingual and full-data evaluations substantially strengthen evidence about applicability, while uncertainty reporting and implementation details improve assessability. These gains outweigh remaining reporting weaknesses: run counts are unspecified, and revised loss settings are not reconciled with retained scores.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same KnowFREE research framework. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial additions and reorganization.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical results and adds multilingual evaluations, full-dataset experiments, additional ablations and synthetic-data LoRA comparisons.

arxiv_record.abstract: This work presents a novel trie (prefix-tree)-based parallel decoding method that addresses the memory inefficiency of batch-based beam search. By sharing a single KV cache across beams with common prefixes, our approach dramatically reduces memory usage and enables efficient decoding. We evaluated our method across three attention architectures, Multi-Head Attention (Phi-3.5-mini-instruct), Grouped Query Attention (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), and Sliding Window Attention (Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct-2501), using CNN/DailyMail for abstractive summarization and HumanEval for code generation. Our experiments demonstrate substantial memory savings (4--8$\times$) and up to 2.4$\times$ faster decoding, without compromising generation quality. These results highlight our method's suitability for memory-constrained environments and large-scale deployments.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains memory-efficient beam search through shared-prefix caches. v2 explicitly qualifies theoretical equivalence by dense attention and changes the abstract's emphasis from preserving inference speed to quantified memory savings and faster decoding. These refine the retained contribution rather than introduce a new one.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive applicability limits involving sparse attention, insufficient prefix overlap and garbage-collection slowdowns for small workloads. It also interprets the separate roles of trie sharing and garbage collection, and discusses reasoning accuracy, sequence length and efficiency tradeoffs. v1 largely emphasizes general applicability and low overhead.

D1.justification: v2 specifies garbage-collection stages and torch.index_select, reports a one-shot setting and clarifies GPU allocation by model. The printed repository owner changes from SpeedReach to brian030128, while v1's commit-specific HuggingFace baseline link disappears. These are documentation and access-information changes, without establishing a different decoding implementation.

E1.justification: CNN/DailyMail summarization and HumanEval code generation remain, while QMSUM meeting summarization disappears. v2 adds MATH500 reasoning with chain-of-thought prompting and reports additional GSM8K and WMT evaluations in Appendix A, substantially revising task and dataset coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds top-k sampling comparisons on MATH500 with k=3 and HumanEval with k=50 in Appendix B. Figure 3 also adds a greedy reference to the memory trajectories. Conventional batched beam search remains the principal comparator.

E3.justification: The Phi-only evaluation expands to Llama 3.1 8B and Mistral-Small 24B, with a limited 70B experiment in Appendix A and model-specific beam widths. Table 1 now states means over 1,000 samples instead of v1's dataset-specific counts, although sampling is unexplained. New protocols include logits checked until first divergence and garbage-collection timing over 1,000 decoding steps.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's memory-trajectory analysis, v2 adds trie-versus-garbage-collection ablations, per-token fidelity checks, garbage-collection overhead measurements, an indirect prefix-overlap analysis and a code-generation error case study. These address component contributions, behavioral fidelity and practical efficiency.

E5.justification: v1 gives an unspecified quality-significance statement with p>0.05. v2 names paired t-tests and McNemar tests, adds confidence intervals and significance markers for efficiency differences, and reports ablation uncertainty and dispersion across appendix settings. Confidence levels, interval construction and repeated-run details remain unspecified; Section 4.2 also inconsistently associates nonsignificance with p<0.01.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces benchmark values under revised reported settings and removes QMSUM results. For example, the Phi/HumanEval beam-15 trie accuracy is 0.6768 in v1 and newly reported as 0.70 in v2, without establishing a same-setting improvement. v2 also adds substantial numerical evidence in Tables 2–4, Figure 4 and the fidelity analysis.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–3 retain the same shared-prefix KV cache, branch-specific masking, positional remapping and periodic garbage collection. v2's marking, pruning and compaction description elaborates the existing procedure; it does not establish a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract and results narrative are substantially rewritten. v1's combined results-and-discussion section becomes separate fidelity and efficiency sections followed by a structured discussion, explicit limitations and appendices. Method explanations are expanded, and title, author and affiliation text also change.

P2.justification: Table 1 is redesigned into side-by-side model comparisons with differences, uncertainty and gain columns. Figure 3 changes its panel organization and visual encoding. v2 adds three tables, a garbage-collection timing plot and a code-comparison figure; the original method illustrations remain with shortened captions.

R1.justification: The speculative-decoding discussion expands beyond SpecInfer to Medusa, staged speculative decoding and dynamic-width speculation, emphasizing global beam-search memory versus local sampling acceleration. v2 adds supporting references for sparse attention, nondeterminism, garbage collection and reasoning, while removing the earlier open-ended-generation discussion. The overall research positioning remains similar.

T1.justification: The algorithmic mathematics and memory-efficiency formula remain unchanged. v2 adds explanations of masking, periodic rebuilding and computational scaling, but no new formal definition, theorem, proof or derivation. Its dense-attention qualification concerns the scope of the equivalence claim.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens support for generality and implementation efficiency: v1's single-model demonstration gains multiple attention configurations, component ablations, fidelity diagnostics, overhead measurements and explicit failure conditions. These address important gaps in the original validation. QMSUM coverage is lost, and reporting problems remain: Section 4.3 claims a 2.42× Phi speedup where Table 1 reports 2.10×, and the 1,000-sample description is unexplained. These weaknesses limit confidence in individual summaries but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in validation and scope qualification.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same trie-based beam-search work and retain matching algorithms and core illustrations. Text, equations, tables and figures are readable throughout, including v2 Appendices A and B. v1 has no appendices.

after.justification: v2 reports original multi-model benchmark results, reasoning experiments, component ablations, fidelity checks and garbage-collection measurements, plus additional empirical results in both appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original Phi-3.5-mini experiments on CNN/DailyMail, QMSUM and HumanEval, measuring generation quality, memory consumption and throughput in Table 1 and Figure 3.

arxiv_record.abstract: The widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs) necessitates reliable methods to detect LLM-generated text. We introduce SimMark, a robust sentence-level watermarking algorithm that makes LLMs' outputs traceable without requiring access to model internals, making it compatible with both open and API-based LLMs. By leveraging the similarity of semantic sentence embeddings combined with rejection sampling to embed detectable statistical patterns imperceptible to humans, and employing a soft counting mechanism, SimMark achieves robustness against paraphrasing attacks. Experimental results demonstrate that SimMark sets a new benchmark for robust watermarking of LLM-generated content, surpassing prior sentence-level watermarking techniques in robustness, sampling efficiency, and applicability across diverse domains, all while maintaining the text quality and fluency.

C1.justification: The central claims about black-box compatibility, paraphrase robustness, quality preservation and sampling efficiency remain. v2 narrows the conclusion's superiority claim to sentence-level methods and removes v1's assertion that resistance to reverse engineering ensures resilience against spoofing.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for weaker detection on short texts, token-level advantages under merging, and the runtime–robustness tradeoff. Its limitations explicitly recognize spoofing through approximate reconstruction using public embeddings or PCA data, substantially qualifying v1's security interpretation. Existing overhead, mixed-text and interval limitations are retained.

D1.justification: v2 adds dataset split identifiers, model variants and sizes, MarkLLM configurations, the Transformers timing implementation, and participant instructions. It also documents settings for the new experiments. Existing hardware specifications, core hyperparameters, paraphrasing prompts and code-access link are largely retained.

E1.justification: RealNews, BookSum and Reddit-TIFU remain the datasets. v2 adds a sentence-merging attack scenario and a small human watermark-identification task, while removing the BookSum sentence-drop scenario shown in v1 Figure 3.

E2.justification: v2 adds UW across all three datasets in Table 1 and to the sentence-perturbation comparisons, adds SIR for Reddit-TIFU, and adds UW, KGW and SIR to text-quality Table 2. These additions substantially broaden comparisons, particularly against token-level methods.

E3.justification: New Gemma3-4B experiments use 300-token generations, different similarity intervals and a BookSum-calibrated threshold transferred across datasets. Budget-sweep, latency and human-study protocols are added. v2 specifies 10 GPT-3.5 bigram candidates versus v1's unqualified 25-candidate description; this revises the reported setting without establishing that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds merging-attack robustness, threshold-transfer testing, sampling-budget sensitivity, measured runtime and human imperceptibility analyses (Figure 4; Appendices D–F and M). The original soft-count and PCA ablations are retained unchanged as Tables 6–7. The BookSum sentence-drop analysis is removed.

E5.justification: Section 4 of v2 newly states that results are from a single run; v1 supplies no run count. This is a disclosure change, with no added confidence intervals, repeated-run variability or significance tests.

E6.justification: All 16 shared Table 1 rows remain numerically unchanged, but v2 adds baseline, Gemma, merging, budget, latency and human-study results. Table 2 revises semantic entropy, including unwatermarked text from 3.10 to 3.32 and SemStamp from 3.17 to 3.32. The separate Euclidean text-quality row and BookSum sentence-drop results are removed.

M1.justification: The rejection-sampling procedure, consecutive-sentence similarity measures, optional PCA, soft counting and detection statistic remain unchanged. The revised black-box description and additional model configurations do not introduce a new algorithmic component.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the document: future work becomes a main limitations section, portions of related work and experimental settings move into appendices, and supplementary sections are rearranged. The introduction, method exposition and discussion are extensively edited, including replacing the posthoc characterization with black-box generation language.

P2.justification: The document adopts an EMNLP layout and adds radar summaries, a sampling-budget figure, Gemma, latency and human-study tables, and a participant-instruction image. The attack figure replaces its BookSum panel with RealNews merging results and adds UW. Existing examples and ablation displays are relocated and renumbered.

R1.justification: New Appendix A.2 substantially expands positioning against post-hoc watermarking through PostMark, Yang et al. and Hao et al., discussing access requirements, cost, quality and robustness. Additional contextual and implementation references are introduced. SemStamp's publication update is the same cited work, not a new comparator.

T1.justification: The soft-count and z-score equations, histogram estimate of p0, and geometric sampling calculation remain unchanged. v2 Appendix G's theoretical analysis retains v1's derivation of approximately 5.1 samples from probability 0.194.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's single-model validation and sampling-count-based efficiency evidence through Gemma tests, stronger baseline and attack comparisons, and measured runtime costs. It also replaces an unsupported spoofing-resilience assurance with explicit limitations. Single-run evidence and the three-person human study remain limited, and BookSum drop-attack and separate Euclidean quality results are removed. Nevertheless, the broader validation and clearer practical boundaries substantially improve the paper's evidential support.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SimMark by the same authors. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching across the revision.

after.justification: v2 retains original SimMark experiments and adds Gemma3-4B evaluations, merging attacks, sampling-budget and latency experiments, and a human study.

before.justification: v1 reports original SimMark detection, text-quality, sentence-drop and ablation results, alongside comparisons drawn from prior work.

arxiv_record.abstract: The prototyping of computer games, particularly card games, requires extensive human effort in creative ideation and gameplay evaluation. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer opportunities to automate and streamline these processes. However, it remains challenging for LLMs to design novel game mechanics beyond existing databases, generate consistent gameplay environments, and develop scalable gameplay AI for large-scale evaluations. This paper addresses these challenges by introducing a comprehensive automated card game prototyping framework. The approach highlights a graph-based indexing method for generating novel game variations, an LLM-driven system for consistent game code generation validated by gameplay records, and a gameplay AI constructing method that uses an ensemble of LLM-generated heuristic functions optimized through self-play. These contributions aim to accelerate card game prototyping, reduce human labor, and lower barriers to entry for game developers. For code repo visit this http URL https://github.com/danruili/Cardiverse

      <pages>29735-29762</pages>
      <abstract>The prototyping of computer games, particularly card games, requires extensive human effort in creative ideation and gameplay evaluation. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer opportunities to automate and streamline these processes. However, it remains challenging for LLMs to design novel game mechanics beyond existing databases, generate consistent gameplay environments, and develop scalable gameplay AI for large-scale evaluations. This paper addresses these challenges by introducing a comprehensive automated card game prototyping framework. The approach highlights a graph-based indexing method for generating novel game variations, an LLM-driven system for consistent game code generation validated by gameplay records, and a gameplay AI constructing method that uses an ensemble of LLM-generated action-value functions optimized through self-play. These contributions aim to accelerate card game prototyping, reduce human labor, and lower barriers to entry for game developers.</abstract>
