C1.justification: Both versions claim the same three contributions: graph-supported novel mechanics, gameplay-validated code generation, and scalable gameplay AI without per-decision LLM calls. The emphasis on game variations clarifies the mutation-based task already described in v1; the additional evaluations support rather than redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 retains earlier caveats about mechanic conflicts, validation cost, and missing opponent-intention modeling. It adds substantive boundaries concerning small controlled variations, detailed human inputs, scaling to other genres, clustering cost, weaker-model code generation, and embedding-metric precision. It also interprets the new sensitivity plateau and subjective design evaluations.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link and identifies the card-description source. It newly specifies UPGMA clustering, n=4 policy generation, 400 games per selection evaluation, three code-generation attempts, explicit sampling defaults, and five-turn baseline histories. These materially improve reproducibility documentation without establishing changes to the previously used implementation.

E1.justification: The original 106-game collection and principal evaluation sets remain. v2 adds human evaluation of Go Fish variants, gameplay comparisons on Leduc Hold'em and Uno, and consistency-evaluation scenarios using deliberately mismatched game descriptions. These introduce substantive new evaluation tasks and conditions beyond the retained benchmarks.

E2.justification: The existing novelty baselines, code-generation ablations, and CoT, ReAct, Reflexion, and Belief agents remain. Appendix C.1 newly evaluates human-designed RLCard heuristics on two games, adding a limited non-LLM comparison outside the retained main gameplay benchmark.

E3.justification: New protocols include five-point ratings of nine summaries per participant, consistency checks using five verified games with five records each and descriptions at 95% or 70% embedding similarity, gameplay comparisons across player orderings, and a policy-population sweep over n=2, 4, and 6. These substantially extend the evaluation design.

E4.justification: v1 already contains ensemble and optimization ablations. v2 adds controlled validation of the PCon judge in Appendix B.4, policy-population sensitivity in C.3, and further graph and generated-game case studies in Appendix A. These address metric validity, parameter sensitivity, and qualitative behavior beyond the original analyses.

E5.justification: Beyond the retained means, standard deviations, and paired t-tests, v2 introduces mixed-effects estimates with standard errors, z-tests, and confidence intervals for human ratings, chi-square tests for heuristic comparisons, and standard-error shading for PCon. It also newly discloses 50 runs per game for ablations; this does not establish an increase in runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1 and 2 retain their point estimates, but gameplay and ablation entries change. For example, Table 3 changes the proposed method's varied-game advantage from 12.5±24.8 to 19.7±30.5 while retaining its overall 16.3±22.6. v2 also adds human-rating, PCon-validation, heuristic-comparison, and sensitivity results. The revised existing scores are not explained as an algorithmic improvement.

M1.justification: The graph-based variation pipeline, gameplay-record code validation, and self-play-selected heuristic ensemble remain substantively the same. v2 expands implementation details and replaces Q-function terminology with heuristic functions. The strategy, metric, and refinement prompts already appear in v1 Section 9; their fuller explanation does not establish a new algorithm.

P1.justification: The introduction, mechanics-related work, and gameplay-AI explanation are substantially rewritten. Code-generation details move into Appendix B, limitations receive a dedicated main-text section, and supplementary material is reorganized into Appendices A–E with a contents list. Terminology changes accompany this broader narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: v2 adds an overall pipeline figure, merges and redraws the mechanics diagrams, and redraws the gameplay-AI and code-generation workflows. Table 2 becomes separate common/varied panels, and new study tables and a PCon plot appear. Existing embedding panels and gameplay radar plots are relocated, while additional explicit mechanic graphs are introduced.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially repositions the work within P-creativity and existing mechanic-recombination research, replacing v1's stronger assertions about missing hierarchical representations. Genuine additions include Conceptual Game Expansion, Chaos Cards, Mechanic Maker, and broader LLM design research. The Large Concept Models connection is removed; publication updates to retained references are not new works.

T1.justification: The policy-averaging, QMS, and win-advantage equations remain mathematically equivalent, with no new proofs. The new limitations discussion adds a brief complexity comparison: O(n^3) for the clustering implementation versus a proposed O(n) Gaussian-mixture alternative.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's reliance on embedding similarity for design evaluation and unvalidated LLM consistency scores through human ratings and controlled PCon checks. Additional AI analyses, clearer implementation details, and better-qualified positioning strengthen support and reproducibility. The user study remains limited to Go Fish summaries, and duplicated matchup labels in Table 6 plus unexplained score revisions weaken reporting clarity, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Cardiverse and retain identifiable methods and experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete supplementary sections support reliable comparison, including material relocated between the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds human ratings, consistency-metric validation, heuristic-opponent comparisons, and policy-pool sensitivity results.

before.justification: v1 reports original game-design, code-generation, and gameplay-AI evaluations, plus component ablations, in Sections 4 and 8.

arxiv_record.abstract: Recent progress in large language models (LLMs) has enabled the automated processing of lengthy documents even without supervised training on a task-specific dataset. Yet, their zero-shot performance in complex tasks as opposed to straightforward information extraction tasks remains suboptimal. One feasible approach for tasks with lengthy, complex input is to first summarize the document and then apply supervised fine-tuning to the summary. However, the summarization process inevitably results in some loss of information. In this study we present a method for processing the summaries of long documents aimed to capture different important aspects of the original document. We hypothesize that LLM summaries generated with different aspect-oriented prompts contain different information signals, and we propose methods to measure these differences. We introduce approaches to effectively integrate signals from these different summaries for supervised training of transformer models. We validate our hypotheses on a high-impact task -- 30-day readmission prediction from a psychiatric discharge -- using real-world data from four hospitals, and show that our proposed method increases the prediction performance for the complex task of predicting patient outcome.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: aspect-specific summaries contain different signals, prediction comparisons can measure those differences, and integrating summaries can improve downstream prediction. The additional baselines provide support without redefining these contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations for weak full-note baselines, including limited data, possible overfitting or distribution mismatch, and input truncation. It also discusses hallucination propagation through the summarization pipeline and distinguishes short-term from long-term outcome prediction in Appendix J. These extend the qualifications around the retained central interpretations.

D1.justification: V1 provides model, library, and hardware information but omits essential training hyperparameters. V2 adds the learning-rate/epoch search, final learning rate 2e-5, 40 epochs, batch size 8, development-loss checkpoint selection, and CNLPT version 0.7.0. It also documents the new Qwen experiments' LoRA rank 12, q_proj/v_proj targets, and training duration. This substantially improves implementation documentation.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same four hospital datasets, patient eligibility criteria, and 30-day readmission task. Table 1 is unchanged. Appendix J's discussion of long-term outcomes introduces no evaluated task or population.

E2.justification: V2 substantially expands supervised full-note comparisons by adding LoRA-tuned Qwen-2.5-0.5B-Instruct and Qwen3-0.6B in Table 3, and a hierarchical transformer in Table 7. Section 5.3 also reports an unsuccessful raw-note Clinical Longformer experiment; its previously reported evaluations used summaries. Existing comparators are retained.

E3.justification: The added experiments introduce 10-epoch LoRA training on full notes with development/test evaluation, and a raw-note Clinical Longformer trial using the first 4k tokens. Existing splits, metrics, and the 0.5 classification threshold remain unchanged. Newly disclosed settings for retained experiments do not establish that their protocols changed.

E4.justification: Appendix B and Figure 6 add a limited qualitative case showing the different content produced by three prompts for one psychiatric note. Existing information-distance, summary-integration, and prediction-distribution analyses are retained. The new hallucination discussion supplies no empirical hallucination test.

E5.justification: Appendix D.1 newly specifies sequential seeds starting at zero, including 0–4 for BiomedBERT, and Appendix C explicitly identifies the Qwen results as single-run. Previously reported repetition counts and Table 4's standard deviations are retained; there is no documented increase in runs or new significance testing.

E6.justification: V2 adds development/test results for both Qwen baselines and hierarchical-transformer scores across all four hospitals. For example, Table 3 reports Qwen-2.5's MGH test AUROC as 0.6109, and Table 7 reports hierarchical-transformer McLean AUROC as 0.5346. These substantially extend the reported baseline evidence. Matched original performance tables, including the relocated zero-shot results, remain numerically unchanged.

M1.justification: The proposed pipeline retains the same three summarization prompts, information-distance approach, merged and union datasets, and soft/any voting procedures. The added Qwen and hierarchical-transformer models are comparison methods, rather than new components of the proposed method.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative sequence are retained. V2 inserts related-work and discussion subsections, reorganizes appendix headings, shortens the zero-shot introduction, and makes local terminology, author-contact, and wording corrections. The revision principally adds material rather than extensively rewriting the existing account.

P2.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the displays: it splits the prompt figure between main text and appendix, relocates the zero-shot table and prediction-distribution plots, revises the Venn diagram's labels and sizing, and reformats appendix text into two columns. New displays include the sample summaries and two full-note baseline tables. Retained result displays preserve their underlying findings.

R1.justification: V2 adds a substantial Related Work section covering prompt tuning, dynamic prompting, self-consistency, aspect-oriented summarization, clinical summarization, and patient outcome prediction. It explicitly positions measuring and combining complementary prompt signals relative to prompt-selection approaches, considerably expanding the earlier version's research context.

T1.justification: Section 3.2.1 corrects the concordant-pair definition: when R1_i > R1_j, v1 incorrectly requires R2_i < R2_j, whereas v2 correctly requires R2_i > R2_j. The distance, dataset averaging, and integration equations otherwise retain their mathematical content.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important gaps in reproducibility and comparative evaluation: Appendix D.1 supplies the previously missing training and checkpoint-selection recipe, while Tables 3 and 7 add supervised neural full-note alternatives to assess the summarization rationale. The corrected concordance definition and substantially expanded research positioning further improve assessability. The Qwen comparisons remain single-run and provide limited evidence for general claims about full-document modeling, but this limitation does not outweigh the substantial documentation and evaluation gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same aspect-oriented summarization study for psychiatric readmission prediction. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

after.justification: V2 retains those original empirical results and additionally reports supervised full-note experiments with Qwen models and a hierarchical transformer.

before.justification: V1 reports original four-hospital experiments, including readmission prediction scores, repeated-training statistics, and comparisons of information signals across summary types.

arxiv_record.abstract: Vision tokens in multimodal large language models often dominate huge computational overhead due to their excessive length compared to linguistic modality. Abundant recent methods aim to solve this problem with token pruning, which first defines an importance criterion for tokens and then prunes the unimportant vision tokens during inference. However, in this paper, we show that the importance is not an ideal indicator to decide whether a token should be pruned. Surprisingly, it usually results in inferior performance than random token pruning and leading to incompatibility to efficient attention computation operators.Instead, we propose DART (Duplication-Aware Reduction of Tokens), which prunes tokens based on its duplication with other tokens, leading to significant and training-free acceleration. Concretely, DART selects a small subset of pivot tokens and then retains the tokens with low duplication to the pivots, ensuring minimal information loss during token pruning. Experiments demonstrate that DART can prune 88.9% vision tokens while maintaining comparable performance, leading to a 1.99$\times$ and 2.99$\times$ speed-up in total time and prefilling stage, respectively, with good compatibility to efficient attention operators. Our codes are available at https://github.com/ZichenWen1/DART.
arxiv_record.authors: Zichen Wen, Yifeng Gao, Shaobo Wang, Junyuan Zhang, Qintong Zhang, Weijia Li, Conghui He, Linfeng Zhang
arxiv_record.title: Stop Looking for Important Tokens in Multimodal Language Models: Duplication Matters More

      <abstract>Vision tokens in multimodal large language models often dominate huge computational overhead due to their excessive length compared to linguistic modality. Abundant recent methods aim to solve this problem with token pruning, which first defines an importance criterion for tokens and then prunes the unimportant vision tokens during inference. However, in this paper, we show that the importance is not an ideal indicator to decide whether a token should be pruned. Surprisingly, it usually results in inferior performance than random token pruning and leading to incompatibility to efficient attention computation operators. Instead, we propose DART (Duplication-Aware Reduction of Tokens), which prunes tokens based on its duplication with other tokens, leading to significant and training-free acceleration. Concretely, DART selects a small subset of pivot tokens and then retains the tokens with low duplication to the pivots, ensuring minimal information loss during token pruning. Experiments demonstrate that DART can prune 88.9% vision tokens while maintaining comparable performance, leading to a 1.99<tex-math>\times</tex-math> and 2.99<tex-math>\times</tex-math> speed-up in total time and prefilling stage, respectively, with good compatibility to efficient attention operators.</abstract>

arxiv_record.abstract: With the different roles that AI is expected to play in human life, imbuing large language models (LLMs) with different personalities has attracted increasing research interests. While the "personification" enhances human experiences of interactivity and adaptability of LLMs, it gives rise to critical concerns about content safety, particularly regarding bias, sentiment and toxicity of LLM generation. This study explores how assigning different personality traits to LLMs affects the toxicity and biases of their outputs. Leveraging the widely accepted HEXACO personality framework developed in social psychology, we design experimentally sound prompts to test three LLMs' performance on three toxic and bias benchmarks. The findings demonstrate the sensitivity of all three models to HEXACO personality traits and, more importantly, a consistent variation in the biases, negative sentiment and toxicity of their output. In particular, adjusting the levels of several personality traits can effectively reduce bias and toxicity in model performance, similar to humans' correlations between personality traits and toxic behaviors. The findings highlight the additional need to examine content safety besides the efficiency of training or fine-tuning methods for LLM personification. They also suggest a potential for the adjustment of personalities to be a simple and low-cost method to conduct controlled text generation.
arxiv_record.authors: Shuo Wang and Renhao Li and Xi Chen and Yulin Yuan and Derek F. Wong and Min Yang
arxiv_record.title: Exploring the Impact of Personality Traits on LLM Bias and Toxicity

arxiv_record.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are capable of generating coherent summaries from very long contexts given a user query, and extracting and citing evidence spans helps improve the trustworthiness of these summaries. Whereas previous work has focused on evidence citation with fixed levels of granularity (e.g. sentence, paragraph, document, etc.), we propose to extract unstructured (i.e., spans of any length) evidence in order to acquire more relevant and consistent evidence than in the fixed granularity case. We show how existing systems struggle to copy and properly cite unstructured evidence, which also tends to be "lost-in-the-middle". To help models perform this task, we create the Summaries with Unstructured Evidence Text dataset (SUnsET), a synthetic dataset generated using a novel pipeline, which can be used as training supervision for unstructured evidence summarization. We demonstrate across 5 LLMs and 4 datasets spanning human written, synthetic, single, and multi-document settings that LLMs adapted with SUnsET generate more relevant and factually consistent evidence with their summaries, extract evidence from more diverse locations in their context, and can generate more relevant and consistent summaries than baselines with no fine-tuning and fixed granularity evidence. We release SUnsET and our generation code to the public.
arxiv_record.authors: Dustin Wright, Zain Muhammad Mujahid, Lu Wang, Isabelle Augenstein, and David Jurgens
arxiv_record.title: Unstructured Evidence Attribution for Long Context Query Focused Summarization

metadata.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are capable of generating coherent summaries from very long contexts given a user query, and extracting and citing evidence spans helps improve the trustworthiness of these summaries. Whereas previous work has focused on evidence citation with fixed levels of granularity (e.g. sentence, paragraph, document, etc.), we propose to extract unstructured (i.e., spans of any length) evidence in order to acquire more relevant and consistent evidence than in the fixed granularity case. We show how existing systems struggle to copy and properly cite unstructured evidence, which also tends to be “lost-in-the-middle”. To help models perform this task, we create the Summaries with Unstructured Evidence Text dataset (SUnsET), a synthetic dataset generated using a novel pipeline, which can be used as training supervision for unstructured evidence summarization. We demonstrate across 5 LLMs and 4 datasets spanning human written, synthetic, single, and multi-document settings that LLMs adapted with SUnsET generate more relevant and factually consistent evidence with their summaries, extract evidence from more diverse locations in their context, and can generate more relevant and consistent summaries than baselines with no fine-tuning and fixed granularity evidence. We release SUnsET and our generation code to the public (https://github.com/dwright37/unstructured-evidence-sunset).

C1.justification: v2 adds a central claim that unstructured evidence, especially after SUnsET training, outperforms fixed-granularity evidence, extending v1's claims about improvements over untuned models. The introduction also adds claims of high synthetic-data quality and diversity comparable to human-written data. The original task, dataset, and positional-bias contributions remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations of citation quality versus coverage and why selecting evidence before summarization may improve summaries. It revises the positional-bias interpretation: standard training can reduce bias, and shuffled training has an explicit Mixtral exception. It also explains training-size plateaus through distribution coverage and adds a limitation concerning differences between synthetic and human-written text.

D1.justification: v2 documents topic-model parameters, DeepSeek-V3 sampling settings, and approximately $200 in generation costs. It omits v1's 200-document validation/early-stopping holdout and five-attempt formatting retry rule, without establishing that those procedures changed. Training hyperparameters, hardware, model identifiers, prompts, and the public MIT-licensed code/data release are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use SUnsET and the same four downstream datasets: SQuALITY, LexAbSumm, SummHay, and ScholarQABench. Their single-document, multi-document, literary, legal, scientific, and synthetic coverage remains unchanged. The added validation analyses reuse these data.

E2.justification: v2 adds an evaluated Fixed Gran. comparator for each of the five open LLMs across the four datasets, substantially expanding the central comparisons beyond unstructured base models and GPT-4o-mini. The earlier synthetic-generation baselines are retained under the names Non-Pipelined and Title + Doc.

E3.justification: The main relevance and consistency evaluator changes from GPT-4o-mini to DeepSeek-V3. v2 also introduces a two-annotator, 100-example assessment using three-point ratings and an LDA-based topic-diversity evaluation. Section 4.1 changes the stated precision averaging unit from citing sentences to citations. These changes materially affect evaluation.

E4.justification: v2 adds human validation of summary responsiveness, organization, and evidential support; topic-diversity comparisons with human-written corpora; and correlations between citation and summary quality. The training-size ablations move from v1 Figures 6–7 to v2 Figures 23–24. The existing 710-summary cross-evaluator correlation check is retained.

E5.justification: v2 extends significance annotations to evidence quality and citation F1, explicitly using non-overlapping 95% confidence intervals against both baselines. v1 specifies bootstrapped intervals for summary comparisons, whereas v2 omits the interval-construction method. v2 also reports human annotator agreement of 93.67%; neither version specifies repeated training runs or random seeds.

E6.justification: Citation F1 and summary-quality scores are extensively replaced, and fixed-granularity, separate precision/recall, and validation results are added. For example, Llama 3.1 8B with standard training has SQuALITY relevance F1 of 35.21 in v1 Table 3 and 27.69 in v2 Table 6; the changed evaluator and metric specification prevent interpreting this as a same-setting decline. Evidence-copy results remain identical in v1 Table 2 and v2 Table 3.

M1.justification: The six-stage generation pipeline, standard and shuffled LoRA training, and chunk-summarize-combine inference are retained. Appendix A's generation, training, and inference prompts match. Renaming Standard to SUnsET does not introduce a method component; omitted procedural details are assessed under D1.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten, an explicit contribution list is added, and the experimental narrative is reorganized around fixed-granularity comparisons and aggregate results. Dataset-specific discussion and training-size analysis are reorganized into appendices. This is extensive narrative restructuring despite the retained method and prompts.

P2.justification: v2 redraws Figure 1, adds the fixed-versus-unstructured example and topic-diversity table, and introduces aggregate bar charts with expanded appendix tables. Evidence-position histograms are merged and redrawn as density curves, omitting the former 1B panel. Training-size plots are relocated unchanged, and Table 1 is compacted by removing title columns.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted references on summary-source alignment, citation planning, precise evidence, and topic diversity, including Ernst, Fierro, Wan, Xiao, and Terragni. Several general motivation and evaluation references disappear. The MDCure publication update and Sentence-BERT bibliographic correction concern already-cited works, rather than new research coverage.

T1.justification: Section 4.1 revises the stated precision definition from averaging over citances, meaning citing sentences, to averaging over citations. These differ when a sentence contains multiple citations. This is a limited mathematical specification change; no theorems or proofs are added.

improvement.justification: The fixed-granularity comparisons and independent human assessment of SUnsET address important gaps in v1's support for its central formulation and synthetic training data. Topic-diversity analysis and separate citation precision/recall results further strengthen that support. Omitted validation/retry details and less explicit confidence-interval methodology weaken reproducibility, but the gains in evaluating the central claims are substantial overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SUnsET research. Their text, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching renamed methods and relocated analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds fixed-granularity comparisons, human assessment of SUnsET, topic-diversity measurements, and citation-summary correlations.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-data analyses, citation and summary evaluations, positional-bias measurements, and training-size experiments.

arxiv_record.abstract: Text embeddings are a fundamental component in many NLP tasks, including classification, regression, clustering, and semantic search. However, despite their ubiquitous application, challenges persist in interpreting embeddings and explaining similarities between them. In this work, we provide a structured overview of methods specializing in inherently interpretable text embeddings and text similarity explanation, an underexplored research area. We characterize the main ideas, approaches, and trade-offs. We compare means of evaluation, discuss overarching lessons learned and finally identify opportunities and open challenges for future research.

C1.justification: V1 presents a three-family primer centered on similarity explanations. V2 broadens the stated contribution to a taxonomy of inherently interpretable embeddings and post-hoc explanations, evaluation synthesis and overarching lessons. Its concluding Perspective additionally argues that most surveyed approaches transfer to decoder-derived embedding models.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands discussion of explanation evaluation, surrogate-model limitations, context-dependent similarity, RAG explanations and applicability to modern embedding models. Its limitations newly acknowledge outdated evaluated models. Conversely, it removes v1's specific warning about misleading contextualized-token alignments and its caution against comparing methods through isolated examples.

D1.justification: Appendix Table 1 adds code-resource links and replaces Sun et al.'s link, which previously pointed to Benara et al.'s repository. However, v2 removes the per-method inference-cost column and Figure 4's explicit N=50 integration steps. These change available technical documentation without establishing altered underlying methods.

E1.justification: The same sentence pairs remain in the three model-output examples. Newly discussed resources, including sentence-relation datasets and Sentence Smith, expand the literature coverage; the survey does not report evaluating models on these additional datasets.

E2.justification: Neither version reports a controlled comparison against a proposed method. Table 1 categorizes surveyed approaches rather than evaluating baselines, and the retained illustrative examples do not constitute a comparative benchmark.

E3.justification: No revised experimental protocol is stated for the retained examples. V2's evaluation section describes procedures used by cited studies. Removing Figure 4's integration-step count reduces documentation but does not establish a changed computation setting.

E4.justification: Figure 4 revises the token-attribution evidence in the case study explaining similarity between the same two sentences. The S3BERT and ColBERT examples remain unchanged. Newly discussed probing and perturbation tests summarize prior research rather than introduce systematic analyses performed by this survey.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals or significance-testing procedures for its illustrative computations. Figure 4's retained attribution error of 0.001 measures approximation error, not statistical uncertainty.

E6.justification: Figures 2–3 retain their results, including similarities 0.76 and 0.965. Figure 4 retains similarity 0.618 and error 0.001 but changes individual attributions, including the beer/EOS interaction's sign. V2 also adds cited qualitative outcomes, such as anchor features approaching reference-model accuracy; these are not new controlled performance gains.

M1.justification: Neither version introduces a new algorithm or model. Newly covered methods are attributed to existing research. Figure 4's change from IG to IJ corrects the name of Integrated Jacobians, which v1 already describes in Section 5.2.1.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method descriptions, discussion and limitations undergo extensive rewriting. Three standalone method families become a hierarchy under Interpretable Embeddings and Post-hoc Explanation; evaluation receives a dedicated section, and the former conclusion becomes an expanded Perspective. Title and authorship details also change.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is comprehensively redrawn around the expanded taxonomy. Table 1 is reorganized into hierarchical groups, expanded, moved to Appendix A and stripped of its inference-cost column. Figure 4 is replotted with revised axis labels and caption; Figures 2–3 retain their plotted results with placement or caption edits.

R1.justification: V2 integrates substantial additional literature on anchors, sparsification, global explanations and surrogate/probing methods, including SPLADE and Conneau's probing work. Some references disappear, including Zhang et al. (2020), despite BERTScore remaining discussed. Sun and Fodor publication-year updates represent retained works rather than new additions.

T1.justification: V2 Section 3.3 corrects the box-containment condition: o(a,b)/s_b equals 1 when b is contained in a, whereas v1 Section 3.2.2 reverses that relationship. Other mathematical descriptions are shortened, including the explicit exact-IJ guarantee. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 fills substantial gaps in the survey's coverage through sparse embeddings, global explanations and surrogate/probing methods. Its clearer taxonomy and new Section 5.1 explain how explanation quality is evaluated and why comparisons are difficult, substantially improving its usefulness as a survey. These gains outweigh the loss of specific alignment caveats, Figure 4 computation details and the BERTScore source citation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same survey despite substantial restructuring and the subtitle change from Primer to Survey. All pages, figures, equations and references are readable. V2's Appendix A contains an expanded version of v1's main-text Table 1.

after.justification: V2 retains the numerical model-output examples in Figures 2–4 and presents a revised interaction-attribution matrix in Figure 4. These illustrative computations qualify as empirical results, although the broader experimental findings discussed throughout the survey are attributed to prior work.

before.justification: Although primarily a survey, v1 reports computed sentence-pair examples in Figures 2–4, including ColBERTv2 similarity 0.965 and interaction attributions with similarity 0.618 and error 0.001. Its limitations describe selecting these examples for the paper; they constitute small illustrative empirical analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: Connecting audio encoders with large language models (LLMs) allows the LLM to perform various audio understanding tasks, such as automatic speech recognition (ASR) and audio captioning (AC). Most research focuses on training an adapter layer to generate a unified audio feature for the LLM. However, different tasks may require distinct features that emphasize either semantic or acoustic aspects, making task-specific audio features more desirable. In this paper, we propose Prompt-aware Mixture (PaM) to enhance the Speech LLM that uses multiple audio encoders. Our approach involves using different experts to extract different features based on the prompt that indicates different tasks. Experiments demonstrate that with PaM, only one Speech LLM surpasses the best performances achieved by all single-encoder Speech LLMs on ASR, Speaker Number Verification, and AC tasks. PaM also outperforms other feature fusion baselines, such as concatenation and averaging. Our code would be available at: https://github.com/shanweiqiao/PaM

      <abstract>Connecting audio encoders with large language models (LLMs) allows the LLM to perform various audio understanding tasks, such as automatic speech recognition (ASR) and audio captioning (AC). Most research focuses on training an adapter layer to generate a unified audio feature for the LLM. However, different tasks may require distinct features that emphasize either semantic or acoustic aspects, making task-specific audio features more desirable. In this paper, we propose Prompt-aware Mixture (PaM) to enhance the Speech LLM that uses multiple audio encoders. Our approach involves using different experts to extract different features based on the prompt that indicates different tasks. Experiments demonstrate that with PaM, only one Speech LLM surpasses the best performances achieved by all single-encoder Speech LLMs on ASR, speaker number verification, and AC tasks. PaM also outperforms other feature fusion baselines, such as concatenation and averaging.</abstract>

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the central prompt-aware fusion and multitask-performance claims. The introduction newly makes an explicit performance claim that audio-only routing produces suboptimal results, referencing Table 11, whereas v1 only identifies its lack of prompt conditioning.

C2.justification: Appendices A.7–A.9 add substantive interpretations of backbone-dependent concatenation failures, task-specific shared-expert tradeoffs, and feature mismatch when initializing from multimodal LLMs. Section 5 also replaces v1's asserted applicability to unseen tasks with a proposal requiring future validation.

D1.justification: v2 adds a planned code-repository address, caption-evaluation tool and model details, and an explicit model-loading workaround in A.4. Section 4.5 newly specifies activated and per-expert parameter counts, and A.11 supplies more prompt examples. Existing training hyperparameters are relocated without substantive changes.

E1.justification: The audio datasets and ASR, SNV, and captioning tasks remain unchanged. Appendix A.11 adds evaluation of previously unseen ASR prompt wording, extending coverage to a distinct instruction-input condition.

E2.justification: Table 11 introduces an evaluated audio-based MoE routing comparator, directly testing the central prompt-routing choice. Table 10 also adds WavLLM comparisons within the previously reported Qwen2.5-7B and LLaMA3.1-8B settings. The original main-table comparator set remains intact.

E3.justification: New evaluation protocols include FENSE, Sentence-BERT, CIDEr, and SPICE for captioning; a four-encoder BEATs configuration; controlled routing variants; and router evaluation on 200 ASR prompts, including 150 unseen prompts. The original training schedule, LoRA settings, and decoding procedure are retained in Appendix A.6.

E4.justification: Table 11 adds audio-based routing, one-expert, no-shared-expert, and no-task-label comparisons. Appendix A.9 adds cross-encoder feature-similarity analysis, and A.11 tests unseen-prompt routing. BEATs and larger-LLM comparisons further extend the existing configuration analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, variability estimates, or significance tests. Average ranks and averages across encoder combinations do not constitute run-to-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The retained result tables match numerically after renumbering and formatting changes. Substantial new results cover additional metrics, BEATs, larger-LLM baselines, routing ablations, and feature similarity. For example, Table 8 reports BEATs-variant SNV accuracy of 49.2% versus 42.8%, alongside worse AMI WER of 13.11 versus 12.79. These compare configurations, not improved reruns of the original model.

M1.justification: The adopted PaM procedure retains multi-layer feature fusion, a shared expert plus one prompt-selected expert, and the same training losses. BEATs and alternative routing configurations are additional experiments within this framework. Revised indexing does not establish a changed implementation.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the prose remain intact. v2 edits terminology and fusion explanations, rewrites the discussion, condenses related work, and moves prompt examples, dataset details, and training settings into reorganized appendix subsections.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial experimental displays in Tables 7–12 and prompt tables 14–16. Figure 2 gains explicit feature, routing, and FFN labels; Figure 1's caption and Figure 4's direction labels are revised. Existing tables and Figure 3 are also relocated or renumbered.

R1.justification: v2 adds Soundwave and references concerning multimodal models, task-level routing, initialization, and decoding efficiency. It removes some general scaling background citations. These extend the context while retaining the core positioning around task-specific multi-encoder fusion.

T1.justification: Section 2.2 revises the formal layer-state definitions, summation bounds, and fusion-matrix dimensions in Equations 4–6, including changing the stated matrix shape from 3 × (L1 + L2 + L3) to K × sum(Li − 1). No theorem or proof is added; inconsistencies between the prose and summation indices remain.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important evidential gap: Table 11 directly tests prompt routing, task supervision, and shared experts, whose contributions v1 did not isolate. Additional metrics and backbone comparisons strengthen evaluation and expose meaningful limitations. These gains substantially improve the empirical justification despite remaining equation/editorial inconsistencies and the continued absence of run-to-run uncertainty.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PaM study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds captioning metrics, routing ablations, encoder and backbone comparisons, feature-similarity measurements, and prompt-generalization results.

arxiv_record.abstract: In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have been widely applied to legal tasks. To enhance their understanding of legal texts and improve reasoning accuracy, a promising approach is to incorporate legal theories. One of the most widely adopted theories is the Four-Element Theory (FET), which defines the crime constitution through four elements: Subject, Object, Subjective Aspect, and Objective Aspect. While recent work has explored prompting LLMs to follow FET, our evaluation demonstrates that LLM-generated four-elements are often incomplete and less representative, limiting their effectiveness in legal reasoning. To address these issues, we present JUREX-4E, an expert-annotated four-element knowledge base covering 155 criminal charges. The annotations follow a progressive hierarchical framework grounded in legal source validity and incorporate diverse interpretive methods to ensure precision and authority. We evaluate JUREX-4E on the Similar Charge Disambiguation task and apply it to Legal Case Retrieval. Experimental results validate the high quality of JUREX-4E and its substantial impact on downstream legal tasks, underscoring its potential for advancing legal AI applications. The dataset and code are available at: https://github.com/THUlawtech/JUREX
arxiv_record.authors: Huanghai Liu, Quzhe Huang, Qingjing Chen, Yiran Hu, Jiayu Ma, Yun Liu, Weixing Shen, Yansong Feng
arxiv_record.title: JUREX-4E: Juridical Expert-Annotated Four-Element Knowledge Base for Legal Reasoning

C1.justification: The central knowledge-base contribution and claim that expert knowledge benefits legal reasoning remain. V2 explicitly broadens its claimed consistency across prompting strategies and model types, and its conclusion adds potential applications in other areas requiring expert judgment.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations of failures to recognize when legal interpretation is necessary, weak discrimination from frequent factual keywords, and information lost when retrieval excludes original case facts. Sections 9 and 12 discuss collaboration shortcomings, annotation costs, and coarse factual–legal integration, substantially extending v1's mainly jurisdictional limitation.

D1.justification: V2 supplies previously missing charge-level generation, charge-prediction, and case-generation prompts in Tables 6, 13, and 14. It also identifies five dataset annotators, CAIL2018-based charge-selection criteria, the 8192-token generation limit, and component model identities. These substantially improve documentation without establishing changes to the underlying retained experiments.

E1.justification: V2 Appendix D adds direct charge-prediction evaluation covering unrestricted, multi-charge and multi-defendant cases, extending the reported task scenarios beyond binary charge disambiguation and retrieval. The 155-charge knowledge base, three disambiguation groups, and LeCaRDv2 retrieval coverage are retained.

E2.justification: V2 adds Farui-plus and Qwen comparisons, differently sourced and combined FETs, an in-context-learning variant, and collaborative annotations. GEAR disappears from the retrieval comparison; most other retrieval baselines move to Table 12. The full-pool table also changes its BERT label to Legal-BERT while retaining identical scores, leaving that comparator's identity unresolved.

E3.justification: New experimental designs include a 300-case pilot with and without a supplied charge list, generation guided by two FET exemplars, additional model configurations, and collaboration using ten factual keywords with expert validation. The original disambiguation sample, retrieval pools, and evaluation metrics are retained; these are added protocols rather than established reruns of the original experiments.

E4.justification: V2 substantially expands analyses of dependence on the generating model, downstream backbone, exemplar guidance, combined knowledge sources, and human collaboration. It also adds a misappropriation failure example and charge-list sensitivity analysis. The original FET-only retrieval ablation and embezzlement case study remain.

E5.justification: V2 introduces paired McNemar tests comparing four LLM-generated FET configurations against expert FETs across three disambiguation groups, reporting twelve p-values in Table 11. V1 contains no corresponding significance analysis. This adds statistical support without establishing an increase in repeated runs or newly specified seed counts.

E6.justification: Original GPT-4o results and full-pool retrieval values are retained, but substantial new results appear. Examples include ICL disambiguation accuracy/F1 of 92.69/93.00, collaborative annotations at 92.84/93.04, and Qwen retrieval MRR of 0.2168 without versus 0.2206 with expert guidance. Appendix D adds pilot findings, while GEAR's results are removed. The introduction's percentage gains are equivalent relative expressions of the retained Table 3 differences.

M1.justification: V2 Section 9 introduces a preliminary collaboration procedure: an LLM retrieves statutes and extracts factual keywords, experts validate them, and the LLM produces refined annotations. This is a limited alternative annotation procedure; the original hierarchical expert annotation and retrieval method, including the 70:30 similarity combination, remain substantively unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, annotation explanations, and results narrative are extensively rewritten. V2 separates Background from Related Work, introduces an early analysis of LLM failures, integrates data statistics into dataset construction, and adds a Discussion section. This substantially reorganizes the argument beyond inserting new experimental content.

P2.justification: V2 adds a failure-example figure, revises the hierarchy diagram, and removes the retrieval workflow diagram. It expands and restructures result tables, relocates retrieval baselines to the appendix, and adds collaboration, significance, and prompt tables. The distribution plots and embezzlement case-study display are retained.

R1.justification: Research positioning expands substantially toward legal LLMs and their reasoning limitations, adding works including Lawyer LLaMA, DiSC-LawLLM, LegalBench, LegalDiscourse, LawBench, and LexEval. Earlier discussion and citations concerning debates between competing crime-constitution theories are condensed or removed, while additional legal-interpretation scholarship supports the revised framing.

T1.justification: No new mathematical definitions, theoretical results, or proofs appear. V1's cosine-similarity and weighted-combination equations are expressed procedurally in v2 Section 8.2 with the same underlying calculation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens conclusions previously supported mainly by one primary LLM: it tests alternative models and prompting strategies, adds paired significance tests, and documents previously missing generation procedures and charge-selection criteria. Its collaboration analysis and concrete retrieval limitations also improve critical assessment. Removing GEAR narrows one comparison, and the unexplained BERT/Legal-BERT relabeling weakens traceability, but these drawbacks do not outweigh the gains in evidential support, reproducibility, and clarity.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe JUREX-4E and retain matching core methods, datasets, and results. Inspection of all pages, including figures, tables, and appendices, supports a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds model and prompting comparisons, a charge-prediction pilot, and an expert–LLM collaboration experiment.

before.justification: V1 reports original human evaluations, similar-charge disambiguation experiments, legal-case retrieval results, and a retrieval case study.

arxiv_record.abstract: In large language models (LLMs), certain \emph{neurons} can store distinct pieces of knowledge learned during pretraining. While factual knowledge typically appears as a combination of \emph{relations} and \emph{entities}, it remains unclear whether some neurons focus on a relation itself -- independent of any entity. We hypothesize such neurons \emph{detect} a relation in the input text and \emph{guide} generation involving such a relation. To investigate this, we study the LLama-2 family on a chosen set of relations, with a \textit{statistics}-based method. Our experiments demonstrate the existence of relation-specific neurons. We measure the effect of selectively deactivating candidate neurons specific to relation $r$ on the LLM's ability to handle (1) facts involving relation $r$ and (2) facts involving a different relation $r' \neq r$. With respect to their capacity for encoding relation information, we give evidence for the following three properties of relation-specific neurons. \textbf{(i) Neuron cumulativity.} Multiple neurons jointly contribute to processing facts involving relation $r$, with no single neuron fully encoding a fact in $r$ on its own. \textbf{(ii) Neuron versatility.} Neurons can be shared across multiple closely related as well as less related relations. In addition, some relation neurons transfer across languages. \textbf{(iii) Neuron interference.} Deactivating neurons specific to one relation can improve LLMs' factual recall performance for facts of other relations. We make our code and data publicly available at https://github.com/cisnlp/relation-specific-neurons.

arxiv_record.title: On Relation-Specific Neurons in Large Language Models

With respect to their capacity for encoding relation information, we give evidence for the following three properties of relation-specific neurons. \textbf{(i) Neuron cumulativity.} Multiple neurons jointly contribute to processing facts involving relation $r$, with no single neuron fully encoding a fact in $r$ on its own. \textbf{(ii) Neuron versatility.} Neurons can be shared across multiple closely related as well as less related relations. In addition, some relation neurons transfer across languages. \textbf{(iii) Neuron interference.} Deactivating neurons specific to one relation can improve LLMs' factual recall performance for facts of other relations. We make our code and data publicly available at https://github.com/cisnlp/relation-specific-neurons.

C1.justification: The central claims of relation-specific neurons, versatility, and interference remain. Cumulativity is strengthened from increasing factual degradation as more neurons are disabled to joint processing with no single neuron fully encoding a fact, explicitly stated in the abstract and introduction.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive arguments separating relation semantics from prompt syntax and general object-generation ability, plus interpretations of post-ablation errors. Appendix B discusses object-distribution imbalance, and the limitations expand to model-family and post-training generalization. The earlier distinct-object-count explanation for sensitivity is removed; the fact-frequency explanation remains.

D1.justification: The release statement changes from planned code availability to stated public code-and-data availability. Appendix K documents the new paraphrase and synthetic-sentence templates. Hardware and Python-environment disclosures remain unchanged; actual repository availability is not established by the PDFs.

E1.justification: The 12 LRE relations, six languages, and Dolma analysis are retained. Coverage expands through alternative English templates for the same held-out triples and synthetic object-containing sentences outside the original factual queries, adding limited input scenarios and a language-modeling task.

E2.justification: The original-model and random-neuron-deactivation comparators remain, as do the neuron-module variants and concept-neuron comparisons. Gemma-7B uses the same comparator types; no new competing identification method is evaluated.

E3.justification: v2 substantially extends the evaluation design: Gemma-7B experiments, intermediate-block ablations across eight consecutive threshold pairs, perplexity measurements on 4–50 synthetic sentences per relation, and 20-token error illustrations. The original 50-triple holdouts and two-token factual-recall evaluation remain.

E4.justification: The single 1,000-versus-3,000-neuron cumulativity check becomes a systematic range analysis in Figure 6 and Table 3. New analyses address template dependence, general language-modeling disruption, generated-error patterns, and robustness across model families. The earlier multilingual, frequency, and neuron-type analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report averaging the main random-deactivation baseline over ten seeds, qualitative stability under negative-sampling seeds, and the same Wilcoxon test with p-values 0.11 and 0.03. v2 introduces no new uncertainty-reporting practice; macro/micro cumulativity averages are metric aggregation.

E6.justification: Core Llama-2 results, including Figure 4 and the original cumulativity table entries, are retained. v2 adds substantial Gemma, template-transfer, cumulativity, perplexity, and error results. For example, its new Table 2 reports ablation perplexity changing from 62.71 to 84.31 for person_occupation. Concept-overlap displays omit food, pokemon, and superhero entries and revise non-overlap counts, while concept validation retains all eleven concepts.

M1.justification: Both versions identify neurons through token-averaged activations, average-precision ranking against counter-relation examples, and zeroing selected neurons during inference. RelSpec is new terminology; the additional evaluations do not establish a changed identification or intervention procedure.

P1.justification: v2 standardizes RelSpec terminology, revises explanatory passages and footnotes, and moves the fact-frequency analysis from Section 5.3 to Appendix E. Supplementary sections are reorganized, but the main narrative framework and much of the existing prose are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds displays for Gemma, cumulativity, prompt transfer, perplexity, and errors, and greatly expands the cumulativity table. Existing multilingual plots replace mirrored bars with bars and horizontal markers; sensitivity plots gain percentage annotations, and concept-overlap heatmaps are transposed and reduced. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering.

R1.justification: v2 connects neuron versatility to polysemanticity and superposition, adding Mu and Andreas, Elhage's superposition work, and Scherlis et al. It also cites Gemma and Sclar et al. for the added experiments. The broader related-work survey and statistics-based positioning remain.

T1.justification: v2 introduces the mathematical definition of cumulativity as 1 minus #affected/#total, with macro and micro aggregation. v1 reports the underlying counts without this metric. Existing identification and accuracy-drop mathematics remain substantively unchanged, and no proofs are added.

improvement.justification: The template-transfer and language-modeling controls test important alternative explanations left untested in v1. Expanded cumulativity validation and Gemma replication further strengthen the central empirical evidence. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses: Section 5.4 says nine concepts while overlap figures show eight and appendix validation retains eleven, and the stronger single-neuron claim exceeds what the group ablations establish.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work, with matching methodology and core experiments. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds Gemma-7B experiments, prompt-template controls, perplexity measurements, and error analysis.

before.justification: v1 reports original Llama-2 neuron-deactivation experiments, multilingual evaluations, fact-frequency analysis, and concept-neuron analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance across various tasks but remain prone to hallucinations. Detecting hallucinations is essential for safety-critical applications, and recent methods leverage attention map properties to this end, though their effectiveness remains limited. In this work, we investigate the spectral features of attention maps by interpreting them as adjacency matrices of graph structures. We propose the $\text{LapEigvals}$ method, which utilises the top-$k$ eigenvalues of the Laplacian matrix derived from the attention maps as an input to hallucination detection probes. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art hallucination detection performance among attention-based methods. Extensive ablation studies further highlight the robustness and generalisation of $\text{LapEigvals}$, paving the way for future advancements in the hallucination detection domain.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's three contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: Laplacian spectral features indicate hallucinations, LapEigvals achieves leading attention-based detection performance, and ablations support robustness and generalization. Expanded experiments provide additional support without redefining those contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of GSM8K transfer failures as domain mismatch, judge agreement as a label-quality proxy, bfloat16 rounding as a stabilizing mechanism, and precision/recall tradeoffs. It also discusses attention-materialization and FlashAttention constraints. Some additions are overstated: Appendix G.4 claims consistent superiority over all-layer hidden-state probes despite Table 10 exceptions, and Appendix F attributes low agreement to TriviaQA although Table 4 shows the lowest agreement for TruthfulQA.

D1.justification: v2 documents bfloat16 storage, feature computation fused with inference, H100 hardware for the 24B model, hidden-state feature construction, a GSM8K prompt, expanded optimal hyperparameters, and labeling-cost estimates. It updates the stated repository destination from lapeig to lapeigvals and replaces the uncertain TriviaQA licensing statement with Apache 2.0. The earlier implementation section is relocated to Appendix C.

E1.justification: v2 adds the GSM8K test set of 1,319 mathematics problems to the six retained QA datasets. This extends evaluation to mathematical reasoning and adds transfers between mathematics and the existing QA domains (Section 4.1 and Table 11).

E2.justification: v1 evaluates attention-derived comparators only. v2 adds a hidden-state comparator family: PCA-projected logistic-regression probes using the last answer token, with both per-layer and all-layer variants (Appendix G.4, Table 10). AttentionScore, AttnLogDet, and AttnEigvals remain.

E3.justification: v2 expands from three to five evaluated LLMs by adding Mistral-Nemo and Mistral-Small-24B at both decoding temperatures. Added protocols include GSM8K exact-match labeling with a dedicated reasoning prompt, precision/recall at threshold 0.5, stratified training fractions, and controlled feature-noise settings. The existing 80/20 stratified split and principal probe settings are retained.

E4.justification: New analyses test agreement between gpt-4o-mini and gpt-4.1 labels, performance with reduced training data, and sensitivity to Gaussian perturbations before eigenvalue sorting (Appendices F, J, K). Precision/recall analysis is also added, and existing eigenvalue-count, layer, and transfer studies are extended to the added configurations.

E5.justification: Appendix K and Table 13 newly report means and standard deviations across five perturbation runs. Both versions retain single-run reporting for Table 1 and standard deviations over ten balanced samples in the temperature study. This is a localized expansion of uncertainty reporting, not an increase in repetitions for the main benchmarks.

E6.justification: Original Table 1 scores and shared extended-comparison results are retained, while substantial new benchmark and diagnostic results appear. For example, v2 reports GSM8K AUROC 0.872 for Llama-3.1-8B LapEigvals versus 0.838 for AttnEigvals, and Table 13 shows deterioration under large perturbations. Some newly reported values conflict internally: Llama-3.2-3B LapEigvals on NQOpen at temperature 1.0 is 0.798 in Table 10 but 0.693 in Table 1; this cannot establish a performance improvement.

M1.justification: Both versions use normalized attention-derived Laplacians, their largest diagonal eigenvalues across heads and layers, PCA, and logistic regression. Equation (2) rewrites the causal degree normalization using T-i; the surrounding description retains the same procedure. New proofs and implementation disclosures do not establish a different algorithm.

P1.justification: The main section order and most prose are retained. v2 revises motivation, method, and baseline explanations, standardizes spelling, corrects several names and cross-references, and relocates implementation details. Appendix organization expands, but the retained narrative is not extensively rewritten.

P2.justification: Main Figures 4–5 now display Mistral-Small-24B, while the original multi-model analyses are retained and expanded in appendix Figures 10–11. Dataset plots and benchmark tables expand, new diagnostic tables appear, and the original extended comparison is split into Tables 6–7. Heatmaps and diagrams are also redrawn, producing substantial display and layout changes.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for GSM8K, the two Mistral models, Wu et al., Mann–Whitney, and FlashAttention. It more explicitly distinguishes LapEigvals from AttentionScore through full-attention information and all-layer features. The broader related-work organization and research positioning remain stable.

T1.justification: v2 corrects the above-diagonal attention constraint from 1 to 0 and adds elementary proofs that Laplacian eigenvalues lie in [-1,1] and include a zero eigenvalue (Appendix B). Appendix L adds an operation-count argument for quadratic degree computation and eigenvalue sorting. These are limited formal additions to the retained mathematical framework.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important validation gaps in v1 through hidden-state controls, mathematics evaluated by exact match, larger model configurations, judge-agreement checks, and training-size and perturbation analyses. These additions substantially improve assessment of the method's usefulness and failure boundaries while preserving the original evidence. Conflicting Table 10 values and overstated interpretations weaken parts of the revision, but do not outweigh the broader validation and practical documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LapEigvals research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, including the rotated tables, and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds results for GSM8K, two Mistral models, hidden-state probes, judge agreement, training-data requirements, and feature perturbations.

before.justification: v1 reports original hallucination-detection experiments on six datasets and three LLMs, statistical feature analyses, and ablations (Table 1, Section 6, and appendices).

arxiv_record.abstract: The success of large language models (LLMs) has attracted many individuals to fine-tune them for domain-specific tasks by uploading their data. However, in sensitive areas like healthcare and finance, privacy concerns often arise. One promising solution is to generate synthetic data with Differential Privacy (DP) guarantees to replace private data. However, these synthetic data contain significant flawed data, which are considered as noise. Existing solutions typically rely on naive filtering by comparing ROUGE-L scores or embedding similarities, which are ineffective in addressing the noise. To address this issue, we propose \textit{RewardDS}, a novel privacy-preserving framework that fine-tunes a reward proxy model and uses reward signals to guide the synthetic data generation. Our \textit{RewardDS} introduces two key modules, Reward Guided Filtering and Self-Optimizing Refinement, to both filter and refine the synthetic data, effectively mitigating the noise. Extensive experiments across medical, financial, and code generation domains demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

arxiv_record.title: RewardDS: Privacy-Preserving Fine-Tuning for Large Language Models via Reward Driven Data Synthesis

snapshot_arxiv_record.abstract: The success of large language models (LLMs) has attracted many individuals to fine-tune them for domain-specific tasks by uploading their data. However, in sensitive areas like healthcare and finance, privacy concerns often arise. One promising solution is to generate synthetic data with Differential Privacy (DP) guarantees to replace private data. However, these synthetic data contain significant flawed data, which are considered as noise. Existing solutions typically rely on naive filtering by comparing ROUGE-L scores or embedding similarities, which are ineffective in addressing the noise. To address this issue, we propose \textit{RewardDS}, a novel privacy-preserving framework that fine-tunes a reward proxy model and uses reward signals to guide the synthetic data generation. Our \textit{RewardDS} introduces two key modules, Reward Guided Filtering and Self-Optimizing Refinement, to both filter and refine the synthetic data, effectively mitigating the noise. Extensive experiments across medical, financial, and code generation domains demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the same central claims: reward-driven synthetic-data improvement through Reward Guided Filtering and Self-Optimizing Refinement for privacy-preserving fine-tuning. The additional experiments support these claims without redefining the main contribution.

C2.justification: V2 introduces explanations linking attack resistance to divided privacy budgets, proxy performance to model compatibility and reward-model capacity, and scarce-data performance to refinement. It presents measured overhead as minimal and removes the limitations paragraph explicitly emphasizing additional reward-model training cost. These substantially expand and change the paper's interpretation of effectiveness and practicality.

D1.justification: Appendix G newly documents attack construction, 10-token prefixes, greedy decoding, and a 256-token output limit. V2 also supplies runtime information and a promised code/data repository location. Core training, hardware, and prompt details remain; the baseline appendix loses v1's detailed DP-Instruct clustering/histogram and KnowledgeSG BLEU-filter descriptions, without establishing implementation changes.

E1.justification: The medical, financial, and code-generation datasets and tasks remain. V2 adds medical-data reconstruction and membership-inference scenarios, involving partial private-text prefixes and augmented nonmember examples (Section 6.4 and Appendix G). These extend evaluation coverage without adding another domain.

E2.justification: The main benchmark and target-backbone comparator sets remain unchanged. V2 adds a No Protection control to the attack evaluation and explicit reward-based filtering controls in Table 4. Its revised case study also compares RewardDS directly with DP-Generation, DP-Instruct, and KnowledgeSG.

E3.justification: Reported medical training/synthetic sample counts change from 3,364/6,728 to 3,210/6,420, while development and test counts remain fixed (v1 Table 2; v2 Table 7). V2 substantially expands evaluation protocols through privacy attacks, varying total privacy budgets and synthetic-data quantities, alternative proxy configurations, and cost measurements. The count revision does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds privacy attacks, refinement-stage downstream evaluation, cost profiling, filtering-only comparisons, data-quantity and privacy-budget sensitivity, and proxy-model heterogeneity/scale analyses. The case study becomes a baseline-response comparison. V1's financial/code reward-distribution panels disappear, while existing target-backbone and k/N analyses are retained and reorganized.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The additional experiments continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial results in Tables 2–6 and Figures 4–6, including 448 minutes for RewardDS versus 315 for DP-Generation and new attack, filtering, sensitivity, and proxy-model outcomes. Table 1 and the retained target-backbone table keep their numerical entries despite revised medical sample counts. The case-study responses change, and the financial hyperparameter plots change their R1/RL series attribution.

M1.justification: The proxy-model training procedure, reward loss, filtering, and iterative refinement remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 and all eight prompt templates match across versions. Testing different proxy models does not introduce a new method component.

P1.justification: Related work, the experimental narrative, and the appendices are substantially reorganized. LLM-judge discussion moves into Main Results and Appendix E; medical k/N and privacy-allocation analyses move to appendices; an appendix overview is added. Baseline, case-study, and limitations prose is rewritten, although the core method text remains largely stable.

P2.justification: V2 introduces five new tables, privacy and budget plots, a redesigned Figure 5, and an expanded multi-method Figure 7. Figure 1 is redrawn and relocated, Figure 3 is reduced in size, and existing hyperparameter displays are relocated and split. The financial-QA plots also change their metric-to-series mapping.

R1.justification: Section 2 and new Appendix A recast related work into anonymity-, encryption-, and synthesis-based approaches. V2 adds substantive discussion of encryption methods, including Lou, Frery, and You, alongside Hou and privacy-attack references. Earlier discussions of API-based generation and multi-model synthesis are removed, materially changing the research positioning.

T1.justification: Equation 1, Algorithm 1, and Section 5's DP post-processing and sequential-composition argument remain unchanged, including the total budget of (2ε, 2δ). No new theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the unchanged method. Privacy attacks and filtering-only comparisons address central evidence gaps in v1, while cost and sensitivity analyses make practical tradeoffs more assessable. These gains outweigh reporting weaknesses, including the unexplained medical-count revision with unchanged headline scores, labeling 642 of 6,420 samples as 1%, and using parameter counts as a GPU-memory proxy.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RewardDS, with matching core methods and experiments. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds privacy attacks, runtime measurements, filtering comparisons, and additional sensitivity and proxy-model experiments.

before.justification: V1 reports original QA and code-generation experiments, component ablations, LLM-judge evaluations, hyperparameter analyses, and comparisons across target-model backbones.

arxiv_record.abstract: Graph-theoretic problems arise in real-world applications like logistics, communication networks, and traffic optimization. These problems are often complex, noisy, and irregular, posing challenges for traditional algorithms. Large language models (LLMs) offer potential solutions but face challenges, including limited accuracy and input length constraints. To address these challenges, we propose MA-GTS (Multi-Agent Graph Theory Solver), a multi-agent framework that decomposes these complex problems through agent collaboration. MA-GTS maps the implicitly expressed text-based graph data into clear, structured graph representations and dynamically selects the most suitable algorithm based on problem constraints and graph structure scale. This approach ensures that the solution process remains efficient and the resulting reasoning path is interpretable. We validate MA-GTS using the G-REAL dataset, a real-world-inspired graph theory dataset we created. Experimental results show that MA-GTS outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in terms of efficiency, accuracy, and scalability, with strong results across multiple benchmarks (G-REAL 94.2%, GraCoRe 96.9%, NLGraph 98.4%).MA-GTS is open-sourced at https://github.com/ZIKEYUAN/MA-GTS.git.
arxiv_record.authors: Zike Yuan, Ming Liu, Hui Wang, Bing Qin
arxiv_record.title: MA-GTS: A Multi-Agent Framework for Solving Complex Graph Problems in Real-World Applications

These problems are often complex, noisy, and irregular, posing challenges for traditional algorithms. Large language models offer potential solutions but face several challenges, including limited accuracy, input length constraints, and suboptimal algorithm selection. To address these challenges, we propose MA-GTS(Multi-Agent Graph Theory Solver), a multi-agent framework that decomposes these complex problems through agent collaboration.
