C1.justification: The abstract newly claims robust performance with both closed- and open-source base models. The introduction and conclusion extend the comparison claim explicitly to existing multi-agent frameworks. The central contributions—MA-GTS, G-REAL, and agent collaboration for graph problem solving—remain the same.

C2.justification: Appendix D adds a rationale for studying 8–25-node graphs based on semantic difficulty and interprets the new experiments as supporting scalability and runtime efficiency. Section 6.7 adds a stability interpretation. Section 3.3 also softens 'optimal or near-optimal' solutions to 'suitable' solutions. The dedicated limitations paragraph remains unchanged.

D1.justification: Table 9 adds the specific DeepSeek-V3-0324-660B version and its access link. The abstract now explicitly states that G-REAL is released alongside MA-GTS. Existing agent prompts, knowledge-base examples, and algorithm-library examples are retained; these disclosures do not establish an underlying implementation change.

E1.justification: G-REAL expands from three tasks to four by adding Target Navigation, a shortest-path task with noisy text and implicit graph structure. This extends the input conditions beyond the existing NLGraph shortest-path evaluation. The previous G-REAL, GraCoRe, and NLGraph tasks remain.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds DeepSeek-V3-660B under direct and CoT prompting, plus OWL and GraphTeam using GPT-4o-mini. These introduce evaluated general-purpose and graph-specific multi-agent competitors, substantially expanding comparison beyond v1's individual LLM baselines. Existing comparators remain.

E3.justification: v2 adds a DeepSeek-based MA-GTS configuration and several distinct evaluation protocols. Appendix D tests TSP and coloring at 25, 30, 35, and 40 nodes with five instances per size, and measures end-to-end runtime on five randomly selected 15-node TSP graphs. These extend the experimental design; the original accuracy definition remains unchanged.

E4.justification: Section 6.7 adds repeated-query stability analysis, while Appendix D adds larger-graph scalability tests and runtime comparisons. The node-size plot also gains the new G-REAL shortest-path task. These substantially extend the analyses beyond v1's size sweep and layer ablations; Table 4's original ablation results are retained.

E5.justification: v1 provides no repeated-query uncertainty analysis. v2 reports five queries per selected problem and gives per-query accuracy, variance, standard deviation, and mean in Table 5. This introduces statistical reporting for a supplementary experiment, without adding uncertainty estimates to the main comparison table or establishing increased repetitions of its experiments.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for the new task, baselines, base model, and supplementary analyses. MA-GTS with GPT-4o-mini scores 91.7% on G-REAL shortest path; its six original Table 2 scores remain unchanged. The abstract's G-REAL average changes from 94.2% to 93.6% because task coverage expands. Reported o3-mini NLGraph cycle scores change from 98.9% for both prompting methods to 97.3% direct and 97.8% CoT.

M1.justification: The three-layer architecture, six agents, algorithm selection, tool execution, and self-checking procedure remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 and all six appendix prompts are retained. Evaluating DeepSeek as another base model does not establish a procedural modification.

P1.justification: v2 revises the abstract and introduction, condenses several agent descriptions, and adds an introductory notation overview in Section 3. It also updates affiliations and corresponding-author information and adds acknowledgments. The main section sequence and much of the original prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds a motivation figure and substantially redraws the architecture diagram. Dataset, performance, and cost tables gain columns or rows, and the node-size plot gains another curve. Four new tables present stability, larger-graph results, runtime, and benchmark characteristics. Appendix figures and the model-details table are also rearranged, while their retained content remains identifiable.

R1.justification: Research positioning expands through discussion of OWL, GCoder, GraphAgent, ProGraph, GraphArena, and GLBench. Appendix E and Table 8 add an explicit benchmark comparison concerning noise, naming, contamination, and data generation. DeepSeek and CoT references are added, while Anim-Director is removed. The expansion makes competing graph and multi-agent approaches substantially more central to the positioning.

T1.justification: Equations (1)–(3), Algorithm 1's mathematical relationships, and the appendix's algorithm-complexity descriptions are retained. The new opening of Section 3 restates the existing setup; no substantive mathematical definitions, assumptions, proofs, or derivations are added.

improvement.justification: The decisive improvement is Table 2's addition of OWL and GraphTeam with the same GPT-4o-mini base, addressing v1's important absence of evaluated multi-agent competitors. The second base model and new stability and scalability experiments further strengthen assessment of the framework's applicability. These gains outweigh remaining weaknesses: supplementary samples are small, the above-90% claims need qualification given the new results, and the runtime-advantage interpretation overlooks OWL's shorter time in Table 7 (139.39 versus 148.48 seconds).

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MA-GTS and G-REAL. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including matching retained material across renumbering and relocation.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds task and model evaluations, repeated-query measurements, larger-graph experiments, and runtime comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, node-size analyses, inference-cost measurements, and layer ablations for MA-GTS.

arxiv_record.abstract: Personalizing large language models (LLMs) is important for aligning outputs with diverse user preferences, yet existing methods struggle with flexibility and generalization. We propose CoPL (Collaborative Preference Learning), a graph-based collaborative filtering framework that models user-response relationships to enhance preference estimation, particularly in sparse annotation settings. By integrating a mixture of LoRA experts, CoPL efficiently fine-tunes LLMs while dynamically balancing shared and user-specific preferences. Additionally, an optimization-free adaptation strategy enables generalization to unseen users without fine-tuning. Experiments on UltraFeedback-P demonstrate that CoPL outperforms existing personalized reward models, effectively capturing both common and controversial preferences, making it a scalable solution for personalized LLM alignment. The code is available at https://github.com/ml-postech/CoPL.
arxiv_record.authors: Youngbin Choi, Seunghyuk Cho, Minjong Lee, MoonJeong Park, Yesong Ko, Jungseul Ok, Dongwoo Kim
arxiv_record.title: CoPL: Collaborative Preference Learning for Personalizing LLMs

      <abstract>Personalizing large language models (LLMs) is important for aligning outputs with diverse user preferences, yet existing methods struggle with flexibility and generalization. We propose CoPL (Collaborative Preference Learning), a graph-based collaborative filtering framework that models user-response relationships to enhance preference estimation, particularly in sparse annotation settings. By integrating a mixture of LoRA experts, CoPL efficiently fine-tunes LLMs while dynamically balancing shared and user-specific preferences. Additionally, an optimization-free adaptation strategy enables generalization to unseen users without fine-tuning. Experiments on TL;DR, UltraFeedback-P, and PersonalLLM datasets demonstrate that CoPL outperforms existing personalized reward models, effectively capturing both common and controversial preferences, making it a scalable solution for personalized LLM alignment.</abstract>

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive limitations concerning annotation overlap, uninformative common-pair feedback and majority bias under imbalance. It distinguishes stable preference clusters from declining minority accuracy, interprets the new sensitivity results, and discusses semantic graph construction, active learning and reweighting as possible remedies.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a code repository link and construction details for TL;DR and PersonalLLM, including Dirichlet concentration 0.1, response and reward-dimension subsampling, and pair filtering. The existing GNN, MoLE, optimizer, hardware and adaptation specifications are retained.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates only UF-P with discrete preference groups. V2 adds TL;DR summarization preferences and PersonalLLM with continuously mixed user preferences, substantially broadening task and preference coverage. It also evaluates imbalanced user populations.

E2.justification: The benchmark baselines and existing adaptation comparators are retained; Oracle is renamed G-Oracle. Table A4 adds three evaluated message-passing comparator variants removing negative edges and/or activation and feature transformations. The new 27B comparison reuses VPL.

E3.justification: Existing UF-P protocols are retained. Added experiments introduce a 27B Gemma 2 backbone, group-ratio sweeps, 5,000–20,000-user evaluations with an annotation-doubling control, and expert-count sweeps. These substantially expand the evaluation design.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component, adaptation and pseudo-label analyses, v2 tests majority/minority robustness, user-count and annotation sufficiency, expert-count sensitivity, and the contributions of negative edges, activation and feature transformations. Figures 4 and 7 and Appendix E provide substantial new diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: Three-seed reporting and uncertainty values are retained for existing experiments. Appendix E explicitly introduces a single-seed exception for the new 27B evaluation because of hardware limits; Table A3 reports point accuracies without uncertainty.

P1.justification: V2 expands the introductory explanation of sparse supervision, rewrites the dataset narrative, condenses main-text related work while preserving it in Appendix C, and organizes additional experiments in Appendix E. arxiv_record.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in tool learning. In real-world scenarios, user queries are often ambiguous and incomplete, requiring effective clarification. However, existing interactive clarification approaches face two critical limitations: reliance on manually constructed datasets, which inherently constrains training data scale and diversity, and lack of error correction mechanisms during multi-turn clarification, leading to error accumulation that compromises both accuracy and efficiency. We present AskToAct, which addresses these challenges by exploiting the structural mapping between queries and their tool invocation solutions. Our key insight is that tool parameters naturally represent explicit user intents. By systematically removing key parameters from queries while retaining them as ground truth, we enable automated construction of high-quality training data. We further enhance model robustness through error-correction pairs and selective masking, enabling dynamic error detection during clarification interactions. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that AskToAct significantly outperforms existing approaches, achieving above 57% accuracy in recovering critical unspecified intents and enhancing clarification efficiency by an average of 10.46% while maintaining high accuracy in tool invocation. Our framework exhibits robust performance across different model architectures and successfully generalizes to entirely unseen APIs without additional training, achieving performance comparable to GPT-4o with substantially fewer computational resources.

C1.justification: The three central contributions remain automated data construction, self-correction, and unseen-API generalization. The abstract and introduction revise recovery/efficiency claims from above 79%/48.34% to above 57%/10.46%, shift the robustness emphasis from complexity levels to model architectures, and claim comparability to GPT-4o instead of GPT-4.

C2.justification: V2 Appendix G substantially extends interpretation: weaker backbones benefit more, excessive augmentation may induce over-correction or overfitting, and increasing ambiguity or tool counts strains clarification and planning. It adds interpretations of conversational robustness and practical utility from case and human studies. Conversely, v1's specific limitation about simulations failing to reproduce partial or inconsistent human responses is removed.

D1.justification: V2 substantially expands reproducibility documentation through dataset provenance, licensing and API-overlap checks, revised prompts and transformation records, explicit correction templates, and metric aggregation and strict string-matching rules. Appendix E specifies LoRA rank 8, augmentation replacement proportion, and variant-specific learning rates and GPU configurations. V1's explicit 4096-token maximum sequence length is no longer stated.

E1.justification: V1 uses TaskBench-derived Daily Life data for training and in-domain testing, with Hugging Face and Multimedia domains for OOD testing. V2 introduces xlam-IC, covering Python-library and RESTful-service APIs, for training and in-domain evaluation, while Taskbench-IC becomes the OOD benchmark. It also adds human-authored queries and actual human interactions.

E2.justification: V2 Tables 3 and 5 add xLAM-7b-fc-r and remove LLaMA-2-7B-Chat and Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1 from the main and OOD comparator sets. Most comparators, including ToolLLaMA-2-7b-v2, gorilla-openfunctions-v2, and Mistral-Interact, remain.

E3.justification: V2 replaces the Daily Life 10:1 split and LLaMA-2 training with xlam-IC splits and Qwen2.5 LoRA/full fine-tuning; batch size changes from 16 to 64 and epochs from two to three. The semantic-filter threshold changes from 0.85 to 0.95. The three-level evaluation is replaced by personality simulation and a three-participant, 30-query human study. Simulator restrictions are relaxed, and the ablation changes from 100 to 50 queries and from intent-level to query-level incompleteness.

E4.justification: Beyond revising the existing error-type ablation and adding CPS/PRS measurements, v2 adds human quality assessments of generated queries and augmented dialogues, cross-backbone transfer tests, a 0–50% augmentation sweep, complexity curves, and a contrasting-user-style case study. These substantially expand diagnostic evidence, while v1's separate Level I–III robustness comparison is no longer reported.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. V2's new human-study and verification tables report participant averages without uncertainty estimates or inter-rater agreement.

E6.justification: Benchmark and ablation results are extensively replaced under changed conditions. For example, v1's Level III AskToAct reports ICR 79.54 and PRS 73.40; v2's xlam-IC LoRA/full variants report ICR 57.68/63.88 and PRS 68.71/73.12. These are not same-setting performance changes. V2 also adds human task-completion results of 93.33%/96.67% versus 86.67% for the base model, plus verification and supplementary-analysis results.

M1.justification: The core query transformation, dialogue construction, error injection, and selective masking framework remains. However, v2 Appendix C.1.1 adds transformation rules for optional parameters, repeated API calls, and partial list/matrix obfuscation. Its clearly-stated-intent error-generation prompt also corrects the selection condition from removed=true to removed=false.

P1.justification: V2 extensively rewrites the introduction, method explanations, and experimental narrative. It moves the full related-work review into the appendix, separates metrics into their own section, reorganizes the appendices, and expands procedural explanations and examples. These changes substantially alter the document's organization beyond renumbering.

P2.justification: The dataset table changes from a domain-by-complexity grid to split and aggregate-statistics columns. Main comparison tables replace level-based columns with grouped model categories and seven metrics, and the ablation gains CPS/PRS columns. V2 adds human-evaluation, verification, correction-template, and supplementary-analysis tables plus complexity plots in Figure 3. Figure 2 is revised and relocated.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations to LoRA, APIGen, and TaskBench. The existing three-part related-work review is largely retained in Appendix A, with a short main-text summary. Positioning around automated clarification data and self-correction remains substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: The incomplete-clarification error rate is redefined from unclarified intents divided by total unspecified intents in v1 Section 4.5 to the proportion of queries containing any unresolved intent in v2 Table 6. This is a limited mathematical-definition change. Appendix F.3 otherwise supplies formulas for existing metrics; neither version introduces theoretical proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation beyond v1's single trained backbone and simulated interactions. Human checks of 400 queries and 200 augmented dialogues directly assess generated-data quality; the human-interaction study and cross-backbone tests address practical applicability and generality. Augmentation and complexity analyses expose useful operating limits, while expanded implementation details improve reproducibility. The controlled three-level comparison is lost, and the human study remains small without uncertainty reporting, but the overall evidence is substantially stronger. Changed headline scores do not establish a direct performance improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe AskToAct and retain its central clarification and self-correction framework. Their complete main texts, appendices, tables, figures, and equations support comparison despite substantial experimental revisions.

after.justification: V2 reports original benchmark, human-interaction, ablation, and data-verification results, plus transferability, augmentation-proportion, and complexity analyses.

before.justification: V1 reports original model comparisons, out-of-domain evaluations, and an error-correction ablation in Tables 3–5, with expanded results in Appendix D.

arxiv_record.abstract: Preference learning extends the performance of Code LLMs beyond traditional supervised fine-tuning by leveraging relative quality comparisons. In existing approaches, a set of n candidate solutions is evaluated based on test case success rates, with the candidate demonstrating a higher pass rate being labeled as positive and its counterpart with a lower pass rate as negative. However, because this approach aligns entire failing code blocks rather than pinpointing specific errors, it lacks the granularity necessary to capture meaningful error-correction relationships. As a result, the model is unable to learn more informative error-correction patterns. To address these issues, we propose Target-DPO, a new preference alignment framework that mimics human iterative debugging to refine Code LLMs. Target-DPO explicitly locates error regions and aligns the corresponding tokens via a tailored DPO algorithm. To facilitate it, we introduce the CodeFlow dataset, where samples are iteratively refined until passing tests, with modifications capturing error corrections. Extensive experiments show that a diverse suite of Code LLMs equipped with Target-DPO achieves significant performance gains in code generation and improves on challenging tasks like BigCodeBench. In-depth analysis reveals that Target-DPO yields fewer errors. Code, model and datasets are in: https://github.com/JieWu02/Target-DPO.

metadata.abstract: Preference learning extends the performance of Code LLMs beyond traditional supervised fine-tuning by leveraging relative quality comparisons. In existing approaches, a set of n candidate solutions is evaluated based on test case success rates, with the candidate demonstrating a higher pass rate being labeled as positive and its counterpart with a lower pass rate as negative. However, because this approach aligns entire failing code blocks rather than pinpointing specific errors, it lacks the granularity necessary to capture meaningful error-correction relationships. As a result, the model is unable to learn more informative error-correction patterns. To address these issues, we propose Target-DPO, a new preference alignment framework that mimics human iterative debugging to refine Code LLMs. Target-DPO explicitly locates error regions and aligns the corresponding tokens via a tailored DPO algorithm. To facilitate it, we introduce the CodeFlow dataset, where samples are iteratively refined until passing tests, with modifications capturing error corrections. Extensive experiments show that a diverse suite of Code LLMs equipped with Target-DPO achieves significant performance gains in code generation and improves on challenging tasks like BigCodeBench. In-depth analysis reveals that Target-DPO yields fewer errors. Code, model and datasets are in: https://github.com/JieWu02/Target-DPO.

C1.justification: The principal contributions remain iterative-debugging preference construction, the CodeFlow dataset, targeted preference optimization and improved code-generation performance across models and benchmarks. The new emphasis on understanding code and additional supporting experiments do not materially redefine these claims.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive arguments about the five-iteration cutoff, synthetic-test validity, dataset diversity, random-negative generalization and applicability across teacher models. V1's general warning about generated-test quality becomes a more specific appendix qualification that tests can be simple and miss edge cases; the dataset-size limitation remains.

D1.justification: V3 supplies generation and judging prompts, a generated-test example, coverage-evaluation tools, benchmark software versions, a 3% warm-up specification and separate prompt/generation limits. V1 promises future code/data release; v3 states that code, models and datasets are available through a supplied repository. These substantially expand reproducibility information.

E1.justification: The HumanEval, MBPP, BigCodeBench and LiveCodeBench task coverage is retained. V3 adds EpiCoder training-data comparisons and auxiliary dataset analysis involving Alpaca, CodeFeedback, Evol-Alpaca and OSS-Instruct (Tables 2 and 17), extending data coverage within the existing research focus.

E2.justification: V3 adds reported CodeDPO and PLUM comparisons (Figure 4; Table 12), EpiCoder-SFT comparisons, and vanilla DPO rows for StarCoder2-15B and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B in Table 1. The evaluated AceCoder comparison in v1 Figure 5 disappears, although its related-work mention remains.

E3.justification: V1 specifies two training epochs for instruction-tuned models and five for base models; v3 Appendix A.3 specifies three epochs and no longer documents validation-loss checkpoint selection. This is a reported protocol revision, without establishing that retained experiments were rerun. Added experiments also introduce model-size, training-volume, teacher-model and test-quality evaluation settings.

E4.justification: V3 adds debugging-versus-sampling controls, synthetic-test audits, correct-versus-incorrect SFT, hyperparameter and model-size analyses, LCS-versus-prefix/suffix extraction, negative-selection comparisons and alternative-teacher experiments. These substantially extend v1's SFT, context and masking ablations. The original error-frequency and annotation-cost analyses are retained in Appendices C.5-C.6.

E5.justification: V3 introduces sample-level dispersion summaries, including a coverage boxplot with mean and quintile markers and judge-score distribution summaries (Figures 7-8). These describe variability across sampled cases; neither version reports training-run seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: V3 adds extensive results for new comparisons, audits and ablations while retaining most headline scores. Table 1 revises Qwen2.5-Coder-7B/RPO's BigCodeBench-Hard Complete/Instruct scores from 24.3/14.8 to 14.2/13.5, and its average from 42.7 to 41.4. These are changed reported values, not established same-setting performance losses given the revised training description.

M1.justification: IterPref becomes Target-DPO/Target-RPO, retaining iterative debugging, randomly selected failed-iteration negatives, LCS difference extraction and full-positive/masked-negative preference losses. The added audits and alternative-teacher experiments do not establish a change to the proposed algorithm.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and explanatory passages undergo substantial rewriting alongside the title and method renaming. Related Work moves from Section 2 to Section 6, and the main error/cost analyses move into the appendix, substantially reorganizing the narrative around experiments and ablations.

P2.justification: Figure 1 changes from a bar chart to a radial comparison, and v3 adds an ablation diagram, test-quality displays and prompt/example figures. Existing ablation tables are restructured and expanded. V1's iteration plot is redrawn as v3 Figure 6, while its error-frequency chart is redisplayed as Table 18.

R1.justification: V3 adds Hu et al. (2025) on coarse-to-fine process rewards and removes Li et al. (2025) on gradient-based parameter selection. It also identifies CodeDPO as concurrent work and sharpens the contrast with pass-rate supervision, while retaining the broader research positioning.

T1.justification: The LCS algorithm, preference-loss equations and reinforcement-learning objective are retained without substantive mathematical revision. V3's added code-coverage formula explains a standard evaluation metric; no new theorem, proof or formal derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially addresses v1's lack of direct synthetic-test audits and controlled evidence for LCS and random-negative selection through Appendix A.2 and C.7-C.8. Additional baselines and explicit synthesis prompts strengthen the evidential basis and reproducibility. These gains outweigh localized reporting problems, although corrections remain necessary: Qwen Target-RPO's LiveCodeBench score is 32.2 in Table 1 but 33.3 in Tables 9 and 16, and the changed training-epoch statement is unexplained.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CodeFlow and focal preference-alignment research despite the title and method renaming. Text, equations, tables and figures support comparison, including v3's Appendices A-C; v1 ends with references and has no appendix.

after.justification: V3 retains original training results and adds original test-quality audits, controlled comparisons, sensitivity analyses and teacher-model experiments throughout the main text and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original model-training evaluations, ablations, debugging pass rates and generated-code error analyses in Tables 1-2 and Figures 3, 5 and 6.

arxiv_record.abstract: This paper explores targeted distillation methods for sentiment analysis, aiming to build compact and practical models that preserve strong and generalizable sentiment analysis capabilities. To this end, we conceptually decouple the distillation target into knowledge and alignment and accordingly propose a two-stage distillation framework. Moreover, we introduce SentiBench, a comprehensive and systematic sentiment analysis benchmark that covers a diverse set of tasks across 12 datasets. We evaluate a wide range of models on this benchmark. Experimental results show that our approach substantially enhances the performance of compact models across diverse sentiment analysis tasks, and the resulting models demonstrate strong generalization to unseen tasks, showcasing robust competitiveness against existing small-scale models.
arxiv_record.authors: Yice Zhang, Guangyu Xie, Jingjie Lin, Jianzhu Bao, Qianlong Wang, Xi Zeng, Ruifeng Xu

C1.justification: The introduction and conclusion extend the headline size-efficiency claim: alongside the retained 1.2B-over-3.2B result, v2 claims that the distilled 3.2B model surpasses the original 8B model. The two-stage distillation and SENTIBENCH contributions remain the same.

C2.justification: v2 interprets the added student results as evidence of cross-family generalization and proposes combining reasoning enhancement with targeted distillation. Its new Ethics Statement discusses bias amplification and subgroup fairness. The existing limitations concerning unfiltered teacher responses and weak structured extraction remain.

D1.justification: The future release promise becomes a specific repository stated to provide code, data, and weights. v2 discloses construction of 55 demonstrations using GPT-4o and manual verification, supplies additional model-specific hyperparameters, and reports corpus-generation costs: approximately 671 A100 GPU hours using LMDeploy, four 40GB GPUs, and batch size 200. External resource availability was not verified.

E1.justification: The SENTIBENCH task/dataset entries, MMLU evaluation, and distillation source corpora are retained. The teacher-quality audit samples existing distillation tasks, while the reasoning-model comparison uses the existing sentiment benchmark. Neither establishes additional task or domain coverage.

E2.justification: Appendix D.2 introduces comparisons with Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, and DeepScaleR-1.5B-Preview. Appendix D.1 adds a teacher-quality comparison against GPT-3.5. Conversely, the fine-tuned T5-base comparator is removed from Table 2. Alpaca and LaMini distillation comparisons remain.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes demonstration sampling from the training set to the dev set, and Table 1 changes SSA's stated metric from micro_f1 to sentiment_graph_f1. New experiments introduce additional student configurations and training budgets. Appendix D.1 adds Claude-4 evaluation using 50 examples per classification/emotion task and 20 responses per analysis perspective. These reported changes do not establish that retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix D.1 adds systematic evaluation of teacher-output correctness, completeness, explanation quality, and hallucination, extending the earlier teacher-size comparisons and qualitative examples to quantitative data-quality analysis. Existing ablations, MMLU checks, and case studies remain, although Table 2 loses the full-data, per-task KNOWDIST-only and ICLDIST-only results.

E5.justification: Both versions report averaging evaluations over three random seeds. Neither provides new confidence intervals, variability estimates, or significance tests. The teacher-audit sample counts describe a new evaluation design, not additional repeated-run or uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 2 adds distilled Qwen-2.5-1.5B and Llama-3-3.2B averages of 64.01 and 68.41, respectively, plus their generic-distillation comparisons. Tables 22–24 add teacher-quality and reasoning-model results. GPT-3.5's reported average changes from 63.79 to 69.40, but changed stated evaluation settings prevent treating this as a demonstrated same-setting gain. Full-data stage-only result rows are removed.

M1.justification: The KNOWDIST–ICLDIST procedure, analyzing/rewriting prompts, four perspectives, diversification strategies, and training objective remain equivalent. Additional student backbones test the existing method; the newly described demonstration construction does not establish a procedural change.

P1.justification: The abstract is rewritten, selected introduction and conclusion passages are updated, and affiliations change. Ethics and acknowledgments sections are added, while Appendices C and D gain subsections. Most existing methodological prose and the main section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: Table 2 is substantially reorganized into three student-model comparison blocks, and Figure 1 adds the distilled 3.2B result. New appendix tables display model-specific settings, teacher-quality assessments, and reasoning-model comparisons. Existing prompt tables and case-study content are retained; the cases are relocated and recaptioned rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: v2 adds reasoning and ethics references, including OpenAI (2024), DeepSeek-AI (2025), Mohammad (2021), and Sabbagh et al. (2025), while removing Raffel et al. (2020) with the T5 comparison. Appendix B elaborates the benchmark's distinction from Zhang et al. (2024b). The main related-work organization and positioning remain largely unchanged.

T1.justification: v1's negative-log-likelihood minimization in Equations 2–3 becomes equivalent log-likelihood maximization in v2's Equation 2. No substantive mathematical definitions, assumptions, derivations, or proofs are added or revised.

improvement.justification: v1's distillation evidence centers on one student. v2 substantially strengthens support for generality through additional student sizes and another model family, while adding reasoning-model comparisons, teacher-quality assessment, and practical reproducibility information. Some full-data ablation detail is lost, and changed evaluation settings are not reconciled with retained scores. Nevertheless, the broader validation and clearer implementation documentation provide a substantial overall improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Targeted Distillation for Sentiment Analysis. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds experiments with additional students, teacher-response quality evaluation, and reasoning-enhanced model comparisons.

before.justification: v1 reports original SENTIBENCH experiments, component ablations, teacher-model comparisons, MMLU evaluation, and qualitative case studies.

arxiv_record.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability of large language models (LLMs) aims to uncover the internal processes of information propagation and reasoning. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have demonstrated promise in this domain by extracting interpretable and monosemantic features. However, prior works primarily focus on feature extraction from a single layer, failing to effectively capture activations that span multiple layers. In this paper, we introduce Route Sparse Autoencoder (RouteSAE), a new framework that integrates a routing mechanism with a shared SAE to efficiently extract features from multiple layers. It dynamically assigns weights to activations from different layers, incurring minimal parameter overhead while achieving high interpretability and flexibility for targeted feature manipulation. We evaluate RouteSAE through extensive experiments on Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct. Specifically, under the same sparsity constraint of 64, RouteSAE extracts 22.5% more features than baseline SAEs while achieving a 22.3% higher interpretability score. These results underscore the potential of RouteSAE as a scalable and effective method for LLM interpretability, with applications in feature discovery and model intervention. Our codes are available at https://github.com/swei2001/RouteSAEs.
arxiv_record.authors: Wei Shi, Sihang Li, Tao Liang, Mingyang Wan, Guojun Ma, Xiang Wang, Xiangnan He
arxiv_record.title: Route Sparse Autoencoder to Interpret Large Language Models

metadata.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability of large language models (LLMs) aims to uncover the internal processes of information propagation and reasoning. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have demonstrated promise in this domain by extracting interpretable and monosemantic features. However, prior works primarily focus on feature extraction from a single layer, failing to effectively capture activations that span multiple layers. In this paper, we introduce Route Sparse Autoencoder (RouteSAE), a new framework that integrates a routing mechanism with a shared SAE to efficiently extract features from multiple layers. It dynamically assigns weights to activations from different layers, incurring minimal parameter overhead while achieving high interpretability and flexibility for targeted feature manipulation. We evaluate RouteSAE through extensive experiments on Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct. Specifically, under the same sparsity constraint of 64, RouteSAE extracts 22.5% more features than baseline SAEs while achieving a 22.3% higher interpretability score. These results underscore the potential of RouteSAE as a scalable and effective method for LLM interpretability, with applications in feature discovery and model intervention. Our codes are available at https://github.com/swei2001/RouteSAEs.

C1.justification: The abstract and conclusion retain the same claims about efficient multi-layer feature extraction, interpretability, targeted intervention, and the headline improvements. The introduction's new contribution list restates existing contributions; additional experiments support capabilities already claimed in v1.

C2.justification: v1's explicit feature-steering limitation is removed, and v3 interprets its steering examples as evidence of controllable intervention. v3 also interprets training/inference routing distributions as contributions from both shallow and deep layers, and Appendix B newly qualifies soft routing as having shown no clear experimental benefits.

D1.justification: v3 clarifies that KL evaluation substitutes the activation at the highest-weight layer, specifies uniform weights for the Random control, and discloses the steering clamp value of 20. The implementation table, optimizer schedule, preprocessing information, and repository access remain substantively unchanged.

E1.justification: OpenWebText2 training and evaluation coverage remains unchanged. v3 Section 3.6 adds a limited generation-steering task: manipulating Olympic-related and maximal-effort features in responses to two questions, beyond v1's reconstruction and feature-interpretation evaluations.

E2.justification: The ReLU, Gated, TopK, and Crosscoder baselines remain. v3 adds Random routing, described as assigning uniform layer weights, to the KL-divergence, feature-count, interpretation-score, and reconstruction comparisons. Crosscoder remains excluded from KL evaluation.

E3.justification: The principal training settings remain unchanged, including the 100-million/10-million-token allocation and 512-token context. Added evaluation designs include threshold sweeps over 10, 15, and 20; human–GPT-4o assessment of 100 RouteSAE features; original-versus-clamped generation with activation set to 20; and TopK activation profiles on Pythia-160m in Figure 1.

E4.justification: v3 substantially expands validation through a routing-control ablation, threshold sensitivity analysis (Figure 5), human assessment of automatic interpretation (Figure 7), inference-time routing analysis (Figure 9b), and steering case studies (Figure 10). These supplement v1's sparsity comparisons, training-time routing analysis, and extracted-feature examples.

E5.justification: Both versions average interpretation scores over 100 sampled features per SAE and retain the same stochasticity caveat. Neither introduces repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new human–GPT-4o disagreement histogram reports validation outcomes rather than uncertainty in benchmark estimates.

E6.justification: v3 reports substantial new results for activation profiles, thresholds, human agreement, inference routing, and steering. Random routing sometimes extracts more features than RouteSAE but scores lower on interpretation; higher thresholds yield fewer, more interpretable features. The abstract's 22.5% feature-count and 22.3% interpretation-score gains remain unchanged.

M1.justification: The sum-pooled inputs, linear softmax router, probability-scaled layer selection, shared TopK SAE, and reconstruction objective remain unchanged. Equations 1–14, including the appendix hard/soft routing formulations, are retained. The steering examples demonstrate feature manipulation without introducing a revised RouteSAE component.

P1.justification: The narrative is substantially reorganized: related work and reconstruction analysis move to appendices, limitations follow the conclusion, and routing analysis precedes the case study. The introduction gains a contribution summary, while several methodological and interpretive passages are condensed or rewritten.

P2.justification: The conceptual Figure 1 is replaced by an activation-profile plot; architecture diagrams and existing performance plots are redrawn. New threshold, human-comparison, steering, and inference-routing displays are added. Table 1 and reconstruction results move to the appendix, whose formerly full-width example boxes adopt a two-column layout.

R1.justification: The cited-work coverage and positioning against single-layer SAEs and Crosscoder remain substantively unchanged. v1's related-work section is preserved in v3 Appendix A; reference formatting and shortened author lists do not constitute new research positioning.

T1.justification: The SAE definitions, routing probabilities, selection rule, reconstruction objective, and hard/soft routing equations are unchanged. No formal assumptions, theorems, or proofs are added; the expanded routing discussion is conceptual.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens validation of the central mechanism and evaluation: the uniform-routing control tests the value of learned routing, while human comparison and threshold sensitivity address weaknesses in v1's automatic interpretability assessment. These gains outweigh limited steering coverage and the retained Figure 6 caption claiming maximal feature counts despite Random sometimes exceeding RouteSAE.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RouteSAE research. Their text, equations, figures, table, and appendices support comparison, including material relocated between the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains original evaluations and adds random-routing comparisons, threshold sensitivity, human–GPT-4o comparisons, inference routing weights, and feature-steering results.

before.justification: v1 Sections 4.2–4.7 report original reconstruction, interpretability, feature-extraction, and routing-weight results on Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct. Appendix C supplies additional extracted-feature examples.

arxiv_record.abstract: Long-form writing agents require flexible integration and interaction across information retrieval, reasoning, and composition. Current approaches rely on predefined workflows and rigid thinking patterns to generate outlines before writing, resulting in constrained adaptability during writing. In this paper we propose WriteHERE, a general agent framework that achieves human-like adaptive writing through recursive task decomposition and dynamic integration of three fundamental task types: retrieval, reasoning, and composition. Our methodology features: 1) a planning mechanism that interleaves recursive task decomposition and execution, eliminating artificial restrictions on writing workflow; and 2) integration of task types that facilitates heterogeneous task decomposition. Evaluations on both fiction writing and technical report generation show that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across all automatic evaluation metrics, demonstrating the effectiveness and broad applicability of our proposed framework. We have publicly released our code and prompts to facilitate further research.

C1.justification: The central claims remain a unified planning view of writing, heterogeneous recursive decomposition, adaptive task scheduling, and improved narrative/report quality over the original baselines. Naming the framework WriteHERE and adding supporting human evaluation do not materially redefine these claims.

C2.justification: V3 adds a qualified interpretation of the human study, describing comparable performance and differences in clarity versus breadth, depth, and novelty. It also adds process-diagnostic limitations and framework-specific qualifications about unreliable retrieved information, synthesis errors, and absent built-in debiasing. The earlier computational-efficiency and human-feedback limitations remain.

D1.justification: V3 substantially expands reproducibility documentation through memory/context-selection details, module descriptions, a worked execution trace, and narrative-generation prompts. These disclose atomicity guidance, task schemas, dependency rules, and planning constraints. It also specifies GPT-4o-mini for retrieval ranking/summarization and provides LongReport access information, evaluation rubrics, preprocessing instructions, and dataset licenses. These disclosures do not establish that existing settings changed.

E1.justification: V3 adds LongReport: 12 detailed, time-sensitive prompts covering complex retrieval, information integration, and analytical writing, evaluated with reports exceeding 10,000 words. This substantially extends the task requirements beyond the retained TELL ME A STORY and WildSeek evaluations.

E2.justification: Gemini Deep Research with 2.5 Pro is added as the comparator in the new LongReport evaluation. E2E, Agent's Room, STORM, Co-STORM, and Perplexity Deep Research remain in their original comparisons; the appendix baseline variants are also retained.

E3.justification: The new LongReport study introduces a substantially different evaluation protocol: Gemini 2.5 Pro generation, five human annotators assessing every report pair, anonymous and randomized presentation, five rubric dimensions including clarity, and overall preferences. It also standardizes formatting and removes titles and report appendices, explicitly excluding citation-source fidelity. The original benchmark protocols are largely retained.

E4.justification: The recursion/type ablations, 2K–8K narrative-length analysis, and STORM/Co-STORM configuration comparisons are retained. Appendix B.4 adds case analyses of human judgments, including Gemini's incomplete report in Sample 7 and WriteHERE's very long but less-preferred report in Sample 6.

E5.justification: Appendix B introduces aggregation of five human ratings per report, reporting mean rubric scores and per-topic preference counts that expose annotator disagreement. The original 14-trial LLM judging and Davidson scoring remain unchanged. Neither version reports generation-seed variability, confidence intervals, or new significance tests.

E6.justification: The original numerical results are unchanged, including Tables 1–2 and v1 Tables 3–4, now v3 Tables 7–8. New LongReport results report WriteHERE/Gemini breadth scores of 4.5/4.2 and depth scores of 4.0/3.8. The reported 7:5 outcome counts topic-majority wins; individual preference votes total 30:30. Report-length statistics are added, while v1's generated DeepSeek R1 report example is removed.

M1.justification: The typed recursive decomposition and state-based DAG scheduling remain. However, v3 explicitly adds context retrieval and goal updating to Algorithm 1, while no longer stating v1's mandatory reasoning task after retrieval sequences. The PDFs do not establish whether these reflect procedural changes or expanded and condensed documentation of the existing implementation.

arxiv_record.abstract: Existing large language model (LLM) evaluation benchmarks primarily focus on English, while current multilingual tasks lack parallel questions that specifically assess cross-linguistic reasoning abilities. This dual limitation makes it challenging to comprehensively assess LLMs' performance in the multilingual setting. To fill this gap, we introduce MMLU-ProX, a comprehensive benchmark covering 29 languages, built on an English benchmark. Each language version consists of 11,829 identical questions, enabling direct cross-linguistic comparisons. Additionally, to meet efficient evaluation needs, we provide a lite version containing 658 questions per language. To ensure the high quality of MMLU-ProX, we employ a rigorous development process that involves multiple powerful LLMs for translation, followed by expert review to ensure accurate expression, consistent terminology, and cultural relevance. Building on this, we systematically evaluate 36 state-of-the-art LLMs, including reasoning-enhanced and multilingual-optimized LLMs. The results reveal significant disparities in the multilingual capabilities of LLMs: While they perform well in high-resource languages, their performance declines markedly in low-resource languages, with gaps of up to 24.3%. Through MMLU-ProX, we aim to advance the development of more inclusive AI systems and promote equitable access to technology across global contexts.

C1.justification: The central contribution expands from an ongoing 13-language benchmark to a 29-language resource with both full and efficient lite versions. The introduction explicitly adds the lite benchmark and broader model evaluation to the contributions. The central claim of persistent multilingual performance disparities remains.

C2.justification: v1 emphasizes inconsistent benefits from reasoning enhancement; v2 emphasizes benefits observed for DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen3 thinking modes, adds interpretations of language-dependent scaling, and argues that lite evaluation preserves performance patterns. New limitations explicitly acknowledge incomplete expert verification, residual translation errors, and exclusion of multimodal inputs.

D1.justification: v2 adds initial-translation, self-reflection, and editing prompts in Appendix F; detailed scoring rubrics in Appendix E; and annotator qualifications and labor information. It newly discloses vLLM inference and the 70-question validation allocation. Reported total evaluation compute increases from approximately 4,000 to over 10,000 GPU hours, reflecting expanded work rather than a documented per-run budget change.

E1.justification: Evaluated language coverage expands from 13 to 29 while retaining the original languages and reasoning-question domain. Added languages include Wolof, Yoruba, Zulu, Telugu, Nepali, and Ukrainian, substantially broadening the linguistic populations represented in the results.

E2.justification: The evaluated model set adds GPT-4.1, GPT-4o, o4-mini, full DeepSeek-R1/V3, Qwen3 variants, and Gemma3, among others. Gemma2, Llama3.1-405B, and Mistral-7B disappear from the corresponding full 5-shot comparison. The full zero-shot comparator set also changes substantially. Appendix D additionally compares the translation pipeline against reasoning-based translation and native-speaking translators.

E3.justification: v2 adds a separate lite evaluation with 588 test questions and full-versus-lite comparisons, alongside explicit Qwen3 thinking-enabled/disabled configurations. The existing 5-shot and zero-shot framework remains. Section 5.3's sampling description is inconsistent: 20 items from each of 14 disciplines does not yield the stated 658 total items, leaving the precise lite-selection procedure unresolved.

E4.justification: v1 already analyzes model scale, reasoning enhancement, and prompting; v2 revises these analyses for the expanded model set. It also adds full/lite representativeness analysis in Section 5.3 and a direct English-to-Japanese translation-quality comparison in Appendix D, testing aspects of benchmark efficiency and pipeline quality previously unexamined.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or inter-rater agreement. v2 adds mean ratings and accuracy-difference plots but no uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Tables 6–9 substantially expand model-language and full/lite result entries, while Tables 4–5 add numerical translation evaluations. Retained entries also change: QwQ-32B's reported English 5-shot accuracy changes from 70.7% to 75.9%, without enough inference detail to establish a same-setting gain. Overall averages across 13 versus 29 languages are not directly comparable.

M1.justification: The Claude 3.7 translation, self-reflection, and external/expert verification approach remains. Section 3.3 changes external verification from GPT-4o reviewing and refining translations to o3 for four African languages and GPT-4.1 elsewhere, flagging discrepancies for human review. This is a limited component revision; expanded stage descriptions alone do not establish an entirely new method.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and related work are extensively rewritten, contributions become explicitly enumerated, and results are reorganized into separate Experiments and Analysis sections. A limitations section and Appendices A–G substantially change the narrative organization beyond merely adding experimental content.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one-column to two-column layout. v2 introduces seven figures, including pipeline and performance visualizations, and additional comparison and verification tables. Main results are transposed into a language-grouped table, while expanded detailed results appear in rotated appendix tables.

R1.justification: Sections 1–2 substantially revise the benchmark landscape, adding discussions of HLE, MGSM, XCOPA, XGLUE/XTREME-R, and language-specific MMLU benchmarks. v2 strengthens its critique of heterogeneous translation quality and positions MMLU-ProX around parallel reasoning evaluation, supported by a new benchmark-comparison table and positioning figure.

T1.justification: Neither version presents formal theoretical results, proofs, or mathematical derivations. The added rating rubrics, prompts, and language classifications are empirical documentation rather than new theory.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens benchmark validation and reproducibility: v1's ongoing verification and preliminary averages gain support from detailed 15-language expert results, a translation-method comparison, explicit rubrics, and reusable prompts. Broader evaluations and full/lite testing further improve usefulness. Reporting defects temper these gains: the lite sampling arithmetic is inconsistent, and Figure 4 gives Telugu's maximum as 71.9% despite a 77.9% entry in Table 3. These defects weaken particular analyses but do not outweigh the substantial improvements in validation evidence and documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MMLU-ProX and support a reliable comparison of text, tables, and figures. v1 ends with references and has no appendix; v2's Appendices A–G were included. Retained content can be matched despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

after.justification: v2 reports original model evaluations across 29 languages, full/lite benchmark results, expert translation ratings, and translation-method comparisons in Tables 3–9.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 25 models with 5-shot prompting and seven with zero-shot prompting across 13 languages in Tables 1–2.

arxiv_record.abstract:
LLMs often adopt an assertive language style also when making false claims.
Such ``overconfident hallucinations'' mislead users and erode trust. Achieving
the ability to express in language the actual degree of uncertainty around a
claim is therefore of great importance. We find that ``verbal uncertainty'' is
governed by a single linear feature in the representation space of LLMs, and
show that this has only moderate correlation with the actual ``semantic
uncertainty'' of the model. We apply this insight and show that (1) the
mismatch between semantic and verbal uncertainty is a better predictor of
hallucinations than semantic uncertainty alone and (2) we can intervene on
verbal uncertainty at inference time and reduce confident hallucinations on
short-form answers, achieving an average relative reduction of ~30%.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction narrow the headline reduction claim from hallucinations generally to confident hallucinations. The three central contributions—linear VUF discovery, combined-uncertainty detection, and MUC steering—remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 attributes Qwen's lower steering sensitivity to larger embedding norms under normalized VUFs, discusses potential judge circularity, and explains correctness losses through semantic-entropy noise causing false abstentions (Sections 3.2 and 4.2; Appendix G.3). The existing short-form QA and generalization limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-availability link, the exact accuracy-judge prompt in Appendix A.3, full ESU/EUU prototype-expression lists in Appendix E.2, and the 70B intervention cap of 4.0 in Appendix G.1. These substantially expand the implementation and measurement information available for reproduction.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate closed-book short-form QA on TriviaQA, NQ-Open, and PopQA. The added model, controls, and case study remain within this existing dataset and task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds EigenScore to the SEP comparison in Table 2 and random-vector steering to Table 5. Existing uncertainty-based comparisons and SEP results are retained.

E3.justification: Evaluation expands to Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct as a generator, extends Qwen steering sweeps from ±1 to ±10, and adds overall hallucination rate alongside confident hallucination rate. New random-vector controls match intervention strength and vector-value range. These substantially extend the evaluation design; existing dataset splits and sampling settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds random-direction controls testing whether mitigation specifically benefits from VUF steering, causal validation using the previously described ESU extraction method to address judge circularity, and a correctness-loss case study (Table 5, Appendix E.5/Figure 13, Appendix G.3). Qwen sensitivity testing is also extended. Existing transfer and alternative-score similarity analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Section 2.3 newly reports MANOVA significance for the four response groups, with p-values below 0.0001. v1 presented the distributions without this test. No new repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, or error-bar reporting are introduced.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for EigenScore, random controls, ESU steering, and the 70B model. Table 3 additionally reports overall hallucination rates: for Qwen on TriviaQA, the post-calibration overall rate is 34.4%, versus 23.4% confident hallucinations. Previously reported table values are retained. The headline reduction changes from 31.9% to 29.6% across an expanded model set, so this is not a same-setting performance decline.

M1.justification: The specified VUF extraction rule changes from the raw difference of mean activations in v1 Equation 1 to an explicitly L2-normalized direction in v2 Equations 2–3. This changes the specified steering-vector scale. The detector and adaptive SU–VU intervention rule remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish whether the underlying implementation changed.

P1.justification: v2 locally rewrites the uncertainty definitions, reorganizes Section 3.2 around effective-layer selection, clarifies terminology, and gives existing appendix examples descriptive headings. The overall narrative and section structure remain intact.

P2.justification: Tables 2, 3, and 5 gain comparator columns, metric columns, or experimental rows. Qwen plot axes are extended, Figure 13 is added, and existing figures are relocated, including the exchange of Figures 4 and 5. The underlying visual style and most displays remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The research bibliography, related-work discussions in Sections 2.4 and 5, and positioning relative to prior approaches are unchanged. The added terminology footnote does not revise the research positioning.

T1.justification: Section 2.2 replaces the informal VU definition with VU(U|C) = 1 − Pr(P|U,C), interpreted through a listener's subjective probability, and specifies an ordering between answers. Section 3.1 also adds the normalized-vector equation. These are limited formal-definition additions.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important weaknesses in validating and communicating the central result. Random-direction controls and ESU-based causal validation strengthen attribution to VUF steering. Separating overall from confident hallucinations corrects the ambiguity in v1's headline and table labeling, while Appendix G.3 explains the correctness–abstention tradeoff. Together with substantially improved reproduction information, these provide meaningful gains in evidential strength and transparency despite the method's retained accuracy tradeoff.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VUF and Mechanistic Uncertainty Calibration study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds 70B-model evaluation, comparison methods, control experiments, and a failure case.

before.justification: v1 reports original feature-extraction, steering, hallucination-detection, and mitigation experiments on TriviaQA, NQ-Open, and PopQA.

However, generating these lengthy reasoning sequences is computationally expensive and time-consuming. To address this inefficiency, we leverage the inherent parallelizability of certain tasks to accelerate the reasoning process. Specifically, when multiple parallel reasoning steps exist, we decode multiple tokens per forward pass via a tree-like attention mask within a single sequence, avoiding additional memory usage. Experimental results show that our method achieves up to nearly 100\% speedup in decoding while basically maintaining the answer quality.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains training-free parallel reasoning within one sequence. The abstract changes the speed claim from over 100% to up to nearly 100%, while the introduction qualifies applicability to specific scenarios. The conclusion narrows the cache-recomputation claim to caches from prefilling.

C2.justification: v4 adds an important applicability boundary: reasoning models such as QwQ-32B can fail because their thinking output ignores formatting instructions, extending v1's small-model limitation. It also attributes SoT's memory cost to long contexts and CoD's quality losses to overly concise reasoning, substantially expanding interpretation of the efficiency tradeoffs.

D1.justification: v4 newly documents generation temperature, normal-baseline prompting, SoT's batch_outline mode, average prompt lengths, and planning-data construction. Appendix C supplies the complete grading prompt, temperature, and token limit; Appendix B adds QA and planning input examples. These substantially expand reproducibility information. Both versions already link to the same code repository.

E1.justification: v4 adds a planning task using 100 examples covering topics such as technology, politics, and business. This extends evaluation from retrieval and document-grounded QA to short-prompt analysis and planning using model knowledge. The original retrieval and QA datasets remain represented.

E2.justification: v1 evaluates only normal decoding against the proposed parallel decoder. v4 Table 1 adds actual comparisons with Skeleton-of-Thought, Chain-of-Draft, and CoD+Ours, including on the retained tasks. Skeleton-of-Thought was previously discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: The QA evaluator changes from GPT-4 to GPT-4o-2024-11-20, and GPU memory becomes an evaluation metric. v4 drops the 30-student configuration and the 14B retrieval/QA evaluations, uses 7B for the main comparisons, and introduces planning evaluations with additional models and SoT/CoD comparison procedures.

E4.justification: v4 adds exploratory CoD compatibility and model-generalization checks, including a qualitative report that QwQ-32B fails to follow the required format. The 10-versus-30-student scaling comparison disappears. The worked retrieval example in Appendix B is retained rather than newly added.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. v4 describes a QA score increase as normal fluctuation without adding an uncertainty estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Reported 7B ten-student retrieval accuracy changes from 93%/95% for normal/parallel decoding to 100%/100%. QA ratings change from 3.57/3.49 to 2.77/2.88 under the changed evaluator. v4 also adds planning, baseline, memory, and model results while removing 30-student and 14B retrieval/QA entries. These are revised reports, not established same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The three-stage decoder, branch-isolating attention, position handling, padding, and cache reuse remain unchanged; renaming the mask from belt-like to tree-like does not establish an algorithm change. v4 adds an optional CoD+Ours variant using concise-reasoning prompting and refines the stage-1 prompt in Appendix A.

P1.justification: The overall section order and three-stage method exposition are retained. v4 edits the abstract, introduction, and conclusion, clarifies method terminology, renames the data subsection, expands appendix headings, and adds an affiliation. Much of the additional text documents new experiments rather than reorganizing the existing narrative.

P2.justification: The separate retrieval and QA tables are replaced by a task-grouped comparison table with a memory column; Table 2 becomes a smaller cross-model planning table. Figure 1 gains explicit step numbering, revised labels, and an expanded caption. These substantially restructure the presentation of the central evidence.

R1.justification: v4 adds references for Chain-of-Draft, Phi-4, and QwQ-32B, and replaces the GPT-4 report with the GPT-4o System Card. The introduction expands the comparison with MEDUSA's retrained prediction heads, while the existing related-work framework remains largely intact.

T1.justification: Neither version contains formal theorems, proofs, or substantive mathematical derivations. The operational descriptions of branch attention and position IDs retain the same underlying reasoning.

improvement.justification: v4 addresses an important weakness in v1: efficiency and memory advantages now receive direct comparison against relevant alternatives, including SoT, with measured memory and timing results. Planning evaluations, documented model failures, and the grading prompt improve scope assessment and transparency. Removing the 30-student and 14B retrieval/QA evaluations weakens some evidence, and uncertainty reporting remains absent, but the comparative validation and reproducibility gains substantially improve the paper.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same parallel decoding work. All six pages of v1 and eight pages of v4, including their figures, tables, and appendices, support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v4 reports original experiments across retrieval, multi-document QA, and planning, including method comparisons, memory measurements, and additional model evaluations.

before.justification: v1 reports original retrieval and multi-document QA experiments, including accuracy, answer ratings, decoding speed, and time in Tables 1–2.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are commonly trained on multi-domain datasets, where domain sampling strategies significantly impact model performance due to varying domain importance across downstream tasks. Existing approaches for optimizing domain-level sampling strategies struggle with maintaining intra-domain consistency and accurately measuring domain impact. In this paper, we present Domain Impact-aware Data Sampling (DIDS). To ensure intra-domain consistency, a gradient clustering algorithm is proposed to group training data based on their learning effects, where a proxy language model and dimensionality reduction are employed to reduce computational overhead. To accurately measure domain impact, we develop a Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) guided metric that quantifies how domain-specific parameter updates affect the model's output distributions on downstream tasks, with theoretical guarantees. Furthermore, to determine optimal sampling ratios, DIDS combines both the FIM-guided domain impact assessment and loss learning trajectories that indicate domain-specific potential, while accounting for diminishing marginal returns. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DIDS achieves 3.4% higher average performance while maintaining comparable training efficiency. The code is available at https://github.com/shiweijiezero/DIDS.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same three methodological contributions, 3.4% average-performance claim, comparable-efficiency claim, and emphasis on using approximately 10% of the training data. Additional appendix evidence supports these retained claims.

C2.justification: New appendix discussions explain performance through more decisive domain reweighting, interpret clustering by instructional format and shared reasoning patterns, and discuss specialization/general-data tradeoffs. They also interpret graceful degradation under corrupted partitions and cross-task transfer, including specialization effects on unrelated tasks. The original limitations section is unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link, documents downstream-task adaptations of baselines, and supplies baseline proxy sizes, computational stages, and practical implementation guidance, including FIM batch sizes of 16–32. These are substantial documentation additions; they do not establish that unchanged benchmark results were rerun.

E1.justification: v2 adds OpenHermes-2.5 training data, HumanEval and MT-Bench evaluation in Appendix G, and unseen WMT16 English–German, TLDR, ARC-Challenge, and MBPP tasks in Appendix J. These substantially broaden coverage beyond the retained Tulu-3 and nine-task experiments.

E2.justification: The principal benchmark comparator set is retained. Table 10 adds fixed code/math-versus-general mixing strategies, while Table 12 extends the computational-cost comparison to DoReMi, DoGE, and Velocitune beyond the earlier DGA comparison. Newly cited DRPruning and DDK are not evaluated.

E3.justification: Added experiments introduce another reported 7B model configuration, a full 1,000k-sample OpenHermes control, static-mixture sweeps, swapping half of each domain's data, and unseen-task evaluation using BLEU, win rate, accuracy, and Pass@1. These are additional protocols; the original training hyperparameters and three-shot evaluation description remain.

E4.justification: Appendix D extends component ablations from four to all nine tasks and adds domain-weight trajectories, selection overlap, and clustering observations. Appendices G, H, and J add static-mixture sensitivity, corrupted-partition robustness, and generalization under diverse versus single-task guidance. Earlier sensitivity and irrelevant-data tests are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or experimental error bars. The added tables continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and the original plotted results are unchanged, including DIDS averages of 62.3 and 63.7. Tables 5–14 add extensive results, including a 63.7-to-60.2 decline under corrupted partitioning and a reported 53.5 average on unseen tasks. These concern newly reported conditions, not same-setting improvements over v1.

M1.justification: The gradient clustering, FIM-based impact calculation, loss forecasting, and sampling updates remain unchanged, including Algorithm 1. Appendix E discusses alternative divergences as possible extensions without establishing an implemented procedural change.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section order are preserved. Local edits clarify post-training terminology, standardize model names, revise author information, add acknowledgments, and expand related-work and baseline explanations. New appendix sections extend the supplement without extensively rewriting the original narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 5–14 with model/dataset comparisons, expanded ablations, temporal domain weights, robustness, costs, and unseen-task results. Existing tables are regrouped and their captions moved below; Algorithm 1 becomes full-width and moves to the end. Figures 1–3 remain visually unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds DRPruning and DDK, distinguishing their pruning-recovery and knowledge-distillation settings from DIDS. Three introductory references, Li et al. (2023, 2024) and Wu et al. (2024), are removed. The central positioning against existing sampling strategies remains.

T1.justification: The original KL/FIM derivation and Johnson–Lindenstrauss material are retained. Appendix E adds a Cramér–Rao connection, properties asserted for the quadratic approximation, and a generalized metric-tensor expression for alternative divergences in Equation 19, without a new proof.

improvement.justification: v1's reported validation centers on one training dataset and tasks used to guide sampling. v2 substantially addresses this evidence gap through another training distribution, unseen-task evaluations under two guidance regimes, and corrupted-partition tests, supported by fuller ablations and reproducibility information. Reporting ambiguities temper these gains: Appendix B.3 claims shared gradient clustering despite Table 3's BERT-based DGA costing, and the added 'Mixtral-7B' name conflicts with its Mistral-7B footnote. Nevertheless, the broader tests substantially strengthen assessment of generalization and robustness.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DIDS research. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, tables, figures, and algorithm are readable and support reliable matching despite expanded supplementary material.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds model/dataset evaluations, domain analyses, robustness tests, and unseen-task results in its appendices.

before.justification: v1 reports original nine-task evaluations, component ablations, computational costs, and sensitivity experiments in Tables 1–3 and Figures 2–3.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are susceptible to adversarial attacks such as jailbreaking, which can elicit harmful or unsafe behaviors. This vulnerability is exacerbated in multilingual settings, where multilingual safety-aligned data is often limited. Thus, developing a guardrail capable of detecting and filtering unsafe content across diverse languages is critical for deploying LLMs in real-world applications. In this work, we introduce a multilingual guardrail with reasoning for prompt classification. Our method consists of: (1) synthetic multilingual data generation incorporating culturally and linguistically nuanced variants, (2) supervised fine-tuning, and (3) a curriculum-based Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) framework that further improves performance. Experimental results demonstrate that our multilingual guardrail, MrGuard, consistently outperforms recent baselines across both in-domain and out-of-domain languages by more than 15%. We also evaluate MrGuard's robustness to multilingual variations, such as code-switching and low-resource language distractors in the prompt, and demonstrate that it preserves safety judgments under these challenging conditions. The multilingual reasoning capability of our guardrail enables it to generate explanations, which are particularly useful for understanding language-specific risks and ambiguities in multilingual content moderation.
arxiv_record.authors: Yahan Yang, Soham Dan, Shuo Li, Dan Roth, Insup Lee
arxiv_record.title: MrGuard: A Multilingual Reasoning Guardrail for Universal LLM Safety
