C1.justification: Alongside the retained multilingual guardrail and state-of-the-art claims, v3 makes consistency and reasoning-fidelity evaluation an explicit contribution and claims validation of reasoning reliability in the conclusion. The abstract also strengthens the performance claim to an advantage of more than 15%, which Table 2 does not support uniformly across comparisons.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive discussion of reasoning failures, including cultural uncertainty and unsupported risk attribution. Its new limitations section addresses restricted language and seed-data coverage, bias from using one LLM for generation and verification, imperfect automated judgments, and the small human study with limited annotation. v1 lacks these qualifications.

D1.justification: v3 adds a code-availability statement, planned model/data release information, human-annotation qualifications and scoring instructions, and the reasoning-evaluation prompt in Figures 8 and 17. Most existing hardware, libraries, LoRA settings, learning rates, and generation/inference instructions are retained.

E1.justification: The five benchmarks and existing attack scenarios remain. Appendix G.2 adds Hebrew on RTP-LX, Filipino on Aya, Bengali on XSafety and MultiJail, and Korean on Wildchat. This extends language coverage within the existing task and datasets.

E2.justification: The five external benchmark baselines remain unchanged. However, v3 removes the SFT and SFT+GRPO rows from the full five-benchmark comparison, retaining aggregate ablations on only three benchmarks. Figure 1 also replaces the Llama-Guard-3 illustration with a GuardR comparison.

E3.justification: v3 adds Llama-3.2-3B and Qwen2.5-3B configurations, automated consistency/fidelity/language-match evaluation, and human evaluation protocols using 100-example samples. Reported training sizes also change: Appendix B gives 30.3K rather than 20.3K English examples, while Table 1 gives 6K rather than 2K multilingual examples. These are reported setting revisions; the PDFs do not establish whether corresponding experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v3 adds cross-lingual consistency analysis, automated and human explanation assessment, human validation of synthetic translations, a reasoning-failure taxonomy, difficulty-threshold sensitivity, and a language-match ablation. Appendix G also analyzes performance by script, language family, and resource availability. Earlier attack tests and the fixed-versus-curriculum reward comparison remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The new evaluations still report point estimates. The retained uncertainty reward is a training component, not statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive results for smaller models, additional languages, explanation quality, human validation, and sensitivity analyses. Existing reported values also change: Table 2's 8B RTP-LX ID/OOD scores move from 91.08/85.87 to 91.04/86.32, and MultiJail sandwich F1 changes from 92.37 to 90.63. XSafety code-switching values are revised in Table 16. These changes do not establish a uniform same-setting performance improvement.

M1.justification: The synthetic-data generation, bilingual supervised fine-tuning, three-stage curriculum, four reward components, and GRPO procedure remain unchanged. Explicitly naming cross-entropy clarifies the existing training description; the additional backbones apply the same method.

P1.justification: The title and model name are revised, with targeted rewriting of the abstract, contributions, results discussion, and conclusion. Section 5 becomes a broader Discussion, and GRPO and XSafety material move to appendices. Much of the original introduction, related work, and method prose remains intact.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the language-performance bar charts as radar plots, redesigns Figure 1, and separates the paired attack tables between the main text and appendices. It adds consistency and unseen-language plots, annotation instructions, failure examples, and numerous analysis tables. Existing qualitative examples are also redistributed.

R1.justification: v3 adds citations to the Llama 3 model report and She et al.'s MAPO work for cross-lingual consistency. Its related-work discussion and positioning against English-centric and multilingual guardrails otherwise remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Sections 5.2–5.3 introduce quantitative definitions of cross-lingual consistency, explanation fidelity, and language-match rates for the new evaluations. The existing difficulty function, reward equations, and GRPO mathematics remain unchanged; the GRPO objective is relocated to Appendix E. No new proofs or theoretical guarantees appear.

improvement.justification: v1 supports its central explanation-quality claim mainly through examples. v3 substantially strengthens that evidence with automated and human assessments, synthetic-data validation, failure analysis, and explicit limitations, making the reasoning claims more assessable. Additional backbone and sensitivity tests further strengthen validation. The small human samples and reporting problems, including the unqualified more-than-15% claim and duplicated ablation row, limit confidence but do not outweigh these substantial gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same multilingual reasoning guardrail and retain matching methods and experiments. Their full texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, including material relocated in v3.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds model configurations, language evaluations, automated and human assessments, and further ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original multilingual classification results, code-switching and sandwich-attack experiments, reward ablations, and qualitative outputs.

arxiv_record.abstract: Video question answering benefits from the rich information in videos, enabling various applications. However, the large volume of tokens generated from long videos presents challenges to memory efficiency and model performance. To alleviate this, existing works propose to compress video inputs, but often overlook the varying importance of static and dynamic information across different queries, leading to inefficient token usage within limited budgets. We propose a novel token selection strategy, \textsc{explore-then-select}, that adaptively adjusts static and dynamic information based on question requirements. Our framework first explores different token allocations between key frames, which preserve spatial details, and delta frames, which capture temporal changes. Then it employs a query-aware attention-based metric to select the optimal token combination without model updates. Our framework is plug-and-play and can be seamlessly integrated within diverse video language models. Extensive experiments show that our method achieves significant performance improvements (up to 5.8\%) on multiple video question answering benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/ANDgate99/Explore-Then-Select .
arxiv_record.authors: Yumeng Shi, Quanyu Long, Wenya Wang
arxiv_record.title: Static or Dynamic: Towards Query-Adaptive Token Selection for Video Question Answering

C1.justification: Both versions claim training-free, query-adaptive allocation of static and dynamic information under limited token budgets, with plug-and-play applicability across models. The abstract and introduction retain the headline improvement of up to 5.8%; additional experiments support the existing central claims.

C2.justification: v2 explains smaller short-video gains through simpler scenes and coherent motion, and distinguishes increasing encoding cost from approximately stable selection cost. It also reframes the metric rationale around cumulative attention. Existing positional-encoding limitations and first-token latency qualifications remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code URL, specifies GPT-4o mini, discloses disabled generation sampling and an alternative 80GB A100 configuration, and documents the qualitative example's full search space. It also adds MLVU prompt/output details. Conversely, Appendix A.2 omits v1's explicit statement that reproduced LongVU uses top-K pruning to meet the budget.

E1.justification: v2 adds MLVU long-video multiple-choice evaluation and ActivityNet-QA open-ended evaluation, retaining EgoSchema, VideoMME and MSVD-QA. These additions broaden the evaluated video collections and extend coverage to MLVU videos described as lasting up to two hours.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds reference comparisons with VideoChat2, LongVA, mPLUG-Owl3 and trained LongVU, explicitly acknowledging their limited comparability. Original, Retrieval, Similarity and reproduced LongVU accuracy comparisons remain. However, v1's direct runtime comparison against LongVU is removed.

E3.justification: New configurations include Qwen2.5-VL-7B evaluations and a sweep of 32–512 sampled frames with a fixed 32-frame budget in Table 6. Existing main experiments retain their sampling and budget settings. Table 7 lists Original at 256/128 sampled frames, so equivalence to the main tables' within-budget Original settings cannot be assumed.

E4.justification: Table 5 adds ablations testing query inclusion in attention keys and maximum versus mean aggregation. Table 6 replaces the brief timing comparison with a sampling-size analysis of accuracy, encoding cost and selection cost. The stage ablation extends to MLVU, while the existing qualitative and search-space analyses remain.

E5.justification: v2 newly states that reported timing measurements are averaged over 10 runs; v1 gives no repeat count. This adds run-reporting information without establishing an increase in runs. Neither version reports accuracy confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial benchmark, backbone, ablation and timing results, including 54.4% MLVU accuracy for Qwen2-VL at 256–64. Retained main benchmark scores match, but Figure 5 changes EgoSchema quarter/half search-space accuracies from 66.7/66.6 to 66.6/66.7. v1's 0.43-second versus 2.24-second LongVU timing comparison disappears; the new timings concern different experimental conditions.

M1.justification: Uniform frame selection, cosine-difference token selection, candidate construction and second-layer attention scoring remain unchanged. Static/dynamic frames are renamed key/delta frames; the expanded equations and explanations describe the same procedure.

P1.justification: Substantial prose editing spans the abstract, related work, method exposition, experimental discussion and limitations. Frame terminology is standardized throughout, ablations are divided into stage and metric subsections, and the appendix is reorganized into additional experiments and prompt details.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is substantially redrawn, and Figure 4 replaces displayed frames while retaining the same questions and token ratios. Tables gain benchmark columns and comparator blocks, with new metric, efficiency and Qwen2.5-VL tables. The original LongVU Table 4 moves to Appendix Table 9 and gains another model block.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations for Qwen2.5-VL, MLVU, ActivityNet-QA, mPLUG-Owl3 and video GOP coding. The central positioning against KV-cache compression and training-dependent pre-input compression remains unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 rewrites v1's top-token selection equation as an explicit difference score followed by index selection, preserving the same mathematical operation. Frame indexing, budget relationships and attention scoring remain equivalent. No new theorem, proof or substantive formal assumption is introduced.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1's validation: Table 5 tests previously unablated metric choices, Table 6 measures encoding as well as selection costs, and additional datasets and a third backbone better test generalization. Clearer exposition and the code URL improve reproducibility information. This paper explores State Space Models (SSMs) as a promising alternative for code understanding tasks such as retrieval, classification, and clone detection. We introduce CodeSSM, the first SSM-based model trained on code corpora to assess its effectiveness. Our results demonstrate that SSMs are more sample-efficient and can extrapolate to longer contexts beyond the pretraining length. Extensive experiments show that SSMs offer a viable alternative to transformers, addressing several their limitations. Additionally, CodeSSM reduces memory usage by up to 64\% compared to transformers at a context length of 2048, with greater savings as context length grows.

C1.justification: v3 adds a headline quantitative claim of approximately 64% lower inference memory at context length 2048 and gives greater prominence to outperforming transformers on longer unseen contexts. These extend the principal contribution beyond v1's sample-efficiency and code-understanding claims, which remain central.

C2.justification: v3 adds expressivity and parameterization limitations, phase-based mechanism arguments, and a single-kernel explanation for failures in complex local contexts. It also qualifies when larger datasets favor transformers. Conversely, it drops v1's large-model overfitting exception and broadens the dropout-based claim that CodeSSM does not overfit.

D1.justification: v3 supplies numerical learning-rate and weight-decay settings, dataset split counts, additional model configurations, and code/weight links where v1 only promised weights. It revises the GPU description from A180 to A100. However, v1's explicit context-dependent batch sizes, 120k-step GitHub-issues stage and BertCoder initialization details are no longer specified; CodeSSM initialization and tokenizer details are mainly relocated.

E1.justification: v3 adds StackOverflow answer retrieval, DiverseVul vulnerability detection and seven-class Java complexity prediction. The original four tasks remain, with defect detection now identified as Devign and text-to-code search as NLCodeSearch. CodeSearchNet and StarCoder remain the pretraining corpora.

E2.justification: RoCoder and Zamba enter comparisons on retained benchmarks. Devign additionally includes GraphCodeBERT and CodeT5, while the new complexity-prediction comparison includes UniXcoder. These are reported comparison entries, whereas several corresponding models were only cited or absent in v1; CodeBERT and BertCoder remain.

E3.justification: v3 adds 256-context StarCoder pretraining comparisons, 1024-token SQA and complexity evaluations, and inference benchmarking at lengths 512, 1024 and 2048. The six- and 23-layer configuration evaluations disappear. Some original 512-context evaluations remain in Appendix H, so that configuration was not entirely removed.

E4.justification: Length-extrapolation comparisons expand, dropout robustness is examined on the small complexity benchmark, and Appendices F–G add kernel spectra and a worked type-inference failure case. Conversely, v1's model-depth scaling study and downstream failure results for the DFT variant disappear. The original MLM architectural ablations remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report benchmark point estimates without seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals or significance tests. The MLM plots retain shaded traces without defining a statistical uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: v3 adds results for three benchmarks, new comparators and configurations, and memory/throughput measurements, while removing model-depth result rows. StarCoder-trained 2048-context search MRR changes from 28.37 to 29.88. Its type-inference F1 is inconsistent within v3: 0.625 in Table 2 versus 0.619 in Table 11, which retains v1's value. These are reporting differences, not established same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The proposed 12-layer bidirectional gated SSM, MLM objective, tokenizer and initialization remain unchanged. Positional-embedding, dropout, DFT and unidirectional variants are retained under revised names. The omitted model-depth experiments concern configuration coverage rather than a revised computational procedure.

P1.justification: The title and model terminology change throughout, and the introduction and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. The combined results/discussion becomes separate Results and seven Research Questions sections; implementation material moves into appendices, and limitations and ethical considerations receive separate sections.

P2.justification: v3 redraws the architecture diagram, adds an efficiency overview and kernel-spectrum figures, and consolidates several benchmark tables. Detailed clone and type-inference metrics move to Appendix H, and the appendices change from single-column to two-column layout. Existing MLM plots and many table entries are redisplayed rather than newly introduced.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning against hybrid/selective SSMs and recent work on state tracking, token selection and SSM parameterization. New discussion includes Zamba2, Mamba, Merrill and colleagues, Nishikawa and Suzuki, and spectral state-space models, extending beyond v1's emphasis on attention efficiency and convolutional alternatives.

T1.justification: Appendix F adds a short mathematical comparison of SSM transfer functions and self-attention, including magnitude, phase and transformation assumptions in Equations 7–9. The background SSM and BiGS equations remain unchanged, and no new theorem or formal proof is provided.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important evidential gaps through a RoPE baseline, 256-to-1024-context SQA evaluation, and direct memory/throughput measurements, strengthening support for its central extrapolation and efficiency claims. Failure analysis and concrete reproducibility information add further value. Conflicting type-inference values in Tables 2 and 11 and Appendix F's unjustified claim that transformers cannot forget information are material weaknesses, but the empirical and reproducibility gains still constitute a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same BiGS-based code-understanding study, renamed from BiGSCoder to CodeSSM. Their main text, figures, tables, equations and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds benchmark evaluations, baseline comparisons, inference resource measurements, kernel analyses and a qualitative failure case.

before.justification: v1 reports original MLM training and validation results, four downstream benchmark evaluations, and architectural and training ablations.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) perform strongly in complex reasoning tasks via Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, but often suffer from verbose outputs, increasing computational overhead. Existing fine-tuning-based compression methods either operate post-hoc pruning, risking disruption to reasoning coherence, or rely on sampling-based selection, which fails to remove redundant content thoroughly. To address these limitations, this work begins by framing two key patterns of redundant reflection in LRMs--Confidence Deficit, wherein the model reflects on correct intermediate steps, and Termination Delay, where reflection continues after a verified, confident answer--through a confidence-guided perspective. Based on this, we introduce ConCISE (Confidence-guided Compression In Step-by-step Efficient Reasoning), a framework designed to generate concise reasoning chains, integrating Confidence Injection to boost reasoning confidence, and Early Stopping to terminate reasoning when confidence is sufficient. Extensive experiments demonstrate that compared to baseline methods, fine-tuning LRMs on ConCISE-generated data yields a better balance between compression and task performance, reducing length by up to approximately 50% under SimPO, while maintaining high task accuracy.

The central contributions—two redundancy patterns, two intervention mechanisms, and approximately 50% compression under SimPO while retaining strong accuracy—remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of robustness at thresholds 0.5–0.7, inadequate checking at 0.4, and training-free accuracy/compression tradeoffs. Its limitations replace the model-dependency discussion with unexplored RLVR integration and broaden remaining compression opportunities. These qualify the retained confidence-based explanation rather than replace it.

D1.justification: v2 substantially completes the training recipe: Appendix B documents the approximately 1,900-example common correct subset, exact data-generation sampling settings, LlamaFactory, effective batch size 32, gradient accumulation, four A800 GPUs, and training maximum length 10,240. These are newly disclosed details; the PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: Both versions use MATH training questions and evaluate on Math-500, GSM8K, AIME24, and GPQA_diamond. The validation and annotated-analysis datasets retain their coverage. Additional models and training-free procedures do not introduce new datasets, domains, or task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 retains OverThink and SPIRIT and adds evaluated training-free comparators TALE and DEER, including DEER settings of 0.95 and 0.98 (Section 4.4, Figure 6, Table 6). TALE's underlying work was cited in v1 but was not experimentally compared there.

E3.justification: v2 extends evaluation from two DeepSeek configurations to include Skywork-OR1-7B-Preview and Qwen3-8B. It also introduces direct-decoding comparisons and downstream SFT evaluations across stopping thresholds 0.4–0.7. Existing benchmark decoding settings, generation-length limits, and SFT/SimPO epoch counts remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's component ablations and stopping-point distributions, v2 tests how stopping thresholds affect fine-tuned performance (Table 5), reports unsuccessful alternative probing prompts, and expands confidence-mechanism validation across four models (Figure 4, Table 4). The existing DeepSeek-1.5B reflection analyses are relocated, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: Both versions report means over eight samples for AIME24 and GPQA_diamond. No new seed reporting, repeated-training-run information, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests appear. Expanded model-confidence measurements do not constitute statistical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The original DeepSeek benchmark and component-ablation scores are retained apart from rounding. Substantial new results cover Skywork, Qwen3, threshold sensitivity, and training-free methods (Tables 1, 5, 6). For example, Qwen3 ConCISE-SFT/SimPO report average accuracies of 80.6/79.4 with compression ratios of 92%/50%. Some benchmark-specific step plots are replaced by aggregate summaries.

M1.justification: The reported stopping procedure changes substantially: v1 Algorithm 1 terminates on confidence alone, whereas v2 requires a prompted answer to match ground truth, explicitly generates a concluding summary, and discards incorrect traces. Section 4.4 separately evaluates ConCISE-Decoding without ground-truth verification. Confidence Injection and SFT/SimPO training remain.

P2.justification: v2 adds a workflow overview and training-free comparison plot, expands and reformats Table 1, redraws confidence-validation plots, and adds Tables 5–6. improvement.justification: v2 addresses important gaps in v1's validation and reproducibility through additional model families, relevant training-free comparisons, downstream threshold tests, and explicit correctness checks and training settings. arxiv_record.abstract: The impact of Large Language Models (LLMs) has extended into literary domains. However, existing evaluation metrics for literature prioritize mechanical accuracy over artistic expression and tend to overrate machine translation as being superior to human translation from experienced professionals. In the long run, this bias could result in an irreversible decline in translation quality and cultural authenticity. In response to the urgent need for a specialized literary evaluation metric, we introduce LITRANSPROQA, a novel, reference-free, LLM-based question-answering framework designed for literary translation evaluation. LITRANSPROQA integrates humans in the loop to incorporate insights from professional literary translators and researchers, focusing on critical elements in literary quality assessment such as literary devices, cultural understanding, and authorial voice. Our extensive evaluation shows that while literary-finetuned XCOMET-XL yields marginal gains, LITRANSPROQA substantially outperforms current metrics, achieving up to 0.07 gain in correlation and surpassing the best state-of-the-art metrics by over 15 points in adequacy assessments. Incorporating professional translator insights as weights further improves performance, highlighting the value of translator inputs. Notably, LITRANSPROQA reaches an adequacy performance comparable to trained linguistic student evaluators, though it still falls behind experienced professional translators. LITRANSPROQA shows broad applicability to open-source models like LLaMA3.3-70b and Qwen2.5-32b, indicating its potential as an accessible and training-free tool for evaluating literary translations that require local processing due to copyright or ethical considerations.

C1.justification: The core claims remain a reference-free, translator-informed QA metric, stronger evaluation performance, benefits from translator weighting, and applicability to open models. V4 foregrounds the student-level human benchmark and professional-performance gap already acknowledged in v1 Section 5.2; the scientific contribution is not redefined.

C2.justification: V4 adds interpretations of complementary question aspects, hypotheses explaining limited XCOMET adaptation, and failure explanations involving cultural context and prompt complexity (Sections 5.3, A.2.3, A.4). It also discusses expert disagreement and adds qualifications concerning genre/style variation, broader audiences, and deployment risks.

D1.justification: V4 newly specifies the mt-metrics-eval version and commit, metadata modification, dependency versions, annotator background details, and code licensing. It updates the code/data repository location and explicitly states split availability. Existing finetuning hyperparameters and development-set sizes are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate on LITEVAL-CORPUS, LITERARYTRAN, and PAR3-ANNOTATED and finetune using PAR3-UNANNOTATED and WMT24. Language coverage and literary translation tasks are retained; the added analyses use existing coverage.

E2.justification: V4 adds TREQA-QE to the LITEVAL-CORPUS and LITERARYTRAN comparisons in Tables 3–4; v1 discussed TREQA but explicitly deferred evaluating it. Existing baselines remain, and the PAR3-ANNOTATED comparator set is unchanged.

E3.justification: The new ablation protocol scores each of six question aspects alone and excludes each aspect in turn on LITERARYTRAN (Section 5.3). Existing dataset splits, evaluation metrics, finetuning budgets, and base-model configurations remain unchanged; relocated development-set details do not indicate a new split.

E4.justification: V4 substantially expands diagnostic evidence through aspect-isolation and aspect-removal ablations, agreement analysis comparing all versus selected questions, and qualitative success and failure cases (Table 5, Figure 3, Tables 15–16). These examine component contributions, expert consistency, and template-specific failures beyond v1's retained analyses.

E5.justification: V4 introduces permutation-test significance reporting against the best baseline in Table 3, significance assessments of translator weighting in Section A.3.8, and pairwise Pearson/Kendall agreement distributions among translators. V1 lacks these statistical assessments. No increase in repeated runs or seeds is documented.

E6.justification: Original benchmark rows remain unchanged, but v4 adds substantial results for TREQA-QE, ablations, agreement, significance, and qualitative cases. For example, removing tone/authorial-voice questions yields ACC-EQ 0.428 versus 0.519 for the full set. V4 also corrects prose summaries: LITEVAL adequacy gains of 15.2/16.9 points become 14.7/16.4, matching the retained table.

M1.justification: The question-selection procedure, 25 selected questions, prompting templates, answer-to-score mapping, and translator weighting remain unchanged. XCOMET losses and layer configurations also match. Renaming the metric and analyzing question subsets do not establish a revised proposed method.

P1.justification: V4 renames the metric, edits and condenses passages, moves some dataset and development details into Appendix A, and adds descriptive subsections. The main introduction–related work–datasets–methods–results–conclusion structure and much of the narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1 expands from a small first-page column figure to a full-width overview. V4 adds an ablation table, agreement plots, and two extensive qualitative tables, while reorganizing appendix displays and adding significance markers. New Figure 4 visualizes the existing weighting comparison rather than introducing a separate experiment.

R1.justification: V4 adds AskQE to the QA-metric discussion and references Alexander, Ji et al., and Eger et al. for statistical reporting and broader context. The ChatEval discussion/reference is removed. Positioning around professional question design remains substantially the same; AskQE is not an evaluated baseline.

T1.justification: No mathematical definitions, training losses, theorems, or proofs are substantively changed. V4's explanations of correlation-metric suitability and agreement reporting add rationale rather than new formal derivations.

improvement.justification: V4 substantially strengthens validation of the unchanged method. The directly relevant TREQA-QE comparison, statistical assessments, aspect ablations, and explicit failure cases address important gaps in v1's evidence for comparative performance and professional question design. Corrected numerical summaries and clearer reproducibility information further improve reliability. Dataset coverage and existing generalization limitations remain unchanged.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research, renamed from TransProQA to LiTransProQA. Their main texts, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching retained experiments and question lists across renumbering.

after.justification: V4 retains these empirical results and adds TREQA-QE evaluations, question-aspect ablations, translator-agreement analysis, significance tests, and qualitative examples.

before.justification: V1 reports original metric evaluations on three literary translation datasets, XCOMET finetuning experiments, professional translator ratings, and comparisons across prompting templates and base models.

arxiv_record.abstract: Despite impressive progress in areas like mathematical reasoning, large language models still face significant challenges in consistently solving complex problems. Drawing inspiration from key human learning strategies, we propose two novel strategies to enhance the capability of large language models to solve these complex problems. First, Adaptive Difficulty Curriculum Learning (ADCL) is a novel curriculum learning strategy that tackles the Difficulty Shift phenomenon (i.e., a model's perception of problem difficulty dynamically changes during training) by periodically re-estimating difficulty within upcoming data batches to maintain alignment with the model's evolving capabilities. Second, Expert-Guided Self-Reformulation (EGSR) is a novel reinforcement learning strategy that bridges the gap between imitation learning and pure exploration by guiding models to reformulate expert solutions within their own conceptual framework, rather than relying on direct imitation, fostering deeper understanding and knowledge assimilation. Extensive experiments on challenging mathematical reasoning benchmarks, using Qwen2.5-7B as the base model, demonstrate that these human-inspired strategies synergistically and significantly enhance performance. Notably, their combined application improves performance over the standard Zero-RL baseline by 10% on the AIME24 benchmark and 16.6% on AIME25.
arxiv_record.authors: Enci Zhang, Xingang Yan, Wei Lin, Tianxiang Zhang, Qianchun Lu
arxiv_record.title: Learning Like Humans: Advancing LLM Reasoning Capabilities via Adaptive Difficulty Curriculum Learning and Expert-Guided Self-Reformulation

C1.justification: The first contribution changes from theoretical insights about human learning mechanisms to conceptual and empirical insights identifying Difficulty Shift and supporting stable expert-knowledge integration. The central ADCL/EGSR contributions and the headline AIME24 and AIME25 improvement claims remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive limitations concerning fixed re-estimation frequency, dependence on expert-demonstration quality, and untested training paradigms and domains. It introduces ZPD and self-explanation interpretations and interprets Table 2 as evidence of broader model applicability. Conversely, it removes the detailed explanation that gradual post-training shifts make local re-ranking preferable to full-dataset SPL.

D1.justification: Appendix C newly specifies SFT's learning rate of 2e-5 with decay, maximum length of 8192, and gradient accumulation of 1. It separately assigns gradient accumulation of 4 to GRPO. These clarify previously underspecified SFT settings without establishing that the original experiment was rerun.

E1.justification: Both versions use BaseSet-7K and AugSet-10K derived from S1 and DeepScaleR, and evaluate mathematical reasoning on MATH-500, AIME24, AIME25, AMC23, and Minervamath. The shortened MATH table heading does not indicate a different dataset. Additional model configurations do not extend task coverage.

E2.justification: The corresponding Qwen2.5-7B comparisons retain the same comparator membership, including SFT, standard RL, PCL, and direct off-policy replacement. The added model evaluations and training plots reuse existing comparison strategies rather than introduce new baseline methods.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 and Table 2 extend evaluation from Qwen2.5-7B to Qwen2.5-1.5B and Llama3.1-8B-Instruct across four retained benchmarks. This substantially expands the tested model scales and families. Table 2 specifies the same experimental setup as Table 1; the original benchmark metrics and data construction remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds explicit testing of generalization across model families and scales, plus EGSR versus RL/off-policy reward dynamics and SFT optimization diagnostics in Figures 5–6. The original perplexity, pass@32, and reasoning-case analyses remain. The NIR analysis moves to Appendix D, while Figure 4 largely redisplays existing ADCL curves.

E5.justification: The existing perplexity distributions and rank-deviation quantiles are retained. V2 adds no reported seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty estimates, confidence intervals, or significance-testing procedures; its additional training traces do not specify a new uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: Table 2 adds substantial results for two model configurations: combined ADCL/EGSR obtains MATH scores of 69.80 versus RL's 59.00 on Qwen2.5-1.5B, and 60.60 versus 53.20 on Llama3.1-8B-Instruct. Figures 5–6 add training outcomes. All numerical entries in the original Tables 1 and 3 and the relocated NIR table are unchanged.

M1.justification: The ADCL batch re-ranking procedure and EGSR guided-trajectory replacement remain unchanged. Equations 1–4 and Algorithms 1–2 match; the condensed method descriptions and additional model evaluations do not introduce a new procedure.

P1.justification: V2 substantially streamlines the introduction, related work, method exposition, and conclusion, including replacing ADCL's numbered explanation with prose and removing duplicated perplexity discussion. It reorganizes the analysis section, moves NIR discussion into Appendix D, and adds a dedicated limitations section.

P2.justification: V2 adds the two-model Table 2 and Figures 4–6, expands the hyperparameter table, and relocates the NIR table to Appendix D. Figures 1–3 retain identical graphics, while Figure 4 redisplays ADCL dynamics. The later appendices switch from full-width presentation to two-column layouts, substantially reflowing prompts and the case study.

R1.justification: V2 grounds the human-learning motivation in Vygotsky and Cole's ZPD and Chi et al.'s self-explanation work, replacing the informal exercise-book analogy. It also adds the Llama and Qwen model-report citations. The broader positioning against static curricula and direct off-policy learning remains.

T1.justification: Equations 1–4 and the mathematical reasoning in the retained case study are unchanged. The new educational-psychology motivation introduces no formal assumptions, mathematical results, derivations, or proofs.

improvement.justification: V1's evidence for broadly useful training strategies depended on one Qwen2.5-7B backbone. V2 substantially strengthens that evidence by testing a smaller Qwen model and a different Llama family with the existing comparison strategies, demonstrating combined-method gains over RL across four retained benchmarks. arxiv_record.abstract: Recent advances in LLM agents have largely built on reasoning backbones like ReAct, which interleave thought and action in complex environments. However, ReAct often produces ungrounded or incoherent reasoning steps, leading to misalignment between the agent's actual state and goal. Our analysis finds that this stems from ReAct's inability to maintain consistent internal beliefs and goal alignment, causing compounding errors and hallucinations. To address this, we introduce ReflAct, a novel backbone that shifts reasoning from merely planning next actions to continuously reflecting on the agent's state relative to its goal. By explicitly grounding decisions in states and enforcing ongoing goal alignment, ReflAct dramatically improves strategic reliability. This design delivers substantial empirical gains: ReflAct surpasses ReAct by 27.7% on average, achieving a 93.3% success rate in ALFWorld. Notably, ReflAct even outperforms ReAct with added enhancement modules (e.g., Reflexion, WKM), showing that strengthening the core reasoning backbone is key to reliable agent performance.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same contribution and claims about goal-state reflection, grounding and advantages over existing reasoning frameworks. The headline 27.7% average improvement and 93.3% ALFWorld success rate are unchanged.

C2.justification: New discussion identifies exploration limits and misunderstood environment rules as ReflAct failure mechanisms, explains output-format problems with Qwen3 thinking mode, and interprets prompt sensitivity and shorter trajectories. This materially expands the account of effectiveness and failure conditions, while retaining the original domain and token-cost limitations.

D1.justification: Appendices D.3 and K supply exact ablation prompts, full environment instructions, action lists, output formats and additional ALFWorld examples. BabyAI implementation information is also added. Hardware disclosures are unchanged. v2 removes the promised post-publication code release without supplying a ReflAct repository link.

E1.justification: Appendix H adds BabyAI, extending evaluation to five tasks involving navigation and object interactions in a 2D grid world. The existing ALFWorld, ScienceWorld and Jericho coverage is retained.

E2.justification: The corresponding existing experiments retain NoThinking, ReAct, Plan-and-Act, Reflexion, WKM, RAFA and MPO. Qwen3 is an additional agent backbone. Newly discussed SwiftSage and KnowSelf are not evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: New evaluations use Qwen3-8B with thinking mode disabled and BabyAI with 10 episodes per task, 50 episodes total, a 128-step limit and average progression. Appendix I adds controlled prompt variants and an average reasoning-step metric. Existing benchmark splits and success criteria remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds instruction and ICL-example paraphrasing tests, reasoning-step comparisons, ALFWorld task-level success breakdowns and diagnoses of Heat/Clean failures. Figure 26 adds a book-and-desklamp case. These substantially extend the retained ablation, hallucination and behavioral analyses.

E5.justification: Neither version reports independent repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. New results remain point estimates; BabyAI episode counts describe evaluation sample size rather than an uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: The original main results are retained, while Tables 3–8 add model, benchmark, prompt-variant, reasoning-step and task-specific results. For example, Qwen3 ALFWorld success is 65.7 for ReAct versus 80.6 for ReflAct, and BabyAI GPT-4o progression is 64.0 versus 76.0. These are additional evaluations, not improvements over v1 under unchanged conditions.

M1.justification: Section 4 retains the same goal-state reflection followed by action generation and the same one-shot prompting approach. The expanded environment-specific instructions document implementation details without establishing a change to the proposed procedure.

P1.justification: Localized copyediting, acknowledgements and revised related-work prose accompany clearer setup and prompt subsections. The appendices gain sections and separate instructions from ICL examples, but the main narrative and section order are largely retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds six result tables, full instruction panels, additional prompt examples and an ALFWorld case-study figure. Existing appendix displays are relocated, and prompt panels gain titles and sometimes span pages. This substantially expands the visual presentation while preserving the original core figures and tables.

R1.justification: Appendix A adds an imitation-learning comparison with ETO, SwiftSage and KnowSelf, emphasizing ReflAct's lack of parameter updates. References for SwiftSage, KnowSelf, Qwen3, BabyAI and BALROG are added. The broader positioning against reasoning backbones and enhancement modules remains intact.

T1.justification: Section 2 corrects the interaction history to end with the thought and action at t−1, instead of including the current outputs at t. This removes circular conditioning from the formal definition. The remaining mathematical definitions and reasoning are retained.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially improves the assessability of this prompt-based method: missing ablation and environment instructions are supplied, prompt sensitivity is tested, and success-oriented examples are complemented by concrete ReflAct failure diagnoses. Qwen3 and BabyAI broaden empirical support while preserving the original results. These gains outweigh the removed code-release pledge, although absent uncertainty reporting and restricted added settings, including disabled Qwen3 thinking mode, still limit the conclusions.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ReflAct, with matching methods and core experiments. The complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables and figures, are readable and support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds Qwen3-8B and BabyAI evaluations, prompt sensitivity experiments, reasoning-step comparisons and task-specific failure analyses.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations on ALFWorld, ScienceWorld and Jericho, including baseline comparisons, ablations, enhancement-module experiments and behavioral analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: We show that training a single $d$-dimensional steering vector per layer with reinforcement learning, while freezing all base weights, matches the accuracy of fully RL-tuned reasoning models on mathematical-reasoning tasks. On an 8 billion-parameter model this adds only $\approx 0.0016\%$ additional parameters and reproduces performance across a range of base models and mathematical-reasoning benchmarks. These results tighten the upper bound on the parameter budget required for high-level chain-of-thought reasoning, indicating that millions of adapter weights are unnecessary. The minimal trainable footprint reduces optimizer memory and inter-GPU communication, lowering the overall cost of fine-tuning. Moreover, a logit-lens analysis shows that the learned vectors amplify coherent token directions, providing clearer insight into the model's internal computations.
arxiv_record.authors: Viacheslav Sinii, Alexey Gorbatovski, Artem Cherepanov, Boris Shaposhnikov, Nikita Balagansky, Daniil Gavrilov
arxiv_record.title: Steering LLM Reasoning Through Bias-Only Adaptation

C1.justification: v1 foregrounds evidence that RL amplifies pre-existing reasoning abilities. v2 instead foregrounds matching full tuning with approximately 0.0016% additional parameters, tightening the empirical parameter budget, reducing memory/communication costs and isolating interpretable parameters. The latent-capability argument remains as secondary motivation and in Appendix E.

C2.justification: v2 explains efficiency through smaller optimizer states and reduced parameter broadcasting, and qualifies the new parity finding with the Llama3.1-8B exception. Existing logit-lens interpretations, regularization and LoRA explanations, and limitations concerning generality and downstream transformations are substantially retained.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents Math-Verify reward checking and its access link, per-update parameter broadcasting to vLLM, and dataset/rank-specific hyperparameter listings. The steering code and hardware disclosure are retained. These are limited reproducibility additions; the new DeepScaleR study lacks a corresponding detailed learning-rate/rollout table.

E1.justification: v2 adds DeepScaleR training and evaluation on AIME24, AIME25, AMC23, MinervaMath and OlympiadBench. The original GSM8K/MATH experiments remain in Appendix E; MATH500 was already represented in v1. This substantially broadens the mathematical problem coverage.

E2.justification: v2 Table 1 adds reported comparison scores for SimpleRL-Zoo/Zero, Open-Reasoner, Oat-Zero and R1-Distill. These are literature reference scores, not documented reruns. The original Base, Full-Tune and LoRA comparisons remain in Table 4; LoRA-1 hyperparameter rows alone do not establish additional evaluated comparisons.

E3.justification: The new study adds Qwen 7B/14B configurations, training and evaluation context limits, PASS@1/AVG@32 metrics, and distinct base-versus-trained decoding procedures. Reported settings for retained experiments also change: Llama3.1-8B rollout counts fall from 128 to 64, and Qwen2.5-1.5B steering learning rates rise from 1e-4 to 5e-4. Identical retained accuracy scores do not establish reruns.

E4.justification: Tables 3 and 5 add a focused analysis of whether parameter efficiency translates into reduced optimizer memory and parameter-broadcast costs. The logit-lens analysis and GSM8K/MATH transfer comparisons are retained, with no new ablation or robustness sweep.

E5.justification: Unlike v1's point estimates without seed information, v2 reports averaging the new evaluation over three seeds and supplies ± values throughout its main results table. This substantially changes uncertainty reporting, although the ± statistic is undefined and evaluation repeats do not establish repeated training runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results under the new settings: average steering/full-tuning scores are 42.3/41.3 for Qwen2.5-14B and 9.1/11.5 for Llama3.1-8B. Tables 3 and 5 add resource measurements. v1 Table 1 is preserved numerically as v2 Table 4; the new results are not same-setting improvements over those earlier scores.

M1.justification: Both versions train one additive residual-stream vector per transformer layer with frozen base weights. The steering implementation, policy-gradient equations and LoRA construction are unchanged. v2 names the objective RLOO and documents Math-Verify, but does not establish a changed optimization or reward procedure.

The original experimental setup and results move into Appendix E, while the appendices are reorganized around the new main study. Affiliations and an acknowledgment are also added.

P2.justification: v2 adds the steering schematic in Figure 1, a new six-benchmark main results table and two resource-cost tables. arxiv_record.abstract: Encoder transformer models compress information from all tokens in a sequence into a single [CLS] token to represent global context. This approach risks diluting fine-grained or hierarchical features, leading to information loss in downstream tasks where local patterns are important. To remedy this, we propose a lightweight architectural enhancement: an inception-style 1-D convolution module that sits on top of the transformer layer and augments token representations with multi-scale local features. This enriched feature space is then processed by a self-attention layer that dynamically weights tokens based on their task relevance. Experiments on five diverse tasks show that our framework consistently improves general-purpose, domain-specific, and multilingual models, outperforming baselines by 1% to 14% while maintaining efficiency. Ablation studies show that multi-scale convolution performs better than any single kernel and that the self-attention layer is critical for performance.

C1.justification: The central contribution and reported 1%–14% improvement claim remain. v2 adds an abstract claim that multi-scale convolution outperforms individual kernels, explicitly claims integration into pretrained encoders without costly retraining or model-specific adjustments, and introduces a below-10% inference-overhead claim.

C2.justification: The original local-feature and attention-redistribution interpretation remains. v2 adds explanations for differing emotion/irony gains, a channel-selection heuristic, a redundancy or oversmoothing hypothesis for stacking, and an explicit limitation that performance on tasks dominated by long-range dependencies has not been tested.

D1.justification: New Appendix A specifies the baseline's final-layer CLS representation, dropout probability of 0.3, and linear classification head. Figure 4 newly identifies the layers supplying baseline and inceptive attention maps. These are additional disclosures; the PDFs do not establish changes to the existing implementations.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate English emotion recognition and irony detection from TweetEval, Bengali emotion recognition, OHSUMED, and CAVES. The dataset statistics are unchanged, moving from v1 Table 1 to v2 Appendix B, Table 7.

E2.justification: v2 Tables 2–3 add ModernBERT and DeBERTa v3 comparisons across all four English tasks. BioBERT-Large also becomes a comparator on CAVES, whereas v1 evaluated it only on OHSUMED. The earlier comparator rows are retained.

E3.justification: Existing sequence lengths, training budgets, optimization settings, metrics, and cross-validation construction remain unchanged. New experiments introduce single-kernel and convolution-free controls, one-versus-two-module configurations, and inceptive BioBERT-Large configurations.

E4.justification: v1 ablates only attention and the dense block. v2 Table 6 additionally tests each of four convolution kernels separately and removes convolution entirely, directly examining the central multi-scale contribution. Appendix G tests stacking depth; additional attention comparisons and an illustrative irony case broaden the diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: Both versions report ten runs per model and dataset, cross-validation means and standard deviations, distributions across runs, and Wilcoxon signed-rank testing at the 0.05 threshold. The added significance-test rows follow the existing reporting practice.

E6.justification: Retained main benchmark rows keep their scores, while v2 adds substantial results for new comparators and architectural controls. For example, Table 3 reports OHSUMED F1 scores of 56.71 for ModernBERT and 64.07 for iMB-128. The full-model OHSUMED ablation value changes from 73.32 to 72.34, matching the retained main result. Appendix G newly reports stacked-model scores of 71.97 on OHSUMED and 83.38 on irony.

M1.justification: The main transformer–inception–attention–pooling–classifier architecture and training objectives remain unchanged. Appendix G introduces an implemented variant with two sequential inception modules; it is a limited architectural extension rather than a replacement for the original model.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, comparative-results narrative, and performance interpretation are extensively rewritten. Related work and limitations gain topical subheadings, model notation receives a dedicated explanation, and the appendices are reorganized around new baseline and dataset material while retaining the earlier supplements.

P2.justification: v2 adds an introductory overview figure, class-distribution charts, word clouds, and a stacking comparison. Performance and ablation tables expand substantially. Attention plots combine baseline and inceptive curves, introduce logarithmic axes in several panels, and add model comparisons; other plots are restyled and the dataset-statistics table moves to the appendix.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for Multi-CLS BERT, DeBERTa v3, and ModernBERT, plus an encoder-versus-LLM discussion supported by three additional studies. It also makes its novelty claim explicit. The earlier positioning as a general architectural enhancement complementary to pretraining modifications remains.

T1.justification: The convolution, feature concatenation, attention, pooling, and classification equations are substantively unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and the added architectural explanations introduce no new formal results.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important gap in v1 by directly comparing the central multi-scale module with single-kernel and convolution-free alternatives. arxiv_record.abstract: Current VLM-based VQA methods often process entire images, leading to excessive visual tokens that include redundant information irrelevant to the posed question. This abundance of unnecessary image details creates numerous visual tokens, drastically increasing memory and computational requirements in VLMs. To address this, we propose Contextual Region-Oriented Visual Token Pruning (CROP), a novel framework to compress visual tokens through a two-step process: Localization and Pruning. Specifically, CROP first employs an efficient model to identify the contextual region relevant to the input query. Subsequently, two distinct strategies are introduced for pruning: (1) Pre-LLM Compression (PLC), which adaptively compresses different image regions with varying ratios, and (2) Inner-LLM Pruning (ILP), a training-free method that prunes tokens within early LLM layers guided by the identified contextual region. Extensive experiments on a wide range of VQA tasks demonstrate that CROP significantly outperforms existing visual token pruning methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance.
arxiv_record.authors: Jiawei Guo, Feifei Zhai, Pu Jian, Qianrun Wei, Yu Zhou

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and contribution list retain the same central claims: contextual-region-guided pruning, a reusable localizer, PLC and ILP strategies, and strong performance without retraining the main VLM for ILP. The additional experiments support these existing claims rather than redefine them.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of overlapping localization with backbone execution, pruning-depth tradeoffs and dependence on localization quality. Appendix E identifies failures when a single region omits relational or global information and proposes multiple regions as future work. These substantially extend v1's discussion, whose explicit limitation concerned training overhead.

D1.justification: V2 replaces the future code/data-release promise with a stated release and repository address, clarifies ground-truth-box use and VisionZip's fine-tuned variant, and removes boundary markers from Appendix A's response template. Most training hyperparameters remain unchanged. Section 4.1 changes localizer training time from 8 to 12 hours, although Section 3.2 still says 8.

E1.justification: The training sources and six VQA benchmarks are retained, as are the question-guided localization and VQA tasks. The new annotated TextVQA study and qualitative cases examine existing coverage; additional backbones change model configurations. ScienceQA remains image-only despite its shortened table label.

E2.justification: V2 removes MustDrop at all three budgets and FasterVLM at 64 tokens from the 7B comparison in v1 Table 2. Conversely, v2 Table 2 adds SparseVLM and PDrop to the 13B comparisons previously reported in v1 Table 3. These materially revise comparator participation.

E3.justification: V2 adds NeXT multi-crop and Qwen variable-token configurations, 13B PLC, timing measurements, a pruning-layer sweep and a 3,000-sample localization protocol with area recall and size-matched controls. The 13B aggregate now includes POPE. Section 4.1 also explicitly includes instruction-following data in localizer training, revising the reported setting without establishing that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The original region-only and anchor-removal studies survive as v2 Tables 5–6. Appendices D–E add pruning-layer sensitivity, localization accuracy against manual annotations, ground-truth/center/random region controls, and success/failure cases examining relational and global-context questions.

E5.justification: Appendix C in both versions says results are averaged across multiple experimental runs. Neither supplies run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new sample counts and recall summaries do not introduce an uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial backbone, timing, pruning-layer and localization results, including mean localization recall of 0.9477 in Table 9. Retained 7B benchmark scores are unchanged. The 13B 64-token aggregate changes from 95.7% to 96.2% after adding POPE; scores on the original five benchmarks remain unchanged, so this is not a same-setting performance gain.

M1.justification: The Qwen2-VL-2B localizer, 8×8 region representation, region-guided ILP and PLC query/anchor fusion remain unchanged, including Equations (1)–(5). Additional backbone evaluations and implementation explanations do not introduce a new pruning rule or compression component.

P1.justification: V2 standardizes much of the terminology from key or continuous regions to contextual regions, edits the introduction, shortens the conclusion, and restructures related work. Additional experiments receive new subsections and appendices, while the core method and original analysis largely retain their wording and organization.

P2.justification: V2 merges the separate 7B/13B tables into a wide side-by-side Table 2, adds six experimental tables and three case-study figures, and revises schematic highlights and grid labels. Existing ablations are relocated and renumbered. Figure 2's caption also acquires stray citation-key text.

R1.justification: Related work expands from two subsections to four, adding general LLM literature and chain-of-thought/locate-then-answer approaches such as V*, TextCoT, Argus and MRFD. V2 explicitly positions coarse block localization against precise bounding-box prediction and model-specific fine-tuning, substantially broadening its research positioning.

T1.justification: The coordinate constraints and mathematical constructions in Equations (1)–(5) are unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs. V2's standard area-recall description supports empirical evaluation rather than introducing new theoretical reasoning.

improvement.justification: V1 supports efficiency mainly through token reduction and validates localization largely through downstream results. V2 adds measured inference times, independent-backbone evaluations, annotated localization controls and explicit failure analyses, substantially strengthening empirical support and applicability assessment. Dropped comparators and reporting defects—including conflicting training times and incorrect NeXT token-count headings—reduce polish and precision, but do not outweigh these substantive gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CROP and are readable throughout, including equations, tables, figures and appendices. Corresponding methods and experiments can be matched reliably. V1's final visualization appendix contains only a heading; v2 supplies substantive additional material.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds evaluations on other backbones, inference timings, pruning-layer ablations, annotated localization measurements and qualitative success/failure cases.

before.justification: V1 reports original CROP evaluations on LLaVA-1.5-7B/13B, region-only pruning experiments and an anchor-token ablation in Tables 2–5.

arxiv_record.abstract: With over 2,000 languages and potentially millions of speakers, Africa represents one of the richest linguistic regions in the world. Yet, this diversity is scarcely reflected in state-of-the-art natural language processing (NLP) systems and large language models (LLMs), which predominantly support a narrow set of high-resource languages. This exclusion not only limits the reach and utility of modern NLP technologies but also risks widening the digital divide across linguistic communities. Nevertheless, NLP research on African languages is active and growing. In recent years, there has been a surge of interest in this area, driven by several factors-including the creation of multilingual language resources, the rise of community-led initiatives, and increased support through funding programs. In this survey, we analyze 884 research papers on NLP for African languages published over the past five years, offering a comprehensive overview of recent progress across core tasks. We identify key trends shaping the field and conclude by outlining promising directions to foster more inclusive and sustainable NLP research for African languages.
arxiv_record.authors: Jesujoba O. Alabi, Michael A. Hedderich, David Ifeoluwa Adelani, Dietrich Klakow
arxiv_record.title: Charting the Landscape of African NLP: Mapping Progress and Shaping the Road Ahead

      <pages>27807-27841</pages>
      <abstract>With over 2,000 languages and potentially millions of speakers, Africa represents one of the richest linguistic regions in the world. Yet, this diversity is scarcely reflected in state-of-the-art natural language processing (NLP) systems and large language models (LLMs), which predominantly support a narrow set of high-resource languages. This exclusion not only limits the reach and utility of modern NLP technologies but also risks widening the digital divide across linguistic communities. Nevertheless, NLP research on African languages is active and growing. In recent years, there has been a surge of interest in this area, driven by several factors—including the creation of multilingual language resources, the rise of community-led initiatives, and increased support through funding programs. In this survey, we analyze 884 research papers on NLP for African languages published over the past five years, offering a comprehensive overview of recent progress across core tasks. We identify key trends shaping the field and conclude by outlining promising directions to foster more inclusive and sustainable NLP research for African languages.</abstract>

C1.justification: The abstract, three introductory goals, and conclusion retain the same contributions: a comprehensive overview, an accessible research resource, and identification of open issues. Updating the corpus size does not redefine the central claims about progress and uneven coverage.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive limitations concerning missing language metadata, testing only one filtering prompt, and the absence of systematic social and ethical assessment. It also explains the inclusion of African-accented European languages. The principal interpretations and future directions remain.

D1.justification: v1 promises a future dataset release; v3 states that both data and code are public and supplies repository access information. v3 also documents the expanded filtering prompt and the ISO 639-3 restriction on Glottolog search languages, substantially improving reproducibility information.

E1.justification: Reported coverage increases slightly from 2,271 to 2,275 African languages and dialects (Section 4.2). The filtering evaluation also changes its target from general AI relevance to NLP relevance. The survey retains its broad African NLP domain.

E2.justification: Neither version evaluates competing methods against a proposed model or screening system. Added models in the resource catalogs are surveyed resources, not experimentally evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: Language search terms expand from 53 NLLB-200 languages to 2,290 ISO-coded Glottolog languages, and searched venues add FAccT and RANLP. The analyzed corpus changes from 734 to 884 papers. Appendix B also increases the balanced filtering audit from 25 to 50 papers per category.

E4.justification: Appendix B revises the screening error analysis for the new NLP-relevance criterion. The larger manual audit reports one false negative, replacing the earlier AI-filter audit whose errors included computer-vision papers. No ablation or prompt-sensitivity experiment is added.

E5.justification: Both versions report descriptive counts, percentages, and filtering accuracy without repeated-run information, confidence intervals, significance tests, or other uncertainty estimates. The increased audit sample size changes the evaluation design, not uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Numerous corpus findings change: the publication peak moves from 2023 to 2024, the leading country pair changes from Mozambique/Nigeria to Mozambique/Uganda, and dataset-creation papers increase from 350 to 401. Appendix B reports 92% versus 99% filtering accuracy under different criteria and samples, not a controlled performance gain. Tables 3-4 add resource entries.

M1.justification: The GPT-4o screening component changes from general AI classification to an explicit NLP-relevance decision rule covering speech, multimodal language tasks, and related applications (Appendix B, Listing 1). The overall retrieval, screening, and manual-coding pipeline remains.

P1.justification: v3 makes localized wording and terminology corrections, expands related-survey explanations, and organizes limitations into labeled paragraphs. The section sequence and most of the narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is redesigned as a full-width horizontal flowchart. Other plots receive revised axes and category labels, Listing 1 expands to full width, and resource tables gain rows. The overall two-column design and figure/table inventory remain.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds Ghanaian surveys and explicit comparisons with tool-focused, bootstrapping, and translation-bias surveys. Appendix D adds a meta-learning synthesis, and the resource catalogs gain references. These extend the literature discussion while retaining the continental landscape positioning.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal mathematical definitions, assumptions, theorems, or proofs. Added descriptions of techniques such as meta-learning remain conceptual literature summaries.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens the survey's collection procedure and reproducibility: replacing the 53-language query list with 2,290 Glottolog languages addresses restrictive retrieval, while explicit NLP screening and reported public code/data access make the evidence easier to assess. Expanded limitations improve qualification of the findings. Bookkeeping remains imperfect: Table 2 reports 27,617 retrieved papers whereas Section 3 and Figure 2 report 27,593. This localized inconsistency does not outweigh the methodological and transparency gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same African NLP survey. Their main text, Figures 1-7, Tables 1-4, and Appendices A-E are available and readable, supporting a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original quantitative analyses of 884 manually annotated papers and a 100-paper evaluation of automatic filtering in Appendix B.

before.justification: v1 reports original quantitative analyses of 734 manually annotated papers and a 50-paper evaluation of automatic filtering in Appendix B.

arxiv_record.abstract: Miscalibration in Large Language Models (LLMs) undermines their reliability, highlighting the need for accurate confidence estimation. We introduce CCPS (Calibrating LLM Confidence by Probing Perturbed Representation Stability), a novel method analyzing internal representational stability in LLMs. CCPS applies targeted adversarial perturbations to final hidden states, extracts features reflecting the model's response to these perturbations, and uses a lightweight classifier to predict answer correctness. CCPS was evaluated on LLMs from 8B to 32B parameters (covering Llama, Qwen, and Mistral architectures) using MMLU and MMLU-Pro benchmarks in both multiple-choice and open-ended formats. Our results show that CCPS significantly outperforms current approaches. Across four LLMs and three MMLU variants, CCPS reduces Expected Calibration Error by approximately 55% and Brier score by 21%, while increasing accuracy by 5 percentage points, Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve by 4 percentage points, and Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve by 6 percentage points, all relative to the strongest prior method. CCPS delivers an efficient, broadly applicable, and more accurate solution for estimating LLM confidence, thereby improving their trustworthiness.
arxiv_record.authors: Reza Khanmohammadi, Erfan Miahi, Mehrsa Mardikoraem, Simerjot Kaur, Ivan Brugere, Charese H. Smiley, Kundan Thind, and Mohammad M. Ghassemi

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same methodological, efficiency, generalizability, and calibration/discrimination claims, including the headline improvement figures.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning semantic token prioritization, perturbation features as the principal performance driver, complementary feature groups, and changing confidence signals with task difficulty. It also interprets MedMCQA results as supporting medical-domain generalization. The existing limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 explains the fixed perturbation hyperparameter choices and feature-vector composition more explicitly. However, it removes v1's disclosures of Unsloth model versions, non-quantized handling, bfloat16 precision, and Transformers/PyTorch usage. Architecture, hardware, and code/data access information otherwise remain.

E1.justification: Appendix I adds MedMCQA evaluation in multiple-choice and open-ended formats. This extends existing medical and general QA coverage; the CT training datasets and original MMLU evaluations are retained.

E2.justification: Self-Consistency is newly evaluated across all four LLMs and three MMLU variants in Appendix K.2 and Table 17. The existing comparator set remains present in the original benchmark comparisons.

E3.justification: New evaluation protocols include token-feature zeroing with POS grouping, controlled 12/63/75-feature comparisons, and 75 distinct feature-removal retrainings per LLM. These substantially expand the experimental controls. Original benchmark settings and metrics remain unchanged; self-consistency sampling details are incomplete.

E4.justification: Appendices K.1, K.3, and K.5 add tests of content-word sensitivity, perturbation versus original-feature contributions, and individual-feature importance through removal and retraining. These extend substantially beyond v1's SHAP analysis, which is retained as K.4.

E5.justification: The existing mean ± standard-deviation tables are unchanged. No new seed counts, confidence intervals, or specified significance tests appear. Token-masking effects are called statistically significant without a reported testing procedure; the 75 retrainings represent distinct ablation conditions.

E6.justification: Original MMLU scores are retained, while Tables 12 and 16–19 add substantial results. For example, MedMCQA multiple-choice Llama ECE is 26.8 for CT versus 11.0 for CCPS; Qwen-14B MMLU-Pro ablation ECE is 21.0, 11.0, and 4.2 for original-only, perturbation-only, and full features.

M1.justification: The frozen-LLM perturbation procedure, 75-feature representation, MC/OE architectures, and two-stage training remain unchanged. The added loss formula and feature accounting document the existing approach without establishing a changed algorithm.

P1.justification: Localized rewrites clarify perturbation choices, evaluation metrics, and semantic grading. New appendices reorganize supplementary material, including moving SHAP into the ablation section. Author/contact and acknowledgment text also change, while the main narrative structure remains recognizable.

P2.justification: Table 1 changes from a narrow vertical arrangement to a full-width layout pairing models side by side. Five supplementary tables are added, and existing tables are renumbered. All 34 figures are retained unchanged apart from their placement and surrounding page formatting.

R1.justification: v2 adds Pal et al. for MedMCQA and Xiong et al. for self-consistency, strengthening the explicit comparison with output-consensus approaches. Several model and software references disappear with the removed language-model paragraph; the broader related-work framing is retained.

T1.justification: Section 3.3 adds an explicit mathematical definition of the previously named max-margin loss. Its self-distance term, ||e+ - e+||, is identically zero and does not support the accompanying claim of pulling correct embeddings together. Existing perturbation mathematics remains unchanged; no theorem or proof is added.

improvement.justification: The controlled feature-group and removal ablations substantially address v1's weak attribution of gains to perturbations, previously supported mainly by SHAP and comparisons with different methods. Self-consistency and MedMCQA evaluations further strengthen the empirical case. These gains outweigh limited documentation losses and new weaknesses, including the inconsistent loss explanation, underspecified sampling protocol, and unsupported statistical-significance wording.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CCPS research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds MedMCQA results, self-consistency comparisons, token-masking experiments, and feature ablations.

before.justification: v1 reports original confidence-estimation experiments across four LLMs and three MMLU variants, with aggregate results, calibration plots, and SHAP analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning has significantly advanced Large Language Models (LLMs) in solving complex tasks. However, its autoregressive paradigm leads to significant computational overhead, hindering its deployment in latency-sensitive applications. To address this, we propose \textbf{DART} (\textbf{D}istilling \textbf{A}utoregressive \textbf{R}easoning to Silent \textbf{T}hought), a self-distillation framework that enables LLMs to replace autoregressive CoT with non-autoregressive Silent Thought (ST). Specifically, DART introduces two training pathways: the CoT pathway for traditional reasoning and the ST pathway for generating answers directly from a few ST tokens. The ST pathway utilizes a lightweight Reasoning Evolvement Module (REM) to align its hidden states with the CoT pathway, enabling the ST tokens to evolve into informative embeddings. During inference, only the ST pathway is activated, leveraging evolving ST tokens to deliver the answer directly. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that DART offers significant performance gains compared with existing non-autoregressive baselines without extra inference latency, serving as a feasible alternative for efficient reasoning.
arxiv_record.authors: Nan Jiang, Ziming Wu, De-Chuan Zhan, Fuming Lai, Shaobing Lian
arxiv_record.title: DART: Distilling Autoregressive Reasoning to Silent Thought

arxiv_record.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in morally sensitive domains, it is crucial to understand how persona traits affect their moral reasoning and persuasive behavior. We present the first large-scale study of multi-dimensional persona effects in AI-AI debates over real-world moral dilemmas. Using a 6-dimensional persona space (age, gender, country, class, ideology, and personality), we simulate structured debates between AI agents over 131 relationship-based cases. Our results show that personas affect initial moral stances and debate outcomes, with political ideology and personality traits exerting the strongest influence. Persuasive success varies across traits, with liberal and open personalities reaching higher consensus and win rates. While logit-based confidence grows during debates, emotional and credibility-based appeals diminish, indicating more tempered argumentation over time. These trends mirror findings from psychology and cultural studies, reinforcing the need for persona-aware evaluation frameworks for AI moral reasoning.
