C1.justification: The abstract narrows the claim that liberal and open personas attain higher consensus and win rates to higher consensus alone. The central contributions concerning multidimensional personas, moral judgments, and persuasion dynamics remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 substantially qualifies the interpretation: Qwen contradicts generalized author-blaming, gender trends differ across models, and the previous middle-class advantage becomes no clear social-class trend. It distinguishes consensus from self-alignment, discusses perspective and positional sensitivity, and adds reasons why rewriting dilemmas from another character's viewpoint could introduce bias.

D1.justification: v2 supplies code and dataset links and reports availability where v1 described a planned dataset release. It newly documents inclusion of full debate history and updates reported API expenditure from $500 to $1000. The original sampling instructions and prompt templates are largely retained.

E1.justification: Both versions retain the 131 SCRUPLES relationship dilemmas, persona categories, and English-language setting. v2 adds first-person narrator and opponent scenarios alongside impartial third-person judgment, extending the roles agents are asked to adopt without adding a dataset.

E2.justification: The corresponding experiments retain no-persona judgments as their baseline. v2 applies the same persona-versus-no-persona comparison to additional model configurations without introducing a different comparison strategy.

E3.justification: Section 3.4 replaces win rate over debates with self-alignment rate conditioned on consensus debates, changing the reported denominator. Evaluation expands from two to four models. New protocols include a 100-persona perspective experiment, reversed action order, and reversed speaking order; these do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Sections 5.1-5.2 and Appendix P add substantive tests of perspective dependence, action-order sensitivity, and speaking-order effects. These expose different vulnerabilities: LLaMA's judgment changes from 2.71 to 3.05 under action reversal, while the speaking-order tests detect no significant confidence or consensus differences.

E5.justification: v2 adds two-sided speaking-order t-tests in Table 20 and explicit significance reporting for persuasion outcomes. Existing ANOVA, Tukey HSD, temporal-change tests, and Figure 7's mean-and-standard-deviation reporting are retained. No increase in repeated runs or seeds is stated.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive Claude and Qwen results, perspective and ordering outcomes, and previously undisplayed efficiency results. Table 1 reports GPT-4o means of 3.30 as narrator versus 1.82 as opponent; Figure 15 shows Qwen mostly above neutral. Self-alignment values replace win-rate values under a changed definition, while original moral-judgment scores and temporal-change tables are retained.

M1.justification: The six-dimensional persona construction, initial moral judgments, disagreement-based pairing, and alternating debate procedure remain unchanged. Appendix D newly states that full debate history is included, but does not establish a procedural change.

P1.justification: v2 selectively rewrites persuasion findings, expands explanations and discussion, adds Section 5.3, and reorganizes model-specific appendices. The overall research-question structure and most methodological, concluding, and limitations prose remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds perspective and speaking-order tables, full Claude and Qwen figure sets, and an expanded GPT-4o persuasion display. Persuasion plots incorporate self-alignment, efficiency, and significance annotations. Figure 7 replaces numerical category indices with meaningful persona labels, and appendix figures are reorganized.

R1.justification: Related work adds persona-induced bias research and concurrent studies of evolving moral dilemmas, including Liu, Kamruzzaman, Wu, and Backmann. Philosophical references support the expanded blameworthiness explanation, while some gender and cultural references disappear with removed interpretations. The central novelty positioning remains unchanged.

T1.justification: The quantitative definition in Section 3.4 changes its denominator from all debates to consensus debates when replacing win rate with self-alignment rate. This is a limited mathematical-definition revision; no new theorem, proof, or derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: The added perspective and ordering controls address previously untested confounds, while Qwen's contrasting results substantially improve assessment of generalizability. Clearer persuasion measurement and explicit code/data access also strengthen interpretability and reproducibility. These gains outweigh localized reporting errors, notably Figure 15's incorrect claim that Qwen means are below 3 and the retained limitation paragraph describing only two models.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with matching research questions, persona framework, and retained experiments. Their main text, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison despite additions and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Qwen3-235B-A22B, and perspective and ordering experiments.

before.justification: v1 reports original GPT-4o and LLaMA-4-Maverick simulations, including moral judgments, debate outcomes, and rhetorical analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: Item (question) difficulties play a crucial role in educational assessments, enabling accurate and efficient assessment of student abilities and personalization to maximize learning outcomes. Traditionally, estimating item difficulties can be costly, requiring real students to respond to items, followed by fitting an item response theory (IRT) model to get difficulty estimates. This approach cannot be applied to the cold-start setting for previously unseen items either. In this work, we present SMART (Simulated Students Aligned with IRT), a novel method for aligning simulated students with instructed ability, which can then be used in simulations to predict the difficulty of open-ended items. We achieve this alignment using direct preference optimization (DPO), where we form preference pairs based on how likely responses are under a ground-truth IRT model. We perform a simulation by generating thousands of responses, evaluating them with a large language model (LLM)-based scoring model, and fit the resulting data to an IRT model to obtain item difficulty estimates. Through extensive experiments on two real-world student response datasets, we show that SMART outperforms other item difficulty prediction methods by leveraging its improved ability alignment.

C1.justification: The central claims remain that IRT-based DPO aligns simulated students with instructed ability and supports difficulty prediction for unseen open-ended items with few training items. The abstract and introduction update the supporting evidence from one dataset to two without redefining that core contribution.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies SMART's advantage over 3B SFT, makes the realism-versus-alignment tradeoff dataset-dependent, and suggests smaller coding models better resemble novices. It adds interpretations of coding cases and the scaling reversal, plus limitations concerning changing abilities across semesters and unreliable evaluation with small item sets.

D1.justification: v2 adds CodeWorkout processing instructions, learning rates, training schedules, A40 hardware information, dataset-access references, and reference-solution prompt templates. Appendix A.4 newly states that GPCM discrimination parameters are fixed to 1; this is newly documented, not established as a change to the earlier implementation. Code release remains conditional.

E1.justification: The original reading dataset, now named Smarter Balanced, is retained. v2 adds CodeWorkout: 50 Java problems with 10,834 first-attempt responses from 246 college students. This substantially expands the evaluated domain, student population, response format, and scoring requirements.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparator set is retained: Diff SFT, random forest, nearest-neighbor mean, two ICL methods, zero-shot response generation, and response-generation SFT. SBERT RF, SBERT kNN Mean, and Response Gen Zero-shot are renamed, not replaced. The same methods are extended to CodeWorkout.

E3.justification: The added coding experiments use first attempts, two generated reference solutions per item, dataset-specific retrieval settings, longer SFT schedules, and 200-epoch ground-truth IRT fitting. Appendix C introduces response-subsampling experiments with a fixed full-data scoring model. The original five-fold reading evaluation is retained.

E4.justification: New Appendix C tests training-response availability at 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%, isolating its effect on SFT and SMART. New Table 5 compares human, SFT, and SMART coding responses, scores, and ability-quartile patterns. The earlier reading examples and failure analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages across five cross-validation folds without seed counts, repeated-seed estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new scaling figure also lacks uncertainty estimates. Added discussion of variability does not change statistical reporting practices.

E6.justification: All original quantitative table values are retained in v2 Tables 1–2. Substantial new CodeWorkout results show mixed rankings: 3B SMART has PCC 0.3929 versus SFT's 0.4256, but SCC 0.4230 versus 0.3648. Scaling results, coding-case scores, and coding scoring-model/IRT accuracy are also added.

M1.justification: v2 extends the ordinal-score pipeline with a continuous-score IRT likelihood for preference construction and fitting, plus continuous response scoring from binary token logits trained with binary cross-entropy. Rubrics become optional, and coding inputs include reference solutions. These change operative components while retaining the three-stage SMART architecture.

P1.justification: v2 converts numbered contributions into prose, shortens baseline and metric names, revises results discussion, reorganizes IRT-fitting explanations, and adds acknowledgments. The overall section sequence and much of the existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: The combined results table becomes two separate tables organized by dataset and evaluation purpose. v2 adds the scaling plot and a multipage coding-example table, and expands prompt tables with dataset-specific blocks. Existing pipeline diagrams and reading examples are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting CodeWorkout, programming student modeling, continuous Bernoulli modeling, continuous scoring, and richer student personas. Section 7's substantive positioning remains largely unchanged. Publication and bibliographic updates to existing references do not constitute new related work.

T1.justification: v2 adds a mathematical formulation for continuous scores in Equation 3 and a continuous scoring rule in Equation 5. These are limited formal extensions, without new theorems or proofs. The existing GPCM step-parameter constraints move from Section 2 to Appendix A.4 rather than being removed.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's reliance on a single private reading dataset by adding public programming-data validation with different students and scoring requirements. The controlled scaling study, coding case analysis, and expanded implementation details strengthen the evidence and reproducibility. The benefit is broader, more informative validation: SMART does not uniformly beat 3B SFT, and statistical uncertainty remains unquantified, but v2 acknowledges important limits more clearly.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SMART by the same authors. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material and renamed baselines.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original CodeWorkout results, a training-data scaling experiment, and a scored programming case study.

before.justification: v1 reports original five-fold experiments on 49 reading-comprehension items, including difficulty prediction, student-simulation metrics, ablations, and qualitative analyses.

arxiv_record.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities in document re-ranking, a key component in modern Information Retrieval (IR) systems. However, existing LLM-based approaches face notable limitations, including ranking uncertainty, unstable top-k recovery, and high token cost due to token-intensive prompting. To effectively address these limitations, we propose REALM, an uncertainty-aware re-ranking framework that models LLM-derived relevance as Gaussian distributions and refines them through recursive Bayesian updates. By explicitly capturing uncertainty and minimizing redundant queries, REALM achieves better rankings more efficiently. Experimental results demonstrate that our REALM surpasses state-of-the-art re-rankers while significantly reducing token usage and latency, improving NDCG@10 by 0.7-11.9 and simultaneously reducing the number of LLM inferences by 23.4-84.4%, promoting it as the next-generation re-ranker for modern IR systems.

C1.justification: The three principal contributions and claims of improved ranking quality, stability and efficiency remain unchanged. V2's abstract adds numerical improvement ranges already reported in v1 Section 4.2; the introduction's contribution statements and conclusion retain their scientific scope.

C2.justification: V2 replaces a generic future-work sentence with a specific limitation concerning untested skew-normal relevance distributions and their potential costs. It also interprets the lambda sweep as a quality-cost tradeoff, iteration counts as supporting potential parallelization, and RankGPT failures as consequences of model context limitations.

D1.justification: V2 discloses the initial pivot tie-breaking rule, adds a source-code repository link in Appendix B.4 and reports iPapers integration in a title footnote. Existing hardware, baseline hyperparameters and substantive prompt instructions are retained. The PDFs establish these added disclosures, not independent verification of the linked resources.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates TREC DL 2019 and 2020. V2 adds Covid, SciFact, DBpedia and NFCorpus from BEIR, substantially extending coverage beyond general web search to biomedical, scientific fact-verification, entity-centric and consumer-health retrieval domains.

E2.justification: RankGPT, previously discussed but not evaluated, is added in Appendix C.1/Table 5 for both TREC datasets and three Flan-T5 sizes. The original four LLM baselines and BM25 remain; the BEIR experiments reuse that original comparator set.

E3.justification: V2 introduces a controlled lambda sweep over 0, 1/3, 2/3 and 1 on TREC DL 2020 and adds mean refinement iterations as an efficiency measure. Existing TREC query counts, BM25 top-100 candidates, top-10 evaluation, model configurations and default lambda = 2/3 remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Figure 3 adds sensitivity analysis of the partition-mixing parameter, and Appendix C.3/Table 7 examines recursive iteration requirements. These focused additions supplement the retained component ablations, initial-order robustness test and pairwise model-capability analysis.

E5.justification: Appendix B.1 in both versions reports dataset-averaged scores from a single run. V2 adds no seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or repeated-run uncertainty estimates. Its new iteration counts describe inference rounds, not experimental replications.

E6.justification: V1 Tables 1-4 retain their numerical contents as v2 Tables 1, 3, 4 and 6. Substantial new results include REALM's BEIR NDCG@10 scores of 78.4, 69.3, 45.9 and 36.4 with Flan-T5-Large, RankGPT scores, lambda sensitivity and an overall mean of 4.89 iterations. These extend the evidence rather than improve previously reported TREC scores.

M1.justification: Gaussian relevance modeling, probabilistic TrueSkill updates, recursive pruning and pivot optimizations are retained. Section 3.3 newly specifies a median-score initial pivot when uncertainties tie, filling an implementation gap without establishing a change to the previously implemented procedure.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized introduction and language edits, adds quantitative detail to the abstract, revises the author/contact block and adds acknowledgments and several experimental or appendix subsections. The main section sequence and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V2 substantially expands visual reporting with the multi-domain BEIR table, a two-panel lambda-sensitivity figure, and RankGPT and iteration tables. Existing tables are relocated and renumbered, while Figures 1-2 retain their content. The principal change is added visual evidence rather than numerical edits to existing displays.

R1.justification: V2 adds the BEIR citation to Thakur et al. and removes Fukuda and Tomiura's academic-search citation and accompanying discussion. The related-work taxonomy and REALM's positioning remain largely unchanged. MS MARCO attribution and publication-metadata updates refer to retained works.

T1.justification: The preference-probability formula, natural-parameter updates, pivot aggregation, partition formula and complexity statements are unchanged. Appendix A retains the same Bayesian-rating exposition and update equations; no proof or mathematical correction is added.

improvement.justification: V1's benchmark evidence was confined to two TREC collections built on MS MARCO. V2's four BEIR datasets substantially strengthen evidence for applicability across retrieval domains. The sensitivity study better supports the existing default, while the pivot clarification and code link improve reproducibility documentation. BEIR testing remains limited to Flan-T5-Large and results remain single-run, but the additions address a substantial gap in empirical generality.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same REALM framework. Their complete main texts and appendices A-C are readable, and equations, figures and tables can be matched reliably across versions.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds BEIR evaluations, RankGPT comparisons, a hyperparameter sweep and inference-iteration measurements.

before.justification: V1 reports original TREC evaluations, component ablations, initial-order sensitivity experiments and pairwise model-capability results.
